item.title: Hacking The Contra Pocket Player - Hack a Day
item.description:
The My Arcade Contra Pocket Player is a fun little handheld that lets you play the arcade versions of Contra and Super Contra… and nothing else. However, [Rob Simon] put in the work to get the device loading custom games as well.

The work started with the usual—identifying the system-on-chip and supporting hardware, dumping the flash, and just generally mapping out how the device was laced together. From there, [Rob] dived into firmware analysis to figure out how the filesystem was laid out and how it could be re-flashed. It turned out the handheld was basically just feeding ROMs into RetroArch, so it wasn’t too hard to get it playing different games. Though there are certain limitations based on what support was compiled in. Basically, it can play games compatible with the FBAlpha libretro emulation core. Files are on GitHub for those eager to mod their own units.

We love seeing hardware like this hacked to play custom games. We saw similar action with the NES Classic almost a decade ago.

item.title: Crashing Microcontrollers Competitively - Hack a Day
item.description:
[Ani] has produced rather an interesting game. Kacken Open Air (KOA) is a browser-based game, wherein players compete for access to a limited resource—namely, festival toilets. So far, so amusing, but there’s a neat technical twist. You’re actually competing to crash microcontrollers in the real world (German, Google Translate link).

The way the game works is simple enough. There are more players than there are toilets, so players have to fight over them. This is achieved by knocking on the toilet doors in the game. However, paired to each toilet in the game is a real ESP8266 microcontroller. Each knock from a player adds computational load to the microcontroller. Knock enough, and the microcontroller will slow enough, and the player occupying the toilet will be kicked out. Keep knocking, and eventually the microcontroller will run out of memory, crash, and reboot. In game, this causes the toilet to collapse. The whole setup runs on a cluster of microcontrollers, with an ESP32-P4, a bunch of ESP8266s, a few Raspberry Pi Pico 2s, Arduino Dues, and an STM8 working as a hardware watchdog to make sure everything stays alive when it should.

If you want to sample the game, try it out in your browser here. (German, Google Translate link). It’s a really fun concept to combine hardware performance with actual gameplay outcomes. It’s so totally different from other projects we’ve seen that involve gaming on ESP microcontrollers. If you’ve done something similar, or something totally zany and different, bell us on the tipsline either way!

item.title: DabbleCAD Takes Design Offline - Hack a Day
item.description:
These days, there are all kind of online-only and in-browser CAD packages. DabbleCAD is the opposite of all that—a simple, offline, open-source design solution.

DabbleCAD handles 3D design in a similar way to TinkerCAD. It’s shape based modelling, with all the usual tools for stretching, deforming, punching holes, and the like. It’s set up to export your geometry to STL or 3MF so you can throw it straight into a slicer for 3D printing.

However, it’s also a package that can handle design for laser cutters, too. There are simple tools for importing artwork or drawing it from scratch, and it will export the relevant G-code or directly send to a GRBL-compatible laser cutter hooked up over USB. As a nice bonus, there’s also an engraving feature. 3D models or images can be turned into height maps for relief engraving if you’ve got the tools for it.

DabbleCAD doesn’t do anything groundbreaking or new that existing software can’t handle. It’s just a convenient, portable piece of software in an era when so much of what we use is tied to logins and clouds and endless headaches around connectivity. If you’re whipping up your own tools to suit your chosen working ethos, don’t hesitate to let us know on the tipsline.

item.title: Preventing a Garage Door Opener From Rebooting When Offline - Hack a Day
item.description:
It’s always great when a smart garage door opener allows for easy local integration into a smart home network, but it’s not so nice when said device still insists on connecting to certain remote servers, and even reboots constantly due to time-outs. This was the problem that [Kusha] was facing with a LiftMaster MyQ Home Bridge garage door control. The solution ended up being to dump the key for the encrypted MQTT communication and setting up a dummy server.

The encryption key is stored on the Cortex-M4 MCU, with fortunately the debug interface with the SWD pins and everything else left in plain view on the PCB. From there it only takes a bit of creative wiring and a bit of Arduino code to read out the needed data.

After this you still need to set up an MQTT broker with this key installed and capable of serving pings to the device after it connects. For this part [Kusha] provides a Docker configuration to streamline this process if you are into containers. Setting up an existing Mosquito or similar MQTT broker for secure MQTT access isn’t overly complicated otherwise.

Of course the device will still try to connect to the mqdevice.com domains where the manufacturer’s MQTT brokers are running, but with a local DNS server you can gently coax these to be redirected to your own MQTT broker instead. After this the device will be convinced that it’s now Cloud-Enabled and stop trying to reboot all the time to fix the egregious problem of not having internet access after being put on an IoT VLAN or similar.

item.title: A Big Ol’ LED Matrix Cube - Hack a Day
item.description:
You could have a featureless cube in your house, but that would be boring, and we wouldn’t write a Hackaday article about it. Alternatively, you could whip up a cube that is positively covered in LEDs that play all sorts of animations, like [Ross Harvey] did.

The cube that [Ross] built has six faces covered in HUB75 LED panels, each consisting of 64 x 64 LEDs in a 2.5 mm pitch measuring 160 mm square. That’s a total of 24,576 individually addressable LEDs, if you’re counting along at home. Each face has a cell-cast acrylic diffuser sheet, which gives the LEDs a much smoother, more pleasant appearance when lit. Inside the cube lives a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 paired with a custom HUB75 driver board, as well as a power/boost board that draws from a 2-cell lithium-ion pack. There are also two speakers and a microphone hooked up, which provides for both audio feedback and audio reactivity. The cube can display all kinds of things, from various games to music visualizers and even a rather tasteful world clock setup.

You can build the cube yourself if you really want six sides of glowing glory on your desk. However, if you’re strapped for time, [Ross] later developed an off-the-shelf version for all your cubey needs. If you prefer more complicated solids, it’s hard to go past [Greg Davill’s] classic glowing D20 build. Video after the break.

item.title: Digital Badge Gets Reverse Engineered - Hack a Day
item.description:
The JieLi AC707N is a cheap $10 digital badge that actually packs in a fair bit of interesting hardware. [Sabas] reverse-engineered the product and figured out how to flash custom firmware onto sealed OEM-fresh units.

The AC707N badge, of the BR35 family, comes well equipped out of the box. It has a 360×360 pixel round display, driven over QSPI. It comes equipped with a AXS5106L capacitive touch controller for interacting with the screen. There are also two buttons, 4MB of flash, and Bluetooth Low Energy capability on board. Plenty to play with, right there!

[Sabas] gave a talk about how the device was first physically torn down, before the APK was decompiled in Ghidra. From there, it was possible to download the firmware without authentication and then develop an open SDK for working with the cheap device. There’s a custom firmware available on Github that was developed a a result of these efforts, and it can do all kinds of neat things. You can use it as a Bluetooth Mouse, or a Bluetooth scanner, for example. Or, if so desired, you could build on this work and develop your own firmware for the device to suit your own use cases.

We see stuff like this repurposed all the time. The GeekMagic SmallTV is a great example of a cheap device given greater functionality through custom firmware. Video after the break.

item.title: How Apple’s HomeView Actively Resists Repairs - Hack a Day
item.description:
Over the past years there have been hopeful noises about Apple devices becoming easier to service and repair, but as [iFixit] found with their teardown of the new HomeView devices, such optimism may be premature. In this teardown they found that extremely strong adhesive is used for the display, as well as to keep the speakers in place.

Even worse is that the mainboard’s back metal can is effectively glued in place with thermal compound, and the speaker connectors on the mainboard pretty much disintegrate if you try to unplug them, even after trying to scrape off the glue on them.

All of this leads to a pretty miserable teardown experience, with the display removal probably being the easiest part. Even plentiful IPA application and careful prying cannot save one of the big speaker modules, with both their connectors mauled as well.

The rear metal can of the mainboard is left in place, probably requiring liberal dousing in IPA or stronger solvents to loosen up first, as well as borderline inaccessible screws, and the subwoofer in the base is basically impossible to plug back into place after disassembly. Looking at the wall-mounted version of the HomeView, things do not get much better, but it omits the subwoofer and screw issues of the base version.

Overall this seems like the kind of device that’s somewhat repairable if you go in armed with all this knowledge that [iFixit] sacrificed a HomeView for, but it’s disappointing to see such a repair nightmare in 2026. Interestingly, this device is not available in the EU, purportedly due to the privacy nightmare that is the Siri AI feature, but it may run afoul of some right-to-repair regulations too, or at the very least get assigned a very low score.

item.title: Mesh2Cad Automates Re-Modelling - Hack a Day
item.description:
It’s happened to all of us, we find an STL that would just about solve our problems, but the mesh isn’t quite right. Sometimes mesh-editing is good enough, other times you need to rebuild the mesh in a proper CAD environment to get what you need. In that latter case, [Emir Mrkaljevic]’s Mesh2Cad program could save you a whole lot of work, because it does exactly what it says on the tin: turns a mesh to a CAD file.

Even better, [Emir] doesn’t pick the CAD format for you. Sure, it does STEP, but you can also go straight to FreeCAD, CadQuerry or OpenSCAD with these handy scripts. Well, technically the FreeCAD version generates a macro to make the object rather than a .FCSTD, but that’s still pretty handy. Scripts is the right word for mesh2cad, because the whole thing is python and just a pip install mesh2cad away from living on your machine. Of course you don’t need to use pip since the whole thing is on GitHub and available for your eyeballs to audit. Speaking of audit, the scripts apparently check their own work and only give you CAD if they can approximate the mesh within tolerance.

Now there are limits here, if you think it sounds too good to be true. You’re limited to things that can be made of the sort of primitive manipulation OpenSCAD usually deals in — no organic shapes, free-flowing curves, or the like. If it’s a box or a bracket with holes, fillets and chamfers, though, this tool might save you a couple minutes recreating it.

If you prefer to do it yourself or have one of those annoyingly-organic meshes this tool won’t touch, we have a guide for what to do when an STL needs some tweaking.

item.title: Sega Dreamcast Plays Nintendo 64 Cartridges - Hack a Day
item.description:
In many ways, the Sega Dreamcast was the most forward-thinking console ever produced. It included a built-in Internet connection in a time when the Internet was just becoming widely accessible, VGA output when most people connected their consoles to their televisions with composite video or RF adapters, and even supported a custom version of Windows. Its advanced features were partially a cause of its commercial failure, though, although the system is still beloved by a niche community today. Partially because it is a great platform for modding in bizarre and novels ways like this build which adds Nintendo 64 cartridge compatibility.

The controllers were unique and fairly advanced as well. They used a proprietary serial interface called Maple which is a protocol that could handle data transmission at a rate of around 2 megabits per second, which is not too shabby for technology from the late 90s, let alone for the controller on a gaming console. Using that capability to read data from a Nintendo 64 cartridge ought to be fairly straightforward then. To get the peripheral up and running, [Throaty Mumbo] took a cartridge port from a N64 and wired it to an adapter which lets the Dreamcast read the data on the cartridge through the controller port. There’s an N64 emulator available for Dreamcast, although the system is not quite fast enough for this to make games playable. The way around this was to use assets and save data from the cartridge but run games that were recompiled for the Dreamcast instead.

[Throaty Mumbo] finishes out the build with a custom PCB and case which turns it into a usable cartridge reader that easily slots into a controller port. Then, using the same premise, he built cartridge readers for other systems’ games like the SNES and Genesis, making the Dreamcast somewhat backwards-compatible. Although the Dreamcast was technically advanced it didn’t have a DVD capability, but [Throaty Mumbo] covered that in a previous build using a similar controller-based peripheral approach.

item.title: How Hough Transforms Enable Computers to See - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although identifying what we can see with our eyes feels like the most natural thing in the world, the responsible cognitive processes running on our brain’s wetware are quite a marvel. Even when pushed beyond their evolutionary design by e.g. driving a car at high speeds does our vision system mostly manage to keep up. Emulating these cognitive processes with artificial cognition (AC) systems like computer vision required the development of feature extraction algorithms, such as the Hough Transform that’s the topic of this video by [The Synthetic Mind].

The Hough Transform was developed originally by [Paul Hough] in the 1960s for machine analysis of patterns in bubble chamber photographs. From there the basic algorithm has evolved beyond merely detecting the straight lines of particles zipping through said bubble chambers.

Key however remains determining the points in a scene which potentially make up the lines, which requires edge detection. Yet unlike in basic examples, real-life use of these algorithms is made hard by how complex a real-life scene is. Naively checking all possible lines as in the original algorithm would take far too long, which led to the development of optimizations that take considerably less time and deal better with pixel noise.

Of course, after finding all potential lines and borders of objects in a scene the next step for a computer vision is to identify what has been spotted, what it means for the current task and determine an appropriate action. Here getting additional scene information other sensors like radar or Lidar can be incredibly helpful, especially when you’re the system in control of something like a car.

Examples like these definitely promote an appreciation of how hard it is to create AC algorithms that can emulate what we animals can seem to do almost effortlessly. Even before considering the intelligence subset of cognition, one cannot help but marvel at the sheer effort it takes for us humans to not constantly bump into things.

item.title: Tracking Down a Mystery Beep By Giving a Coding Agent a Few Ears - Hack a Day
item.description:
[Simon Willison] recently used a coding agent in an unusual way. A software system temporarily used the microphones on devices scattered around the room to triangulate the source of a mysterious, intermittent beep coming from within one of the many boxes in the room.

The main part of the system is a Python web server, and the listeners can be any old devices one might have hanging around. Scan a QR code, and the device becomes a listening post by leveraging the Web Audio API. With listeners spread around the room, the system has everything it needs to patiently wait, listen, and zero in on the mystery beep. The culprit? An old carbon monoxide detector, buried in a box and emitting a low battery chirp.

That’s neat, but what this project really demonstrates is the benefit of hacking together a way for a coding agent to actually sense the real world, the better for it to design a solution to a physical problem.

The ad-hoc framework of web-based listeners allowed [Simon] to give the agent the ability to gather audio data on its own to refine and recalibrate its approach during development, without any need for him to record audio and pass it on manually.

It’s a bit reminiscent of this WiFi analyzer connected to an AI model, a project that hints at the possibilities of a physical tool that can be steered by an agent. Check out the GitHub repository for beep-locator if you’d like a closer look at the code itself.

item.title: The Mega Tamagotchi Manga Reader - Hack a Day
item.description:
You could read manga in the classic bound paper format. But then you’d have to carry around lots of volumes that take up lots of space. The way around this is to use an e-reader, that stores lots of manga in digital form. [Arnov Sharma] built his own themed after the classic Tamagotchi.

What you’re looking at is a big ol’ 3D printed mega-Tamagotchi. It apes the design of the original digital pet, but is scaled up to a size large enough to host a large screen. In particular, the Waveshare ESP32-P4 Touch LCD 4.3 development board, which pairs the 480 x 800 screen with the capable wireless-enabled microcontroller and even a little speaker. Two, as it happens, because there’s an ESP32-P4 and an ESP32-C6 on the board. Power is via a pair of 2000 mAh lithium-ion cells. Manga is loaded on to the device via an SD card, in JPEG format. [Arnov] uses the ESP32-P4’s hardware JPEG decoder to make flipping pages quicker than the 2-5 seconds it would take to do the same decode in software. There are also some fun tricks in the firmware that improve contrast in black-and-white scans and vibrancy in color scans, too.

If you want to read manga on the go in a device with a fun form factor, consider building something similar yourself. To populate your reader, consider a past project we examined that turns movies into comic books. Video after the break.

item.title: Handheld Motor Cancels Out Every Twist and Turn - Hack a Day
item.description:
It’s one thing to know that input from a motion sensor can steer a motor. It’s another to see and feel the two cancelling out the other in real-time, right in the palm of one’s hand. That’s [cpietsch]’s takeaway from the CAN do GYRO, a brushless motor with a CAN interface and tiny STM32-based development board perched atop it.

It’s essentially a one-axis gimbal with a few thoughtful features. The unit tracks itself fully in three dimensions, so while the motor is limited to one axis, the unit doesn’t get confused by complex movements. It also auto-calibrates, and auto-stops within half a rotation if it detects the motor spinning freely.

The hardware consists of a tiny XIAO STM32C5 microcontroller board with integrated IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) and CAN transceiver, and an M5Stack RollerCAN motor. The motor, handily, has a small OLED screen built into it.

Combined with a battery it’s small enough to be handheld while it shows off what a tight control loop paired with a suitable motor can do. Watch it in action in the video, embedded below.

Of course, accurate gimbals using brushless motors have been around for many years. But one thing that’s plain is just how much the kind of hardware available to individuals has changed. Compare this build to a DIY gimbal project from about ten years ago and you’ll see the function looks about the same, but today’s hardware has evolved considerably.

item.title: Local Prusa Connect Cuts Out the Cloud - Hack a Day
item.description:
One of the ways 3D printing has changed over the last few years has come in the form of cloud services that exist alongside your printer. In some cases they are locked-in to using the thing, while in others such as Prusa Connect, they are an adjunct that provides useful services but doesn’t restrict the printer to using it.

Now Prusa have gone a step further in keeping control closer to the owner of the printer, by releasing a local version. You can run it on your own server, giving all the benefits with none of the ties.

All the code can be found in a GitHub repository, under their Open Community Licence, which makes everything available but puts some restrictions on who can use it, for example requiring that large enterprises have a paid version. As well as in code form it’s supplied pre-built for Apple, Windows, and Linux platforms, on different architectures including the Raspberry Pi. Out of the box it supports Prusa printers, but it’s not restricted to them as there is a driver API should you wish to add a non-Prusa model.

We know there’s a reaction to the heavier reliance on the cloud found in for example Bambu Labs printers, and we know that some users may have commercially sensitive parts they may not wish to pass off their own network. So we see this as a clever move from Prusa, offering a more palatable way towards a networked printer service without relying on the vendor.

Thanks [Renze] for the tip.

item.title: Not-So-Large Language Model Fits On a Floppy Disk - Hack a Day
item.description:
At some point when hackers start pushing edge cases, nomenclature gets weird, like Large Language Models, or LLMs. At some point, the word “large” obviously becomes impossible to justify, but we’re not going to call [WollyMonjac]’s Tiny2.1 DOS PC Chatbot just a ‘language model’ — perhaps “transformer” is the better term. That’s what LLMs and not-so-L-LMs like this one are under the hood, after all.

In any case, this one was written in Turbo C 2.0 by the no-debate ‘large’ LLM Fable 5.2 and trained by Opus 5.5. So for those of you who’ve got this one on their apocalypse bingo card: yes, machines are making machines. This second-gen transformer targets a 486DX or Pentium processor and runs on DOS, and you can get it onto the machine on a single period-appropriate floppy disk.

The actual network is 380 KB of 8-bit weights, while the rest of the floppy would hold the handy interface. As you might imagine, it needs 540 KB of free memory to run in. The transformer holds 3,500 facts in its 367K-parameter but outside of that it makes stuff up with the reckless abandon that these models can’t escape, regardless of size. 

The project is of course more of a conversation-starter than anything else, though if you want to train it on your own 3,500 facts the scripts for that are on GitHub under an MIT license. We’ve seen an LLM on a 486 before, but being able to easily curate exactly what the model knows raises some interesting possibilities.

item.title: Linux in a Browser Tab - Hack a Day
item.description:
Linux was once distributed on CDs and DVDs stuck to the front of computer magazines. Now, technology has advanced to the point where you can simply run a Linux kernel right in your browser. That’s precisely what you get with Unkernel from [pithings].

Unkernel is described as “Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with an MMU.” Yes, thanks to the magic of WebAssembly, you can run Linux in a browser tab at a decent fraction of native speed. All the proper kernel stuff—like syscalls, the scheduler, memory management, file systems, and networking—is compiled code. User programs are then emulated with a just-in-time compiler, so you can run Ubuntu and Alpine packages without any fuss. You get a shell, package manager, persistent storage, sound, and internet access out of the box. It’s basically a whole Linux computer sitting in a single browser tab for your convenience.

It’s generally not as fast as running the kernel natively, but where you need a little Linux on the go, it should come in clutch. We’ve discussed Linux showing up in weird places quite recently on the Hackaday Podcast, too. If you’re sticking kernels where they’re not expected, be sure to let us know on the tipsline.

item.title: Coding on Windows? Redmond May Already Know. - Hack a Day
item.description:
File this one under “shocked, but not that shocked”– hacker [Xusheng Li] did some digging on a recent Windows 11 build and found that it seems to be phoning home with details about not only what AI agents you might be using on your system, but what dev tools are in use too. The full writeup is worth reading before rushing to judgement on this, but no doubt Microsoft has your best interests at heart– they always do, right?

The saga starts with a library called MissionControlAggregator.dll, which contains a list of executable files to look for– things like codex.exe on the agent front, but also dev tools as common as python.exe or gcc.exe–which would be innocent enough, and perhaps even helpful if the OS was watching for these files to do something locally. It might be doing something locally, but [Xusheng] was able to trace the diagnostic that triggers when you launch one of the apps it is listening for, and yes, at least on a default Windows 11 install, it phones home about it. Alas, WSL won’t save you this time, as the same event is apparently generated when you launch the linux version in said subsystem.

Of course the default Windows 11 install does have “optional diagnostics” enabled by default, so you could argue that this is something that the system administrator consented to– provided they knew about it, which they likely don’t. We certainly had no idea that this was part of those “optional diagnostics” and are thankful to [Xusheng] for the tip.

Our own [Jenny List] took Windows 11 for a drive back in June, and emerged rather unimpressed. Your mileage may vary, but if you are, like the majority of the world’s desktop users, on Windows, you might want to double-check those privacy settings.

item.title: A Pen Plotter to Draw You Up (on) the Wall - Hack a Day
item.description:
Back in our day you were told not to draw on the walls; nowadays we have robots for that– like Mural 2.0 by [Nik Ivanov]. If the name doesn’t give it away, this is a large format pen plotter made to draw, well, murals. It’s also not [Nik]’s first rodeo, though this version seems considerably improved from the orignial version.

He’s now using a FluidNC board based on an ESP32 and TMC2209 stepper drivers, while the steppers they drive are a pair of NEMA 17 pancake units. Using pancakes for this application makes sense, as the steppers are on the machine and must pull themselves up against gravity using the single belt that is anchored at ceiling level. The kinematics of that mean you don’t get the full area between the anchor points– you lose 20% at the edges– but you can still get a pretty big mural going. In the demo/build video embedded below, it looks like you’re more limited by marker life, [Nik] cautioning that past about 500 m of line things can start to get a bit weak as the pen dries out. He’s working on a ‘pause and replace pen’ routine for the next firmware version to help with that project.

For now, the WiFi-based interface [Nik] has on the ESP32 gives you that path length in advance, and can even process both SVG and raster images with both a sine-wave style squiggle and finite-curve style space filling. This isn’t the fastest pen plotter we’ve seen on these pages, and it might not quite be the simplest, either, but [Nik] has put together a very easy build that you could do with your nieces and nephews content in the knowledge that the easy-to-use firmware will let them keep making murals when you aren’t there– assuming, that is, that their mother lets them draw on the walls.

item.title: Custom Firmware for Fortinet FortiGate 60 Firewall/Router - Hack a Day
item.description:
When [Matt Williams] found an old enterprise firewall in the trash, he knew he had to do something with it. After cracking it open, he found that this 2000s-era Fortinet FortiGate 60 hardware firewall has some very hackable hardware in the form of a VIA C3 mainboard. This is an x86-compatible CPU that was very popular in small form-factor and industrial solutions around 2000s, meaning that it should be able to run just about anything that’s happy to run on its 400 MHz single core.

Unfortunately it wasn’t a standard Mini-ITX C3 board like the one that [Matt] also has kicking around, as that one features standard DIMMs for the memory modules. For this firewall the 128 MB of SDRAM was soldered to the board, with the only clue as to how to initialize it in the original firmware. Ergo this firmware had to be reverse-engineered to figure out just how this was supposed to happen.

With that done, Linux 2.4 was happy enough to boot on it with a bit more tweaking. Using the framebuffer driver applications like DOOM happily ran, as the above graphic shows. That it’s very much green is due to only the green pin on the VGA connector being probed. Since it’s a firewall Fortinet only added a physical DE-9 port in addition to the internal IDE interface and CF card slot.

If one were to wire up these pads on the mainboard to physical connectors, it would actually make for a pretty decent little system for what the kids call retro gaming these days.

item.title: Testing TISMO Whisker-Reinforced Poticon STD1 PA Filament - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although at first glance potassium-titanite (TISMO) whiskers don’t seem to be much of a change from chopped glass- and carbon fiber in FDM filaments, they’re really quite different. They’re not only much smaller, they’re also less abrasive, and work with 0.2 mm nozzles. Although basically just found in industrial filaments right now, [JanTec Engineering] put a spool to the test to see what these whiskers bring to the party.

While at an event in Japan, [JanTec] got handed a spool of Poticon STD1 NTL34M PA filament, presumably the common PA6, AKA Nylon. In their messaging the company calls it LEXTER, a bio-based polyamide.

This was subsequently put to the test after returning home, with the recommended print settings and the newly constructed testing machine, called the Atlas 2000. This is an open source testing machine that could be handy if you have about $500 lying around and an urgent need to test the tensile, compression and bending properties of materials.

The filament under test is 20% TISMO by weight, with it scoring well in the tensile strength test, while being about as brittle as the datasheet suggests. Such reinforced polymers are generally known for being stiff and brittle, so this is little surprise. Perhaps the biggest advantage of this filament is that you can print finer details with it using an 0.2 mm nozzle, making it an interesting engineering filament in that respect.

Also touched upon in the video are the potential health risks of this filament, with these whiskers being definitely easy to inhale. This also is reminiscent of the potential carcinogenic risks of chopped carbon fiber, where fragments of these already small fibers can pose similar risks as asbestos.

As for the constant brittleness in these purported reinforced filaments, this would seem to be due to poor adhesion between the fiber (or whisker) and the thermoplastic. Unlike with thermoset polymers where there’s an active interface between the fiber and the polymer that creates a strong molecular bond, there’s generally a void between thermosets and additives like fibers due to the lack of any chemical activity while cooling.

item.title: The FM-1: Open Source Hacked Open, Vibe Coding, and Farting Synthesizers - Hack a Day
item.description:
The M-Vave FM-1 was a pretty unremarkable little synthesizer “toy” until the open-source synth hackers took it over. Now, it’s a sweet platform for exploration, the incredible work done by the community has encouraged the manufacturer to release an open SDK, and it has recently taken the global synth nerd community by storm. (It has sadly also gotten about a 50% markup in the last month due to this popularity.)

It’s the perfect storm of inexpensive hardware, vibe-coded software, and easy-to-use tooling that enables synthesizer firmware-hacking for the mainstream. It is also the fashionable box of the moment in a nerdy niche of the synthesizer world at the moment and it’s something that we’re going to see in non-synthesizer contexts as well, so buckle up.

Opening Already Open Software

The funny thing about the FM-1 is that most of the good stuff inside it was open-source all along. As it is sold, it is a Yamaha DX7 emulator, and it appears to be running the same sound engine as Dexed, which is an open-source DX7 clone based on the even older music synthesizer for android (msfa).

Dexed, and its smaller brother MiniDexed, has given birth to many sweet synthesizer hacks that we’ve seen here, including a personal favorite: a Yamaha TX816 clone based on a Raspberry Pi. So it certainly looked to everyone at the time as if M-vave wrapped a not-entirely-inspiring user interface around this sound engine and shipped it.

And that would have been the end of it too, if it weren’t for those meddling kids [AL-255] who did a thorough reverse-engineering of the machine about four months ago, which laid the groundwork for everything else to come. Today, we’re looking at around 250 firmwares for this little beasty, so it’s no exaggeration to say that this opened the floodgates. And along the way, he verified signatures of the msfa code, so everyone’s suspicions proved correct.

The Robots Take Off

A quick note on the LLM / agentic coding elephant in the room here. From reading through [AL-255]’s work, it was most almost certainly worked on and documented by the robots, and we have no idea of the relative contribution of man and machine. Publishing a reverse engineering effort like this enables others in the community to point their robots at the repo, and gives them a tremendous leg up in the next steps along the path. We have just as little clue about how much of any of the subsequent synthesizer and sequencer routines were written with LLM assistance, but at the rate they’re popping up, we’d guess a lot.

About two months after [AL-255]’s work, [Madeline] wrote one of the first reworks of the firmware for the FM-1, working as “Baud Girl”. It added some virtual analog to the cold DX7 tones, but notably wrapped it up in a much nicer UI than the original. It has so far been kept closed-source, but as a proof of what’s possible, it certainly inspired many others.

And then along came [Leo Kuroshita]’s open-source Felucca. This program added a yet fancier sequencer, multiple instruments, drums, and even sound effects. It turned the single-instrument FM-1 into a miniature music-production workshop – what the kids from the 1990’s would call a “groovebox”. [isod89]’s Sloop would refine on Felucca, and is probably the standout application running on the FM-1 platform at the moment.

The Firmware Hub started collecting a list of applications written by the community, and there are 250 of them in about six weeks’ time. Suffice it to say that we can’t even begin to scratch the surface, but they range from serious musical interface explorations, to rainbow-colored kids toys, to fart machines, and then to recreations of iconic synthesizers of the past. Something for everyone? Certainly more interesting than Dexed-in-a-box!

There is no guarantee of quality or of suitability for purpose. On some of them, pitch bend won’t work because the bot or person doing the coding just didn’t get around to it. On others, there will be USB problems. Some have audio glitches, which is a serious issue for a sound-making machine. It’s hard to judge the signal-to-noise ratio of the software output for this device (pun intended); it’s the wild west. And at the rate that applications are piling in, you can only hope to review a snapshot anyway.

If you want a guided tour of some of the best applications as of last week, we love [AudioPilz]’s Tier List, embedded below, that also comes with a heavy dose of synth-nerd inside jokes. [Floyd Steinberg]’s video is full of thoughtful commentary on the state of the art.

Plot Twist: Open Source!

Then the story takes a cool turn. M-vave, the company that makes the FM-1, decided to open-source its firmware and its entire SDK. Well, kinda. The strangest turn of events is that they opened up everything except the sound engine itself, which they release as a binary blob. Why? Nobody knows. Some have speculated that it’s because it is based on the GPL-licensed Dexed and are covering their tracks, which is possible. But if M-vave went further back than that, and based it exclusively on the Apache 2.0-licensed msfa, then they’re in the clear.

Either way, there is now official open-firmware support for this little gadget, and a growing community of folks writing new software for it. Because of this official support, musicians who have never flashed an Arduino are overwriting their stock bootloaders. For their part, M-vave is selling a lot more FM-1s than it would otherwise. It’s a win all around.

Apocalypse? Now? In this Economy?

If you watch a number of video reviews of the FM-1, they range from “Game Changer: The Industry is Doomed!” to “The Only Synth You’ll Ever Need” to “Robot Slop”. We think that’s all a little bit overblown. There have always been awesome open-source projects in the synthesizer space. Mutable Instrument’s [Émilie Gillet] gave us countless amazing open examples, many of which are implemented for the FM-1. Major synth manufacturer Korg flirted around with encouraging users to code their own synthesizers in the Minilogue series. None of the FM-1’s capabilities are new, and not all of it is even musical. As a pure synth, it sounds fine, but it’s nothing to write home about.

But what is interesting about the FM-1 story is the sheer velocity at which things are progressing, the positive manufacturer response to being “hacked”, and the empowerment of a community to write its own oddball sound machines. There is more new firmware coming out for the FM-1 than any one person can hope to keep up with, even though the tooling to do so has never been easier. It’s a microcosm of the creation-overflow that we live in. Will this be seen as the beginning of a new era of custom firmware for commercial devices? Fun times!

item.title: Making an Affordable Two-Axis Solar Tracker - Hack a Day
item.description:
Setting up a photovoltaic panel is simple, but you lose a lot of potential power if you merely bolt said panel into place. With a tracker the panel will instead follow the sun, potentially even adjusting the angle of the panel to optimize how much of the sun’s rays hit it during the day. The two-axis tracker that [Greenhill Forge] built is an example of how to make a tracker using just a steel frame and simple electronics.

As noted in the video, commercial solar trackers tend to use slewing bearings, which support heavy, slow-turning structures like a PV panel array. These are however rather expensive, so instead he opted to use a trailer axle hub as the budget version. The array’s structure including a drive sprocket is built up on top of this axle in such a way that it easily removed for maintenance, mostly using welded steel to create a stable base for the PV panels.

This also contains the second axis, with two bearings to pivot around. The azimuth axis is driven with a large geared electric motor, while the second axis is driven by a linear motor containing a worm gear. This should keep position very well, even in case of power loss or a stiff breeze.

Following this there is the electronics part, which includes a wind sensor in addition to a simple quad photoresistor based light sensor. A couple of limit switches ensure that the system should never move past the point where worrying grinding and shearing noises begin.

With assembly complete, the solar tracker is equipped with a single large panel and compared to a stationary identical panel and charge controller. This shows that the tracker nets one an additional 30-50% of energy in the two scenarios compared over the course of two days of testing. Although you have to subtract the power needed to run the system and the two motors, it does make a convincing argument for maximizing the output of these panels with some fairly basic parts.

item.title: The $50 Per Hour Search Engine - Hack a Day
item.description:
Imagine doing a Google search and getting a bill for $50 an hour — or even $300 an hour. Even worse, that’s $50 for every hour you were even connected. Typing a query, reading output, or even grabbing a soda ran the clock. Want to print something? That might cost extra, too. If you aren’t careful, a simple research project could really add up.

That was the world of DIALOG, one of the earliest commercial online information retrieval services. Long before Google, AltaVista, or even the World Wide Web, DIALOG allowed people to search enormous collections of technical papers, patents, news, and other information from a computer terminal. It wasn’t cheap, and it wasn’t particularly easy to use. But for researchers who needed information, it was revolutionary.

From Rockets to Research

The story starts, surprisingly enough, at Lockheed. In the early 1960s, the aerospace company faced a problem familiar to anyone doing research: how do you find out what someone else has already discovered?

[Roger Summit], who worked at Lockheed, recalled that it was sometimes easier to repeat scientific research than to find out whether someone had already done it. Libraries had card catalogs and elaborate indexing systems, but searching through mountains of technical literature was tedious.

Computers seemed like an obvious answer. But in the 1960s, computers mostly worked in batches. And they didn’t have a global network to draw data from, either. [Summit] and others began experimenting with a better approach. Lockheed established an information sciences laboratory in 1964, and by 1966 the team had a small working prototype of an interactive search system.

The hardware was big for its day but modest by today’s standards. The early system used an IBM System/360 Model 30 with just 32 KB of memory. It could search large collections of references on disk and tape and respond interactively.

NASA became an early customer. Lockheed’s work led to NASA’s RECON (Remote Console Information Retrieval Service) system, which allowed researchers to search documentation produced by the space program.

In 1972, Lockheed introduced DIALOG as a commercial service. The idea was simple: organizations could pay to search large databases without building and maintaining their own information retrieval systems.

Having a DIALOG

Using DIALOG was nothing like using a modern search engine. You needed a terminal, or, eventually, a personal computer with a modem, and a connection to the service.

Connecting to the service could be tricky. In the 1970s and 1980s, that often meant dialing into Telenet (not related to the Internet protocol Telnet) or Tymnet, two commercial packet-switched networks that were, in some ways, precursors to the Internet. Instead of placing an expensive long-distance call directly to Lockheed’s computers, you could dial a local access number with your acoustic coupler or modem. The network would carry your session across the country. At 300 baud, about 30 characters per second, you weren’t going to get much for your $50. After all, even if you could saturate your modem (which, of course, you couldn’t), the most data you could pull in an hour was about 108 KB. Of course, everything you typed got an echo, and there were other considerations, so real throughput would never go that high.

Connecting was a multistep affair. You called the local network node, identified your terminal, supplied the address or name of the service you wanted, and eventually reached DIALOG’s login prompt. Then you entered your account credentials and could begin searching. By the mid-1980s, DIALOG also offered its own DIALNET network, and UNINET was another option. All of these networks charged for communications, typically by connection time, on top of the database charges. So your $50 an hour was really going to be more than that.

What these networks did, though, was allow providers to be in many major cities without having to install banks of modems across the country. Early online networks like CompuServe and the Source were accessible via these networks, too, sometimes with an extra charge tacked on.

The name DIALOG was appropriate because the system encouraged an actual dialogue between the operator and the computer. It was strictly a command line. A search produced a set of matching records, which could then be refined by additional searches.

Some of the important commands were BEGIN, EXPAND, SELECT, and TYPE. You could remember them as BEST. BEGIN selected a database. EXPAND displayed neighboring index terms, helping you discover what the database actually contained. SELECT searched for matching records, and TYPE displayed the results.

For example, a 1981 BYTE article shows a query like this:

SELECT PETROLEUM AND PRICES AND OPEC AND PY=1979

The system would find records containing the specified terms, restricted to the publication year 1979.

Boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT were essential tools. You could search for one concept, save the matching references as a numbered set, search for another concept, and combine the two sets.

There’s a video below from the Committee on Scientific and Technical Information that shows a 1968 DIALOG session (starting around 4 minutes in).

The Department of Education had a database, ERIC, that lived on DIALOG. Their manual has several versions that are still around online, including this one from 1981. This was sophisticated technology. In fact, some capabilities of DIALOG are still awkward or unavailable in ordinary web search engines.

Tick Tock

DIALOG had one enormous drawback: cost. According to that 1981 BYTE article, database charges ranged from $15 to $300 per hour, with the most commonly used databases averaging about $50 per hour. Those were 1981 dollars. There could also be telecommunications charges. A 1983 PC World article quoted approximately $8 per hour to connect through networks such as Tymnet or Telenet.
The good news was that you didn’t necessarily need an hour. A competent searcher might find useful results in ten minutes or less. The bad news was that every minute spent figuring out how to formulate a query was a minute you were paying for.

Experienced searchers planned their queries before connecting. They knew which databases contained the relevant material and how to construct efficient searches. An entire profession of information specialists and search brokers developed around these skills.

Even printing was a consideration. At 300 baud, sending a long bibliography to your local printer could consume expensive connection time. DIALOG offered an alternative: have the results printed on its own high-speed printers and mailed to you.

You could even order copies of the original documents through the service. That’s important because DIALOG usually wasn’t delivering complete articles to your screen. Much of its value was in locating bibliographic records and abstracts that told you where to find the information.

In 1983, DIALOG introduced a service aimed at personal computer owners called Knowledge Index. It provided a smaller selection of databases at night and on weekends for $24 per hour, including communications charges.

Searching Isn’t All of It

DIALOG also offered something resembling today’s automated search alerts. You could save a search strategy and arrange to have it run whenever a database was updated. If new matching material appeared, the service could print the references and mail them to you. Think Google Alerts, except the alert arrived in your mailbox rather than your inbox.

The databases themselves were impressive. In 1981, DIALOG offered roughly 130 databases covering everything from engineering and medicine to business and the social sciences. By 1983, the number had grown to more than 170.

Much of the underlying material was compiled and indexed by specialist publishers and information providers. DIALOG provided the searchable infrastructure that brought these collections together.

Google searches an enormous and often chaotic collection of web pages. DIALOG searched smaller, carefully organized collections of professional information. Neither approach is necessarily superior. They solve different problems.

The Changing of the Guard

DIALOG ultimately became big business. Lockheed established it as a wholly owned subsidiary in 1981. In 1988, Knight-Ridder purchased it for approximately $353 million. The service subsequently passed through several owners, including The Dialog Corporation and Thomson, before ProQuest acquired it in 2008.
You might assume the arrival of the Web and inexpensive search engines killed DIALOG. After all, why pay to search when you could simply type something into Google? But the service didn’t disappear. Today, it survives as Clarivate Dialog, offering specialized research databases, including technical, pharmaceutical, and patent information. Its pricing has changed, and the old connect-time meter is no longer the central feature of the business.

The service still exists because carefully indexed, authoritative information has value beyond what a general-purpose search engine can provide.

Pluses and Minuses

Modern search engines are extraordinarily powerful. We can search billions of pages from a device in our pocket, frequently getting useful results in a fraction of a second. Most of us never think about the computational resources or communications infrastructure required.

DIALOG required more effort, but it offered something interesting in exchange: precise, repeatable searches built from explicit operations on sets of information. The searcher controlled the process instead of relying primarily on an opaque relevance-ranking algorithm. We think of search engines as an Internet invention, but many features we associate with modern information retrieval were developed decades before the Web.

DIALOG’s greatest achievement wasn’t putting a library on a computer. It was demonstrating that finding information could be an interactive process rather than a batch job. Still, imagine if while reading this, you looked at the clock and realized you’d just spent $8 of connect time. Oops.

Not all search engines are equal, of course. Before modern search engines, there were several things similar to DIALOG and, of course, bibliographies.

item.title: Newer Rigol Scopes Get a Custom Linux Firmware - Hack a Day
item.description:
Electronics test equipment is a topic near and dear to many Hackaday readers. The average reader of this article is most likely within 50 feet of a multimeter, and it wouldn’t be much of a surprise to find they own multiple oscilloscopes. [dekajoule] has been working on a new firmware for the DHO series of Rigol oscilloscopes, the OOS (Open Operating System).

The DHO series of Rigol oscilloscopes was released in 2022. This series followed the very popular 1000Z series, which we’ve featured before in hacks that unlock built-in capabilities from budget oscilloscopes. The OOS project that [dekajoule] has been working on is similar, but maybe even more exciting, as it gives you even greater control over the scope. OOS runs on the built-in SD card that comes with the DHO scopes, and better still it can run alongside the existing OS, allowing you to swap back to the original OS if you decide to. There are a few different ways to install OOS, ranging from opening up the scope and cloning the SD card to using ADB over the network.

This project is still relatively new and as such it’s only been tested on a couple of models, but if the community support for the 1000Z series scopes is any indication, there are likely no shortage of users who would be interested in getting a little more out of their scope. For those on the fence, check out the long list of features that OOS brings to the table that aren’t part of the stock OS.

item.title: A 3D Printed Pixel Clock, with a Twist - Hack a Day
item.description:
The availability of cheap addressable RGB LED strips has been a huge boon for hardware hackers, as it makes many projects far more accessible. This usually requires a lot of snipping, followed by the monotony of connecting up a bunch of fiddly jumper wires, but that’s still generally preferable to having to solder all of the LEDs individually.

But what if you didn’t even have to do that? That was the goal of the brilliantly designed PixelClock by [Dom Dominici] — by carefully weaving a continuous 2.5 meter strip of WS2812B LEDs through its 3D printed structure, you can create a 7×19 display without any tedious manual work. Technically you do “waste” a few LEDs in the process since they’ll be on the inside of the folded strip, but that’s literally and figuratively a small price to pay for the added convenience offered by this approach.

We saw this one in person during Hackaday Supercon, and [Dom] tells us the whole idea was to make it as accessible as possible for new players. While we know there’s plenty of readers who actually enjoy the process of stripping and soldering wires, that’s not necessarily true for the average person. Of course the builder still needs to connect the end of the LED strip to the ESP32 WROOM development board that controls it, but that’s still a lot less intimating of a prospect for somebody that doesn’t breathe solder smoke on the regular.

The PixelClock is configured via a web interface running on the ESP32, so there’s nothing you need to install on your phone or computer to get it working. You can even install the firmware via WebSerial, making the build process that much friendlier.

One of the things we liked the most about the design is the printed diffuser — it might look like paper or some kind of opaque acrylic, but in actuality it’s just a couple layers of plastic. You can easily swap filament during the print to come up with different color variations, and for those that are comfortable in CAD, creating custom “pixels” is as easy as changing the shape of the individual LED compartments. Even in the bright Pasadena sunlight, the effect was impressive.

If you don’t mind cobbling together LED strips, this concept can be applied at a much larger scale.

item.title: The Fastest Paddleboard in the World - Hack a Day
item.description:
The world is full of linguistic boundaries that seem obvious during regular communication but can break down upon closer inspection. Is a pizza an open-faced sandwich? Is an ebike a motor vehicle? Are palms actually trees? Is a certain number of grains of sand a heap? Without diving too much into the world of philosophy, we might all at least agree that strapping 12 kW of motors to a paddleboard might turn it into another type of vehicle entirely, likely without the word “paddle” in its name. But either way, this is likely the fastest craft of its kind in the world.

Many other types of vessel of this type use off-the-shelf motor kits with shrouds, exposed bolts, and other drag-maximizing features. [rctestflight] has a lot of experience building custom watercraft without these downsides and figured he could put together something a little more hydrodynamic. His paddleboard incorporates two masts from a previous hydrofoil build, as well as two six kilowatt electric motors positioned at the end of each one. With some batteries in a waterproof case and a remote control to command them, the paddleboard quickly gets up on plane provided the rider is in the appropriate forward position.

For anyone familiar with [rctestflight]’s builds, you’ll know this isn’t just someone who slaps a motor onto a piece of fiberglass and tosses it into a lake. A lot of work went into this build, including some propellers that were developed during a long series of tests to find ideal propeller shapes for various applications. With all of the tuning done it travels across the surface of the water in excess of 40 kph, much faster than any other “paddle” board we’ve seen before.

item.title: Water in the Ancient Desert - Hack a Day
item.description:
The desert of the Iranian Plateau receives very little rainfall, and most of it falls in the mountains before flowing underneath the porous ground of the region. The ancient Persians figured out a way to access the water and build a flourishing civilization in the desert.

Half a million vertical shafts cover the Iranian Plateau and are evidence of the massive hydraulic engineering project that allowed cities to thrive in this hostile climate. Persian mathematician Al-Karaji helpfully wrote the book on the method, called The Extraction of Hidden Waters. After examining the land for clues, a piece of wool on a string was lowered in hole, and if it came back wet, a series of test wells were drilled until you found water.

Dropping approximately 1 m for every 1 km, the tunnel, or qanat, would then be dug from the outlet where the water level is even with the surface back to the mother well where the water was discovered. A crew of four muqanni worked digging the tunnel between vertical shafts spaced about 30 m apart and kept an eye on oil lamps that could warn them of oxygen-deprived air much like coal miner lamps in more recent times.

Once the water was at the surface, a complex series of channels and administration made sure crops were irrigated, public baths were supplied, and drinking water was secured for everyone. There was also water storage for dryer seasons and even the ability to make and store ice despite the lack of electricity.

We’ve covered the ice storage in yakhchāls and ancient windmills that are still operating in Persia before on these digital pages.

item.title: Can’t Get the Right Cassette Mechanism? Have a Go at Making Your Own! - Hack a Day
item.description:
In the world of cassette tape enthusiasts, it’s an oft-repeated factoid that there is only one tape deck mechanism still being manufactured. The truth may be a tiny bit murky on that front, but it’s certain that cassettes are no longer a mainstream medium. So we’re bowled over by [Svofski], who’s creating his own cassette mechanism from scratch.

The mechanism takes the form of a chassis made from PCBs, and with each spindle powered by a separate brushless motor. There doesn’t appear to be a capstan — instead it uses an optical mouse sensor to sense tape speed and thus provide input for motor control. As we understand it, this thing is designed to have more in common with a data backup tape drive than an audio player.

Thus before any cassette fans become too excited it’s worth tempering that enthusiasm. The project in hand is to make a data tape drive rather than a linear cassette player, so while it is a cassette mechanism, it isn’t as it stands one you’d use for audio. And as he explains at length in his GitHub repository and a set of videos, it’s not there yet. But the mere fact of its existence is deeply impressive, and we think you’ll agree. The most recent video of the series is below.

item.title: Binocular Chair Lets You Stargaze in Comfort - Hack a Day
item.description:
Telescopes are great, but sometimes binoculars are the right tool for stargazing. Holding them in front of your face for a long night of observation can get onerous though, so [Dave Selinger] designed the Milky Way Lounge Chair.

The chair allows for viewing at a variety of angles, including the zenith, and can hold its azimuth and altitude once the binoculars are released to give your arms a break. There’s no tracking capability yet, but there’s something to be said for something simple and relatively portable.

Starting with a suitable zero gravity chair, [Selinger] mounted it to a rectangular chair board with a bearing that can rotate around an octagonal ground board. The ground board is equipped with leveling screws to stabilize it for uneven surfaces, although he suggests a folded up tarp or rubber mat to place between the base and ground as well. Plans for the base are available for free, but the binocular holding apparatus and other functions are for sale if you don’t want to figure them out on your own.

This actually isn’t the first binocular chair we’ve seen.

item.title: Making a Universal, Self-Centering Tap Wrench - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although many people will just use the tap wrench that came with the tap and die set, once you get a larger shop it can be nice to not have to allocate a drawer or two just to keep track of the different tap wrenches you’ll inevitably end up collecting.

Thus, if you’re like [Inheritance Machining] you may find yourself yearning for a tap wrench that’s universal and also self-centering for that truly no fuss tapping experience. Cue the prism-based, self-adjusting tap wrench project.

After spotting a design with most of the features he was looking for by [Pferderik] on Reddit, he decided that with a few tweaks it would be perfect, though as said in the video it was already 99% of what he had in mind.

The video covers the machining of the tool from stock, including the four inserts that make up the core of the mechanism. With the single screw through one of the inserts, a user can easily adjust the size of the hole that the tap fits into.

As shown in the video, this makes for a rather smooth adjustment experience, though as [Adam Earl] in the comment section notes, it might be an idea to add a support for the adjustment screw on the other side for even more accuracy. Overall it seems like a pretty useful tool, although you may have similar concerns as with e.g. crescent wrenches – infamously known as nut rounders – if you get too much slop in the mechanism.

item.title: ESP32 WIFI Jam Detector Finds the Raspberry - Hack a Day
item.description:
We’ve seen plenty of ESP32 WiFi projects that test wifi systems with attacks such as Deauth, and even jamming. Today’s project is a bit different. [TheDigital1] created an ESP32 project that uses SDR to detect interference in the WiFi bands.  The detector builds on the popular ESPARGOS ESP-SDR project that we have previously featured, to scan for any interference. The hardware is based on an ESP32-C5, so it covers both the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands. [TheDigital1] used a Waveshare ESP32-C5-Touch-LCD-3.5, but since the project is open source, you should be able to port it to other devices.

The system doesn’t just detect noise. It can categorize the interference into four types: wideband, narrowband, pulsed wideband, and frequency-swept. [TheDigital1] notes that while the system can detect interference, it can’t detect intent, so it’s up to the user to determine if they have a leaky microwave or hackers trying to shut down their WiFi.

The system works great as a portable standalone device. In fact, the interface is pretty slick. Connecting it to a PC via USB opens up even more features. It can be used with Home Assistant as a WiFi Jammer detector. It can even detect if a room is occupied by sensing the noise floor increase from humans moving around.

With all these new ESP32 SDR projects coming up, we can’t wait to see what’s next!

item.title: Follow The Grid With An Arduino Uno - Hack a Day
item.description:
We all know the frequency of our AC grid. 60Hz for Americans, or 50Hz for Europeans, for example.  But the real story has some complexity. In a plural but interconnected grid such as Europe’s, that frequency can drift around a nominal center value. To keep track of this, [Jeroen Brinkman] has created a grid monitor that can show long-term trends as well as instantaneous frequencies.

Hardware-wise, it’s somewhat old-school, with an Arduino Uno and a ubiquitous 2×16 character LCD, but the interest here lies not in the microcontroller. Sensing mains frequency is fraught with spicy high-voltage danger if done directly, so [Jeroen] is performing the task using an optocoupler that toggles an interrupt pin on the Arduino. The monitor stores long-term data by the week, using only four bytes per week. That means the monitor can hold up to 240 weeks, or about 4.6 years, on a Nano R3 and over 2,000 weeks, or around 39 years on a Nano R4. The data can be retrieved via serial transfer over the Arduino’s USB port.

The subject of grid monitoring is a fascinating one, as geopolitical events can show up in it. Back in 2018, we covered the moment when Europe lost six seconds as a result.

item.title: It’s A NAS, For Sony Mavica Disks - Hack a Day
item.description:
At the dawn of the consumer digital camera age, manufacturers tested this new market with a wide array of interesting and unorthodox designs. This era only lasted a few years before they moved toward making models that resembled the 35mm cameras the consumers were used to. Sony’s Mavica offerings were particularly unusual, because they eschewed Flash storage for the then-ubiquitous 3.5″ floppy disk. Where there are files, there might be a need to share them, so [Bigcrimping] has created floppy3.5. It’s a NAS for digital Mavica disks.

Inside, along with the floppy drive, is an interesting dual-processor architecture. An RP2354 runs a Greaseweazle port and reads the floppy drive, to the extent that it can operate as a standalone Greaseweazle device through its USB port. An ESP32-S3 is hooked into the RP2354 via SPI and performs the tasks of decoding the raw floppy data, copying the resulting files to an SD card, and sharing the images over a web interface. There’s also a pleasingly retro display intended to look like a Walkman display of the same era.

This is an interesting project, both for Mavica owners for whom it’s very cool indeed, and as a portable Greaseweazle peripheral in its own right. More than once, we’ve had a random old floppy for which this appliance would have been a huge time saver. As we said earlier this year, it’s now imperative that you copy that floppy!

item.title: VapourDeck is the 486 Handheld You Didn’t Know You Needed - Hack a Day
item.description:
Do you need a 486-based handheld computer for DOS games? Well, we didn’t think so either — until we saw [Sprite_tm]’s impressive and excellently documented VapourDeck homebrew handheld PC. Now we want one for Christmas and to be [Sprite_tm] when we grow up.

There exist industrial single-board computers designed around the Intel 486, and you’d be forgiven for thinking that’s what lives inside this build– but no. [Sprite_tm] was tired of thinking of a motherboard as “deep magic” and decided it was high time he designed his own. He chose the 486 because Intel actually let mere mortals at the documentation in those days, and it would let him play all his favourite DOS games on the fly. The board contains a period-appropriate VGA chip — complete with whopping 1MB of VRAM!– though most of the glue logic, I/Om and sound are on a modern FPGA and ESP32-S3, respectively.

The writeup gives a good idea of the thinking behind this machine, but if you want to build one yourself, you can get all the files on Codeburg, because [Sprite_tm] was kind enough to open-source his work even if he’s not sure anyone else would want to replicate it.

We’ve seen a lot of [Sprite_tm]’s work on Hackaday over the years, including a portable Vectrex he walked us through at Supercon one year.

Thanks to [Vital] for the tip!

item.title: Loop Antennas for Transmitting - Hack a Day
item.description:
Loop antennas are becoming increasingly popular as more radio fans find they can’t erect elaborate outdoor antennas. Like most things, of course, there are trade-offs. But, most often, loop antennas are for receiving. Only a few can handle transmitting, and [FesZ] wanted to build some that could handle transmit power. You can find out what he discovered in the video below.

Loop antennas are very sensitive, and a standard variable capacitor just rotates less than a single rotation. High-precision devices would often have gear reductions, but those are hard to find today. But with a 3D printer, it is reasonably easy to make gear reductions for a variable capacitor, and that’s what [FesZ] did.

In addition, [FesZ] replaced one non-critical capacitor with a bank of fixed capacitors and switches. This isn’t just a build video. There are Spice simulations and even a thermal camera deployed. A lot to learn.

If you build some cool loop antennas, let us know. If you want to look at some commercial receive antennas — including one that is — sort of — infinitely long, we’ve tried a few.

item.title: An Orbital Sanders Crash Course and the Threat of HAVS - Hack a Day
item.description:
Most people know about orbital sanders, as the cousin of sheet sanders, with many people using them every day to make wood and other surfaces smooth. Yet if you have ever wondered at the slightly numb and tingling feeling in your hands after using them for a while, you really want to watch this deep dive by [Five Duck Studio] on how orbital sanders work and why not all vibrations are good vibrations.

First, the basic workings of an orbital sander are explained in the video, including the way that the orbital sanding pattern is created by the spinning disc. These patterns aren’t the same size for each sander, with the ‘finisher’ ~2.5 mm pattern being decidedly more suitable for fine work, while the roughly 5 mm pattern is better for coarser work.

From here, the details spiral into the various brake mechanisms, which prevent the disc from spinning wildly when not on a surface. This can be as simple as an O-ring providing some friction.

Also covered are dust filtration, sanding speed, when to touch that speed dial, the different types of pads and sandpaper, and maybe most important of all, the vibrations. These are what numb your hand while you are using the sander, and although this may seem like something you can just ‘shake off’, it’s actually your body warning you that you’re at risk of vascular and nerve damage. This is called Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS), and can lead to permanent damage, including the loss of fingers.

Fortunately, the EU has some regulations on occupational hazards, with sander manufacturers required to test and report the vibrations from their tools. As demonstrated in the video, manufacturers are of course more than happy to use loopholes in said regulations to skirt by with much more vibration than reported.

Using the EU’s point-based system, you can easily see how many damage points you rack up from a sanding session, though of course the type of wood you’re sanding will play a role too. Either way, this video should hopefully give some good information on how to pick a good orbital sander and how to use it safely, without one becoming a case study for HAVS or COPD from dust inhalation.

item.title: Reverse Engineering Score Perfect to Rescue its Files - Hack a Day
item.description:
There are myriad challenges associated with data preservation – bit rot, loss of metadata, and hardware failures, among others – but one of the hardest is making sure that the data remains usable as software goes out of date. [Maarten Tromp]’s father, for instance, had been using the Score Perfect music notation program for years, but since development ceased in 2012, the files would eventually need to be transferred to more modern software. To do this, [Maarten] undertook a four-year project to reverse-engineer the structure of Score Perfect’s files.

Score Perfect was first released in 1990 for Atari and later ported to Windows, and after version four, it switched to a different file format. It had the option to export to MusicXML, but it only exported notes, not chords, lyrics, or other important details. [Maarten] first tried disassembling the program itself to find the file structure; he had hoped that the Visual Basic code might have been compiled to P-code, which is relatively easy to disassemble, but it had been compiled to native code. Interestingly, through version four, the program had been written for Atari and ran in Windows through a simple emulator. It wasn’t fully rewritten for Windows until later. After some investigation into the file-export function with Ghidra, he moved on to reverse-engineering the file format itself.

This consumed the majority of the project’s time. To investigate the file’s structure, [Maarten] would start by creating an empty file in the program, make one change, and compare the difference in the file written. This gradually revealed the organization of information — the file was arranged into blocks containing different kinds of information, such as measures and notes, and tags, which provided supplemental information. Once again, incremental changes revealed the function of most of these, and [Maarten] was eventually able to write a translation program to export Score Perfect files to MusicXML.

We’ve previously seen a similar effort to reverse-engineer the Altium file format. At least in these cases, though, all the necessary information is contained in the files, unlike the reverse-engineering often necessitated by STL files.

item.title: Making CO₂ Sensors Fail Visibly, Not Silently - Hack a Day
item.description:
CO₂ buildup in a living area can be a serious problem, and a sensor that fails quietly cannot be relied upon. [William Collis] addressed this important issue by creating CO₂ monitors built to fail visibly.

[William] has a nice home setup that can monitor CO₂ levels in two places, but noticed an important issue: the system always displayed the last known-good sensor reading. An unchanging, healthy-looking number is good! Unless it isn’t, because a flat unchanging number is also exactly what a dead sensor looks like.

The solution was for [William] to change how the sensors are treated so a faulty sensor isn’t hidden behind apparently-good values, and the sensor itself flashes a visible fault LED in the case of a problem.

Each monitor is a Sensirion SCD30 CO₂ sensor, paired with a Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 running ESPHome to communicate with Home Assistant, an open-source home automation framework. There was no need to rewrite the ESPHome firmware; all his modifications fit within the context of a configuration file and certainly seem to be improvements over the original.

Sensors that can be relied on are important, but if the system itself needs some ruggedizing maybe consider a homebrewed UPS for Home Assistant.

item.title: ESP32 Flight Tracker on Apple CRT - Hack a Day
item.description:
Sometimes we’re most taken by what’s on the screen; sometimes the screen itself is the most interesting part of the project. In this case, it’s the latter. That’s no slight against [Virtual-Bet-4566], whose ESP32-based flight tracker looks very nice– but a big part of what it makes it so nice is that it’s displaying the ADS-B flight data on an old green-phosphor monitor from the Apple II days.

He’s using an ESP32-WROOM-32, which gives him both the wifi connection needed to grab aircraft locations and flight details– including photos of individual aircraft, when available from Planespotters.net– but crucially has an 8-bit digital-analong-converter that he’s using to drive the composite input on the old Apple monitor. Not all of the expansive ESP32 family have that feature, but at this point you might as well call ESP32 a brand of MCU than a family given the vast differences between them. Since composite video doesn’t need much power, he’s connected the dev board directly to the monitor. It’s that delicious combination of the old and new that really gets us vibing.

Speaking of vibing, yes, this whole thing was vibe-coded, as [Virtual-Bet] freely admits in the Reddit thread. LLMs seem to be really good at making these flight tracking apps, to judge from other posts on that site, but this one stands out for its display method. He’s also apparently got weather and his own local sensor data incorporated in the wifi-controlled display application, and isn’t interested in sharing the code since you could prompt it yourself. Fair enough.

We’ve seen composite-out from the ESP32 family before, more than once— which is probably how the LLM knew to pull it off–but there’s just something about that green glow.

Story via CircuitDigest.

item.title: Borland C++ 2.0 Compiler Source Reconstructed - Hack a Day
item.description:
As the successor to Turbo C++, Borland C++ was a staple of professional IDEs for C and C++ development, starting with the initial 2.0 release in 1991. Being a commercial project the original source code for the toolchains were naturally not made available by Borland, but thanks to the efforts of [Abedegno] we have now got what is claimed to be a byte-perfect recreation, in the sense that the binaries compiled using the toolchain are identical to the original toolchain.

The process of creating the source from the original toolchain binaries is detailed in a separate document, including the use of [Abedgno]’s Claude Code-based Exhume tool to assist in the effort.

Having the source code for BC++ 2.0 available is probably most useful for projects that deal with DOS-based software from the same era, as well as for purely historic interest reason. When BC++ 2.0 was released, the C programming language had only just seen itself standardized in the form of C89, and C++’s initial standard in 1998 was still years away.

Thanks to [Stephen Walters] for the tip.

item.title: X Window System on the ESP32 - Hack a Day
item.description:
There are a lot of things you can do with an Xserver, but run it on a microcontroller? Well, if that microcontroller is an ESP32-S3, [Sergey Zorin]– and Claude– have got you covered with Woodland X11, a full-featured port of everyone’s favourite XServer.

Now, it is just the core Xserver with no extensions, and currently targeted specifically at the Elecrow CrowPanel Advance 4.3″, a device that packages an ESP32-S3-N16R8 with an 800×480 RGB565 IPS panel and GT911 touch. In this implementation, your finger is the Xcursor. There’s even two-finger scroll implemented, though no keyboard. As you can see in the demo video embedded below, it works well enough for those oldschool X applications like xclock, xcalc and– crucially!– xeyes. What’s the point of an Xserver without googly eyes, anyway?

In reality, you’re not likely to set this up just for Xeyes, but the idea of having bringing Linux applications to a little display via WiFi or — as in the video– wired connection has no limit of use cases. Try that with Wayland!

Considering X11’s vintage, it is perhaps not surprising that it fits on the ESP32-S3, a chip we’ve seen emulate an entire 386 PC before– a PC that could run an Xserver, for you youngun’s.
