Thanks to [Sergey] for the tip!

item.title: Using a Toothbrush’s NFC chip to Unlock a Computer - Hack a Day
item.description:
Depending on which type of electric toothbrush you are using, the replaceable brushes may contain an NFC chip that the handle and possibly base station uses to track various details, such as time spent brushing and when to replace the brush. The Philips Sonicare of [Circuit Helper] is one such unit, with its NFC chip tracking aspects like runtime and pressure.

Unsurprisingly it’s easy enough to read and write this same NFC chip with a PN532 NFC reader and ESP32-S3 MCU. This reveals data fields for everything from brush type, to total runtime and expected lifetime, inviting a bit of experimentation on how certain usage patterns affects these data fields.

This much is perhaps not too shocking, but the fun part is what you can do with the chip after you have figured out how to write to its memory. How to unlock these units and their NXP NTAG213 IC has been figured out a few years ago already, so the hardest part was to figure out what to do with this information.

The demonstrated use case in the video is to unlock an Apple Macbook, which is maybe a bit too niche. Also demonstrated is taking the chip and its antenna out of the brush, which turns out to be quite easy. Perhaps salvaging just this one part of the brush is the more practical and hygienic option, as who doesn’t like building up a strategic supply of ‘free’ NFC chips?

item.title: Drop-in Vintage CPU Replacements with the tranZPUter Project - Hack a Day
item.description:
One of the struggles with vintage computer systems is that many of the ICs in them have no modern-day version that you can just purchase and drop-in. Creating replacements that use modern-day ICs inside has consequently become a popular direction, with [Philip Smart]’s TranZPUter being one such example.

Standing for ‘transformable ZPU Computer’, the tranZPUter is transformable in the sense that it features an FPGA or MCU and the initial iteration targeting the ZPU Evo CPU design. This has led to a number of variants of this concept, including a version targeting the Z80, the 6502 and 6809. These are based around the RP2350B MCU, using its PIO peripheral to great effect.

Of these the Motorola 6809 is probably the lesser known MPU, having been launched in 1978 as an 8-bit MPU with some 16-bit features that could beat the 6502 in many metrics courtesy of its more advanced hardware. It being more expensive led to it only being used in systems like the TRS-80 Color, Dragon 32/64, SuperPET and a whole range of arcade systems.

If you have any of those 6809-based systems and the MPU gave up the ghost, you can drop in the Pico6809 board featuring said RP2350B MCU as well as an ESP32 co-processor. Currently it targets the Dragon 32/64 systems, adding not just a fresh MPU, but also adds virtual floppy and cassette devices as well as network support as options.

Overall it seems like a pretty extensive project that might already have found purchase within the retrocomputing community.

item.title: Fixing a Dead Socket LGA 1851 Mainboard with a Resistor - Hack a Day
item.description:
Doing board level diagnosis on a PCB is hardly black magic, but some PCBs are definitely more daunting than others. The Socket LGA 1851 mainboard that [Fix the Pixel] got in for repair being one of the harder cases due to the sheer size and complexity. Adding to the excitement was having to purchase a used CPU for it off eBay to even test the board and work through the boot-up sequence to find the culprit.

A basic understanding of how these mainboards power up and verify that they can move on to the next phase is essential here, starting with the power rails. Although the culprit turned out to be a single missing 5.1 Ohm resistor on an SPI clock line, you still have to reason your way through the diagnosis. For this mainboard the boardview was fortunately available, but that still doesn’t make it easy to spot components that have quietly left the chat.

With the CPU and RAM installed the board doesn’t bother to boot up, with the VRM controller for the CPU’s power phases showing its enable pin to stay low. Going down the list of conditions for this pin to be pulled high the culprit was eventually found, when the PCH – the board’s chipset – never reading the BIOS chip.

Checking the SPI lines on the mainboard near the BIOS chip quickly showed the knocked-off resistor on the SPI clock line. Soldering a fresh resistor in place resulted in the board happily booting up once more. Although having a boardview here available helps a lot, checking such basics like the SPI line resistors around the BIOS can be a quick checklist item before dragging out the big diagnostics guns or shelling out money for a boardview file.

item.title: Hacked Nixie Clock Waits for the Bus - Hack a Day
item.description:
Nixie clocks have become popular enough that these days there’s no shortage of turn-key options that let you experience that warm glow with a minimum of fuss. Many still come as little more than a bare PCB, giving the purchaser some freedom to come up with their own enclosure, but at least the electronics are handled.

But for [Justin Scott], putting his new two-digit Nixie clock board into a handsome box was only half the battle. He also wanted to do something a bit more interesting than just tell the time. To convert the board from a simple clock to a device that could show how many minutes until the next bus showed up at his local stop, he had to hack the firmware and establish a communication link to a Raspberry Pi to do the heavy lifting.

The first step was to get a modified firmware on the clock PCB, and that required a ST-LINK V2 programmer and some time tracing out the pins on the STM8 microcontroller to determine how they controlled the various elements of the Nixie tubes. Fortunately, there were just I/O pins left over to stand up a serial link to a Raspberry Pi Zero through a level converter.

On the Pi side, a Python script hits the bus API to figure out what’s coming and when. There’s some creative blinking of the decimal points to indicate what’s happening behind the scenes, but primarily the display simply shows how many minutes are left before [Justin] should be out waiting for his ride.

It would be nice if all those commercial Nixie boards would talk I2C, but at least projects like this show it’s possible to get more out of them than just the time.

item.title: A Desktop OS for the ESP32-P4 - Hack a Day
item.description:
The ESP32-P4 is Espressif’s high-end application processor, with two blistering fast RISC-V cores for a surprisingly reasonable price. As it’s a very capable computer in its own right, there have been a range of operating systems made for it. Latest among them is [Jthwho]’s BMDS, for Bare Metal Do Stuff, which targets an Olimex board.

At its heart is the FreeRTOS kernel we’ve seen in so many other similar projects, but on top is an OS which is described as being like DOS in its one-user minimally intrusive operation. It runs ELF binaries, and has some POSIX compliance, with BusyBox being a port. Perhaps most noticeable is its GUI, which provides a very slick desktop straight out of the late 1990s.

We can see that had this appeared as a contemporary of Amigas, 68k Macs, and Windows 3.x, it would have immediately been a real contender. But the question is, does such an OS have a niche here in 2026? We think it might, as this processor is slowly establishing itself in a new genre of powerful machines aimed at hackers and tinkerers. Either way it’s an impressive achievement, and we look forward to seeing it develop over time.

item.title: Hacking Meta’s Smart Glasses - Hack a Day
item.description:
Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses have attracted plenty of controversy in the relatively short time they have been available, given their potential for covert and unvanted surveillance. But given the chance to examine one it would be churlish to pass up on the opportunity to test its defences. Which is what [p0pcycle] did when the opportunity came her way.

Given that hardware-probing was not an option, she followed the course of intercepting a software update. A little app decompilation led her to the full firmware, and she was able to probe its secrets. There’s a developer mode allowing applications to be written for the glasses, and it takes the form of an APK that loads the application code. An early firmware version would trust self-signed apps, so she could get arbitrary code on the device. From there after some trial and error she was able to expose a network listener, and there she had it.

The write-up is an interesting walkthrough of the process, and ends with her reporting it through their bug bounty program. So sadly the steps outlined above won’t work on newer firmwares, but we’re guessing that won’t stop others probing this device further.

item.title: Watch That Sound: Your Own Chladni Plate - Hack a Day
item.description:
What if you could see sound? A Chladni plate uses a speaker and small particles, like sand, to give you a visual representation of sound, and [CrazyScience] shows you how to make one. The plate dates back to 1787, created by the eponymous physicist. Of course, back then, there were no speakers, so the original plate was metal with a violin bow raked across the edges.

The modern version uses an ESP32, a speaker, and salt. The patterns depend on the resonance points of the plate. The device has a rotary encoder to tune different frequencies. Check it out in the video below.

There’s also an OLED display to show the frequency and patterns. There is also a 3D-printed enclosure. The patterns, of course, depend on standing waves. We aren’t sure that there’s any practical value for it, but we like the way it looks.

This isn’t the first time we’ve talked about Chladni. Visualizing things before the CRT was interesting, to say the least.

item.title: Upgrade Your CoCo The Modern Way - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Radio Shack TRS-80 Colour Computer may never have achieved the sales volume of its competitors from Commodore or Apple, but it offered a surprisingly capable set of hardware. There were three versions, with the final one being a significant upgrade in many ways. There was no upgrade path for owners of version 1 and 2 machines to have a version 3 back in the day, but now thanks to [Felipe Antoniosi] such an upgrade is possible. How? With a Tang Nano 20K FPGA board, of course!

The CoCo 3 had a paged memory system for expansion up to 512k, as well as a significantly more capable graphics chip which while compatible with the original Motorola part offered enhanced graphics. The upgrade emulates these, and connects to the CoCo via a set of daughter boards that connect to where the various motherboard chips sat. it offers an HDMI output as well as analog video and enhanced sound capability, bringing the machine firmly into the 21st century.

As mods go to classic hardware, this is quite an invasive one. Whether or not you’d prefer to do this to your CoCo is up to you, but ask yourself this, would you have done this had this board been available in the 1980s? Of course you would.

Meanwhile should you become bored with the CoCo, it can also be persuaded to emulate an Apple ][.

item.title: Baochip-1x: A Mostly-Open, 22nm SoC for High Assurance Applications - Hack a Day
item.description:
For most people, just getting any old microcontroller or system on chip (SoC) from our favorite – or cheapest – vendor is more than good enough. But if you’re really into high assurance computing where every transistor has to be accounted for, you got a bit of a problem. This is basically why [Andrew “Bunnie” Huang] pitched in and had the Baochip-1x produced.

This SoC’s design is based heavily on the FPGA-based CPU in the Precursor device, which itself is claimed to be a fully verifiable communicator design. Since it does have an MMU, you can run any software on it that supports the RV32IMAC RISC-V instruction set, with a Coder’s Guide available for those who might feel interested in this SoC, along with the SystemVerilog and Verilog-based sources.

In addition to the DIY assembly process, you can even get a physical hardware version, including the ‘Dabao’ evaluation board with a very Raspberry Pi Pico-shaped form factor. Inside this SoC is a single-core, 350 MHz VexRISC-V core, 4 MB resistive RAM (RRAM) and 2 MB of SRAM, along with a whole heap of security-related features.

item.title: Tiny Transmitters Track Monarch Butterflies - Hack a Day
item.description:
Miniaturization is one thing, but how would you like to design a transmitter that attaches to a butterfly? That’s what the BlūMorpho transmitter is made to do, according to [Tom Jokinen] writing for Be Giant. Apparently, most of these butterflies have a two- to six-week life, but periodically a “super generation” spawns and lives up to nine months. This is enough time to migrate from Canada and the United States to Mexico. In Mexico, they spend the winter, and then return when the weather is more hospitable. Scientists wanted to study this migration pattern, and the tiny transmitter is exactly what they needed.

You can even download an app to track the butterflies yourself. The transmitter looks like a tadpole and weighs 60 milligrams. There’s no battery, but there is a tiny solar cell. The transmitter emits a Bluetooth signal that your phone’s location services can relay.

To affix the transmitter, researchers put a glassine envelope over the butterfly, weigh its wings down with something slightly heavy, and then apply eyelash glue to the transmitter. You can see the process in the video below.

What else could you do with a virtually weightless Bluetooth tracker? It is possible that dedicated tracking stations could have a longer range.

item.title: Espresso, Meet Custom-Machined Stainless Steel Boiler - Hack a Day
item.description:
While pondering some repairs for his Gaggia Classic Pro espresso machine, [Hans Gaensbauer] ended up machining an entirely new boiler from stainless steel.

It was a nontrivial undertaking, since the boiler is an assembly that integrates not only heaters and pump connections, but one end is also the group head into which the portafilter interfaces. [Hans] had to deal with machining out the contours and pockets necessary for a portafilter to lock in securely, complete with the little screen and perforated plate responsible for even water distribution. And of course, the whole thing still has to fit into the original machine. All in all, [Hans] had some constraints to work around, making it a considerably more complex job than just milling a chamber out of a block of stainless steel.

Overall he matches the original as much as possible, but since the original was cast from a mold and not designed with machining in mind, the operation is a bit tricky. This is a common issue when one changes manufacturing methods: a part designed to be molded will tend to have features that prove inconvenient for machining.

In the end it’s a success, complete with brand new seals and some upgraded electric components to address an original thermostat failure. If you want to see the insides of [Hans]’ espresso machine as well as loads of pictures showing the process of machining a whole new boiler and group head, check it out.

Coffee is a topic near and dear to many hackers, so there are plenty of retrofits and repairs but we’ve also seen folks go right back to square one and re-imagine entire espresso machines, rather than just single parts.

item.title: A LEGO 3D Printer - Hack a Day
item.description:
LEGO building blocks are a great toy, but every so often a hacker decides to take the little bricks outside of the toy room and make them an integral part of a build. [Adam Turaj] took that idea further than most with his Studprint, a 3D printer that’s 92% LEGO.

We aren’t just talking LEGO bricks making up part of the frame here, or even the bed — though that’s obviously the case — but [Adam] goes so far that even the motion system is using LEGO leadscrews to drive the axes of this printer. Is it particularly capable? Well, no. He’s not boasting of a remarkable bed size or high speeds here because that’s really not the point. The point is that he made a printer in LEGO and if you don’t see the fun in that, we don’t know what to tell you.

The whole project is open source, and includes the CAD files for the handful of non-LEGO bits you’ll need to mount the electronics, steppers and such. With an unheated bed of ABS bricks, you’re going to be limited in filament choices, but [Adam] has at least made a Benchy, which is all anyone really needs, right?

In light of recent work, we can might suggest that the printer is also a pick-and-place machine. If you want to turn the phrase “LEGO 3D Printer” around, we have seen 3D Printed LEGO before as well. We’d be remiss not to note that this isn’t the first printer to use the ubiquitous building blocks we’ve seen, though this one keeps with the regular filament and extruder rather than hot glue like the 2013 version.

item.title: It’s Elite, For The Commodore Pet - Hack a Day
item.description:
A few times in the life of someone interested in technology, there comes along something which after seeing it, you know the field is never going to be the same again. For a teenage future Hackaday writer this came in seeing Elite, on a BBC Micro. Nowadays an open world game is normal, but in the mid-1980s it was mind-blowing. Of course, such a powerful piece of software couldn’t be ported to any old computer, so owners of less capable machines were left envious of their more well-heeled friends.

It will be a surprise to Commodore Pet owners then, that over four decades later, [David Given] has ported the game to their platform. It’s not such a leap, as the Pet has the same (albeit slower) 6502 as the BBC Micro, and the game requires the Commodore machine to have 32k of memory.

So what you get is Elite, but with the Pet’s block graphics rather than the higher-resolution you’d have seen on the newer machines. He admits it doesn’t play well and that the code is something of a mess, but we suspect 32k Pet owners in 2026 won’t be too bothered by this. All the code and disk images are there in the repository, and you can see it at work in the video below the break. Meanwhile if you’re curious about the Elite codebase, you can take a look at it yourself.

Thanks [Stephen Walters] for the tip.

item.title: Modular, 3D Printed Train Whistles For Everyone - Hack a Day
item.description:
If the word “train” didn’t grab your attention, you’re probably not the target audience for this project. If it did, then there is no need to explain why [AeroKoi] has come up with a modular 3″ train whistle, available on Thingiverse and well explained in the video embedded below. It’s a train whistle. Who doesn’t want their own train whistle?

The great part of this design– aside from requiring less air than his earlier, larger-diameter iterations–is the modularity. With adjustable bell caps, you can alter the size of the resonant chamber and thus the notes the whistle plays on the fly. That’s the key difference between a train whistle, as used in the steam era, and a train horn as you find on a modern diesel or electric– whistles use a resonant chamber, while a horn uses a diaphragm to create the vibrations we call sound. By using the movable chamber caps to change the resonance, you can go from a Santa Fe 5 chime to a B&O 3 chime whistle by matching the measurements in the handy-dandy spreadsheet [TrainArtisan] provided– and doubling up on a couple of chimes.

One excellent tip he gives in the video is to grease all the mating surfaces of the whistles with petroleum jelly, but it’s worth watching the whole thing on YouTube for both full build and tuning instructions, and to learn more than you ever thought you needed to know about whistles– he gets right into the physics of sound waves to explain exactly the limitations of trying to replicate the sound of brass steam whistles with plastic and compressed air. If you just want to hear a bunch of train whistles to see how well it works, jump to the ten minute mark. The disappointing part comes later, where he explains the airflow requirements: if you don’t have a compressor with a big tank, you can’t expect more than one short toot at a time.

Interestingly enough it looks like most of the whistles we’ve written about are locomotive-adjacent, including [AeroKoi]’s earlier work, and a true cast-brass replica for the purists.

item.title: CHIP 8: The Pong Game’s Afoot! - Hack a Day
item.description:
Writing a computer game has always been hard. It is only the nature of the difficulty that changes. A modern game is as much about graphics, sound, and storytelling as it is about programming. But in the early days of computers, writing a game was a challenge because of limited graphics, slow CPUs, and tiny memory capacity. If you wanted to write a game for an early microcomputer, you generally wrote it in assembly language. BASIC was available on many machines, but it was usually too slow for anything requiring fast animation. Assembly language was fast, but it was also difficult to write, debug, and port to another machine.

RCA — in particular [Joseph Weisbecker], the architect of the 1802 — introduced the COSMAC VIP into the primordial 1977 home video game market. In addition to using ready-made games, the idea was that you could create your own. But writing games in 1802 assembly language would be beyond most of RCA’s customers. [Weisbecker] devised CHIP-8, a tiny virtual machine. It wasn’t quite a programming language. Instead, it was a simple instruction set implemented by an interpreter running on a real computer. You wrote programs for the imaginary CHIP-8 processor, and the interpreter made them run on the actual hardware. CHIP-8 is perfect for the kind of games you’d see in those days and still has a following among those who love retro games.

A Different Time: Tiny Interpreters

Today, when we think of interpreters, we often imagine something like Python, where the interpreter reads source code and figures out what to do. However, there’s another approach that was particularly attractive when memory and processor cycles were precious: threaded code.

In a threaded-code interpreter, a program consists of references (like indices into a command table) to routines that perform operations. Instead of decoding complicated instructions, the interpreter follows these references, executing the corresponding routines. There are several variations, including direct threading, indirect threading, and token threading. Forth is probably the best-known example of a language that commonly uses threaded code. In a typical Forth implementation, a program is compiled into a sequence of references to words, and a compact inner interpreter executes them.

Why bother? Because the implementation can be remarkably small. Instead of generating native machine code, a compiler can produce a compact representation that is relatively easy to execute. CHIP-8 belongs to the same general family of ideas, although it is more accurately described as a bytecode interpreter than a conventional threaded-code system. Its instructions are two bytes long, and the interpreter decodes each instruction and executes the corresponding operation. The original implementation was written in RCA 1802 machine code.

History Of CHIP-8

The COSMAC VIP was an interesting machine. A basic system had 2 KB of RAM, a hexadecimal keypad, and a monochrome video display. Programs were generally entered as hexadecimal bytes using the keypad, although expansion options were available. The 1802 CPU inside wasn’t exactly a speed demon. It was an 8-bit processor with sixteen 16-bit registers and an unusual architecture that made it well suited to certain embedded applications. There were versions that were also well-suited for spacecraft, and so the chip is in Magellan, Galileo, and even some parts of the Hubble.

CHIP-8 made programming the VIP considerably easier, especially for games. Rather than dealing with the peculiarities of the 1802 and the VIP’s display hardware, programmers could use a small, consistent instruction set designed around graphics and keypad input.

The CHIP-8 virtual machine provides sixteen 8-bit registers, conventionally named V0 through VF. It also has a 16-bit index register, a program counter, a stack for subroutine calls, and two timers.

The display is 64 pixels wide and 32 pixels high. Pixels are either on or off. There’s no color, no hardware sprites, and no sophisticated graphics processor. There are, however, instructions specifically intended to make games easier to write. You can draw a sprite with a single instruction, test whether a key is pressed, generate a random number, and use timers to control animation.

A sprite is simply a sequence of bytes, with each bit representing a pixel. A typical sprite can be up to eight pixels wide and fifteen pixels high. The instruction set is tiny, with only a few dozen basic operations. Yet it is sufficient to implement games such as Pong, Breakout, and Space Invaders-like shooters.

CHIP-8 subsequently appeared on other systems, and later variants extended its capabilities. The best-known extension is Super-CHIP, which added features including higher-resolution graphics. Today, CHIP-8 survives largely because it is an excellent target for emulator projects. Writing a CHIP-8 interpreter is a manageable exercise, and there are thousands of small programs available to test one. But you don’t need to write an interpreter to experiment with CHIP-8.

Modern Octo

Octo is a modern CHIP-8 development environment created by [John Earnest]. It runs in a web browser and includes an assembler, an emulator, a debugger, and tools for working with CHIP-8 programs. You can write code, assemble it, and run it without installing anything. Octo also supports extensions to the original instruction set, although we’ll stick with ordinary CHIP-8 for this project. Using a higher-level assembly syntax than the hexadecimal opcodes used by early CHIP-8 programmers is handy enough.

You still have to think like an assembly language programmer. There are registers, jumps, subroutines, and a very small instruction set. However, you don’t have to remember that 6A05 means load register VA with the value 5. Instead, you can write va := 5.

That’s much easier to read. Octo also provides labels, constants, expressions, and other conveniences that make it practical to write programs of reasonable complexity.

A Little CHIP-8 Assembly

CHIP-8 has sixteen general-purpose registers, V0 through VF. Most instructions operate on these registers.

For example:

v0 := 10
v1 := 20
v0 += v1

This loads 10 into V0, 20 into V1, and adds V1 to V0. Afterward, V0 contains 30. However, Octo also allows :alias and :const keywords to make things easier:

:const RETRY 10
:alias trycount v0
trycount := RETRY

There are also bitwise operations:

v0 &= v1
v0 |= v1
v0 ^= v1

You can compare registers and values using conditional instructions. One thing that takes some getting used to is that CHIP-8 doesn’t really have conventional conditional branches. Instead, conditional instructions skip the following instruction when the condition is satisfied. Luckily, Octo hides some of that awkwardness with syntax such as:

if v0 == 10 then jump somewhere

Underneath, this is still a conditional skip followed by a jump.

Subroutines are straightforward:

: main
v0 := 10
do_something
jump main
: do_something
v0 += 1
return

Drawing is particularly interesting. To draw a sprite, you first load the index register, i, with the address of the sprite data. Then you use the sprite instruction.

For example:

i := ball_sprite ; load address
sprite v0 v1 1
; address of sprint for ball
: ball_sprite 
0x80

Each sprite is one byte high and eight bits wide. Since only the most significant bit is set, it draws a single pixel. The V0 and V1 registers specify the X and Y coordinates.

Let’s Play Pong

A simple Pong game is a good demonstration of CHIP-8 programming because it requires very little graphics capability but exercises most of the interesting parts of the virtual machine. This version has two paddles, one on each side of the screen, and a single-pixel ball. The left paddle uses keys 1 and 4 to move up and down. The right paddle uses C and D. If you use Octo, this maps to the 1 and Q keys along with the 4 and R keys.

The ball moves across the screen, bouncing off the top and bottom walls. When it strikes a paddle, it reverses direction. If a player misses, the ball returns to the center. The ball doesn’t always bounce straight back. Its vertical direction depends on where it strikes the paddle. A hit in the center produces a horizontal trajectory. Hits above or below the center produce progressively steeper angles.

Since CHIP-8 doesn’t have floating-point arithmetic, we approximate the angles using integer counters. For example, a five-degree trajectory moves vertically approximately one pixel for every eleven pixels of horizontal movement. For a ten-degree trajectory, we move vertically about once every six horizontal pixels. This isn’t a sophisticated physics simulation, but it works well enough for Pong. You can play it directly using Octo in your browser.

The game loop is conceptually simple:

: main
erase_objects
move_paddles
move_ball
draw_objects
wait_for_frame
jump main

The actual program is a little more complicated because we have to handle input, collisions, and boundary conditions. Still, the basic structure is familiar to anyone who has written a simple video game.

You can find the complete Octo source on GitHub. The program uses ordinary CHIP-8 instructions and should run in Octo or another compatible interpreter.

Detecting Collisions

CHIP-8 has a clever feature that makes sprite collisions particularly easy to detect. Whenever you execute a sprite instruction, the interpreter sets register VF to indicate whether any pixels were erased by the XOR drawing operation. If no pixels were erased, VF is zero. If one or more pixels were erased, VF is one. Suppose the display contains a pixel that is already on. If you draw another sprite over that pixel, the pixel turns off. If you draw over it again, it turns back on. This makes it possible to erase sprites simply by drawing them again.

It also provides a simple collision detection mechanism. If you draw a ball over a paddle, some of the ball’s pixels will overlap the paddle’s pixels. The XOR operation erases those pixels, and VF becomes one. In our Pong game, we can use this to determine whether the ball has struck a paddle.

Conceptually, the code looks like this:

i := ball_sprite
sprite v0 v1 1
if vf == 1 then jump collision

There’s a subtlety here. VF doesn’t tell us what the ball collided with, only that the drawing operation erased at least one pixel. For Pong, we can use the ball’s position and direction to determine which paddle is involved. We can then calculate the ball’s position relative to the paddle to determine its new trajectory.

For example, suppose the paddle occupies five vertical pixels. If the ball strikes the middle pixel, it travels horizontally. If it strikes one pixel above the middle, it moves upward at approximately five degrees. Two pixels above produces ten degrees. The same idea applies below the center, except the ball moves downward. This is a simple way to add a little variety to the game without requiring complicated mathematics.

XOR drawing also gives us a way to avoid flicker when drawing. Instead of clearing the entire screen, we can erase the old objects by drawing them again. Then we update their coordinates and draw them at their new positions. This approach avoids repeatedly blanking the entire display and generally produces smoother animation.

However, there is a catch. Remember that drawing a sprite sets VF when pixels are erased? When we intentionally erase the old sprites, VF may also become one. That won’t indicate a collision. It simply means the XOR operation did exactly what we wanted. Consequently, we ignore VF during the erase pass. We only examine it when performing the drawing operation intended to detect a collision. Another important detail is that VF is updated by each sprite instruction. If you draw the ball and then draw a paddle, the second drawing operation overwrites VF. Therefore, you need to test or save VF immediately after the relevant instruction.

How Fast Is CHIP-8?

The original CHIP-8 interpreter ran on a 1970s microprocessor, so nobody was expecting spectacular performance. Modern computers can execute CHIP-8 instructions almost instantaneously. However, running the interpreter as fast as possible would make many old games unplayable.

CHIP-8 has two timers, a delay timer and a sound timer, that decrement at 60 Hz when they are nonzero. Programs can use the delay timer to control animation independently of the interpreter’s instruction execution rate. For example:

v0 := 2
delay := v0
: wait
v0 := delay
if v0 != 0 then jump wait

This waits until the delay timer reaches zero. With a 60 Hz timer, two ticks correspond to approximately 33 milliseconds, or 30 frames per second.

Octo also lets you adjust the interpreter’s execution speed. This is important because CHIP-8 never had a single universally standardized instruction execution rate. Different historical implementations ran at different speeds, and programs sometimes depended on those differences. If you run the interpreter too slowly, the game may become sluggish. If you run it too quickly, the game may run much faster than intended.

For our Pong game, the delay timer provides the primary frame pacing, so the exact instruction execution rate is less critical. However, the interpreter still needs to execute enough instructions between timer ticks to complete each frame. There is also an interesting interaction between interpreter speed and display behavior. Some CHIP-8 implementations synchronize drawing operations with the display refresh, while others don’t. These differences can affect animation smoothness and the apparent speed of a program.

If you’re experimenting with Octo, it’s worth adjusting the speed settings to see how they affect the game.

Everything Old…

CHIP-8 is almost fifty years old, but the underlying idea remains familiar. Consider the Java Virtual Machine. Java source code is compiled into bytecode, which executes on a virtual machine rather than directly on the host processor. CHIP-8 does essentially the same thing at a much smaller scale. Of course, the JVM is vastly more sophisticated. It supports a large instruction set, complex data types, object-oriented programming, garbage collection, security mechanisms, and often just-in-time compilation. Before that, the UCSD P-code system offered a bigger abstraction for early computers.

CHIP-8 has only sixteen 8-bit registers, a few dozen instructions, and a 64-by-32 monochrome display. But all of these systems attempt to separate the programmer’s view of the machine from the actual hardware. CHIP-8 also demonstrates how much can be accomplished with very little. Its instruction set is small enough to learn in an afternoon, and writing an interpreter for it is a reasonable weekend project.

If you want to understand virtual machines, emulators, or even the design of instruction sets, CHIP-8 is a particularly approachable place to start. And if nothing else, it’s a reminder that you don’t need millions of lines of code, gigabytes of memory, or a graphics processor to write a video game. It has even inspired some newer systems.
