item.title: Why Engineers are Forced to Create Junk Designs - Hack a Day
item.description:
It’s become a bit of a platitude to state that products were manufactured better in ‘the olden days’, but as [The Meandrous Engineer] covers in a recent video essay, the truth is a lot more greyscale and nuanced than something so trite.

The very short version is that it is the dominant culture of a nation in which products are manufactured that determines how many shortcuts and potential product life-shortening decisions are made. This same culture works its way down into company culture, including the engagement of the so-called C-suite with the engineers and folk who keep the now mostly automated manufacturing lines running, as well as vice-versa.

Old-school die-cast models and incandescent light bulbs saw their own series of manufacturing shortcuts, including a pre-World War 2 scandal about the artificial limiting of the lifespan of lightbulbs so that customers would buy more of them. This foreshadows what happened as soon as plastics and computer-aided design and manufacturing came on the scene.

Post-WW2, people like W. Edwards Deming were welcome guests in Japan and other rebuilding nations, introducing the Lean method of manufacturing which was at the time not deemed desirable in a post-war USA. For Japan, South Korea and other nations in the region this meant a boom in manufacturing, with a quality level that would ultimately trounce that of their Western equivalents.

The argument here is that Japan’s culture of efficiency, of respect for materials and loyalty both to one’s company and its workers is why this method produces much better results, with better working conditions than in nations with a different culture. This is exemplified by e.g. former Nintendo president [Satoru Iwata] taking a 50% pay cut in 2014 rather than lay off any people.

Although plastics and automated manufacturing with CAD/CAM catch a lot of flak, ultimately it’s about how these tools are used. Cheaper manufacturing and more versatile materials have made life much cheaper and more convenient for many of us, while also allowing for us hobbyists to make projects that would otherwise be impossible, including sending off a KiCad project plus BOM and 3D model for an enclosure to print, extrude or mill to have it produced for effectively peanuts.

If we do want to counteract this penny pinching by certain companies, we need to do more than just voting with our wallets. We also need to understand how these products are made, whether a certain choice like plating a car’s lug nut to make it seem better than it is good or bad. Here the right to repair movement has a lot in common, as it pushes a modicum of responsibility on to the customer to understanding fairly low-level details about a product, rather than to be just a consumer who is happy to e-waste when it breaks and buy a new gadget or appliance.

item.title: This Coffee Machine is DOOMed - Hack a Day
item.description:
Somehow, seeing DOOM on things that were never meant to run DOOM never gets old. It’s probably hard to get further into the “never meant to run DOOM” weeds than a coffee maker, but [Robin M.] has done it, and tells you exactly how in his excellent write-up. It adds a new dimension to hard mode — try and play while you’re waiting for your morning coffee.

Of course [Robin] doesn’t start with just any coffee machine; most sensible percolators won’t have any silicon capable of executing code, much less gaming on. The Spengler PSL50 machine [Robin] is hacking is a smart device with a Linux computer inside, although in this case there’s a point to having the smarts, as it’s meant to be a self-serve, pay-to-drink coffee kiosk. Handling payments and the touchscreen menus seems like justification enough for a microprocessor.

As you might expect, all the ‘smarts’ of this coffee maker are on the touchscreen module which aside from the brains of the operation — i.MX 6 ARM Cortex A9 processor — happens to have a handy a debug port. With just a little probing to find the right pins, he gets a console connection via that debug port to the 2013-era Linux build that runs the device, and then it’s off to the races. To make life even easier for [Robin], there was no uboot password set, nor any protections. So a simple setnv gets him into an sh prompt, and then he’s set. As for DOOM, he’s using fbDOOM, a version that renders directly to the framebuffer, and compiles it as a self-contained binary so he doesn’t have to care that everything on the Linux system is 13 years out of date.

Spengler made hacking this device relatively easy with their almost complete lack of security, and the resulting project is well documented, well executed, and tickles our funny bones the same way seeing DOOM on a toaster did. We haven’t covered DOOM on a refrigerator but it’s only a matter of time before the whole kitchen is killing demons, including the thermostat in the hall.

Thanks to [robidev] for the tip!

item.title: Print & Place: Add Embedded Electronics While FDM Printing - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although combining electronics and 3D-printed structures is fairly common, this usually entails some level of manual assembly. This contrasts strongly with the Print & Place approach demonstrated by [Oliver Child] et al. in their research article titled Print & Place: Using a 3D printer for Continuous Assembly of Electronic Devices.

An accompanying video is also provided which covers all the basics and showing a few ways in which a regular FDM printer can be used without modifications to embed these components. Rather than requiring a custom tool head the thermoplastic is used as a temporary adhesive to pick up parts that are placed in a printed tray elsewhere on the build plate.

This parts tray is created parametrically before being printed. Following this an operator has to populate this tray with the requisite parts so that the print head can pick them up when they are needed. This is done during the printing of the actual parts, with regular G-code added to move the head over to the needed part before using a bit of extruded plastic to adhere to it and lift it to its new home.

Subsequently these parts can be printed over to fully embed them, with this method supporting a range of parts. In the three demonstrations everything from small pre-populated PCBs to strips of conductive wire and braid were used together with rivets to provide paths between conductive traces.

Of course, with this being an open loop system you can expect many of the typical issues here, ranging from pick failures, placement misalignment and contact inconsistencies, as the authors encountered during their experiments. Here one could conceivably pitch adding a camera system as on typical pick & place machines to add a feedback loop that the firmware could then use for adjustments and to signal the human operator to assist.

item.title: Watching the Watchers - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although it used to be a much more rare event, now almost any time at dawn or dusk, provided clear weather, a human observer can walk outside, look up, and spot an artificial satellite passing overhead. This has caused some consternation among astronomers who have another source of pollution to deal with in their data, but has benefited society in other ways such as more reliable internet and better weather predictions. To keep an eye on what exactly is passing overhead, take a look at this tool built by [Armaan].

The browser-based satellite tracker uses simplified perturbations models (SGP4) to model the passes of every satellite that has passed a given location on Earth in the past seven days. The modeling is all done locally within the user’s browser, and can even be self-hosted through a fairly simple method that involves forking the project with a tool called Vercel. Not only does this tool find the satellite passes for that given location, though, but it also automatically downloads any imagery that those satellites sent back down to Earth.

The project itself is open source, so users can engage with the code without using Vercel if they choose. Beyond just checking out what happened to fly overhead in the last few days and checking out weather data without needing your own satellite dish to download the data yourself, this could also be useful for radio operators looking to make contacts with satellite repeaters or those wanting to keep tabs on crewed satellites like the International Space Station while it still remains in orbit.

item.title: Gesture Controls With Only a Camera - Hack a Day
item.description:
Back in 2002, [Takahiro Yonemura] and others built a system that used a single webcam-like device to track a user’s hand and generate inputs for a computer. Given that this was more than 20 years ago, the technological limitations were much greater than they are today. It wasn’t until nearly a decade later that we got something like the Microsoft Kinect, and even now many VR and gesture controls require something more than a simple camera. Although [Takahiro Yonemura]’s original paper (Japanese, Google Translate link) is now many decades old, he’s recently picked the project back up and used it to develop this game.

The original system worked by attempting to automatically identify the user’s fingers and head. The team had focused on user inputs for standard PCs, drawing characters in the air and allowing the software to interpret them and pass them to a computer. In the modern iteration the scope is slimmed down a bit. The system instead detects an open or closed hand, and can recognize when it leaves the camera’s view. For the game built around this concept, the player controls a dragon who whips his tail around a map. Closing and opening a hand generates a click in the game, and moving a hand off-screen pauses the game.

Although the game has relatively simple controls, these types of games can be quite fun and popular. From the video clip on the Steam page it looks like [Takahiro] is having plenty of fun playing it. Although we’d prefer it be open source so others can experiment with his gesture controls, we can also experiment with other camera-only gesture controls like this project which allows the user to move and interact with 3D objects in a virtual space.

item.title: How CRISPR Could Mark Mutated Cancer Cells for Termination - Hack a Day
item.description:
Over the past decades CRISPR, short for “clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats”, has become somewhat of a household name, holding the promise of directly addressing genetic mutations by effectively removing, silencing, or even fixing them. Yet the original purpose of CRISPR is slightly less cute and cuddly: the evolutionary origin of these DNA sequences is that of a core component of the prokaryotic immune system.

In most medical applications today we only try to use CRISPR to detect sequences and then apply enzymes such as the well-known Cas9 to cut DNA at specific locations in the process of gene-editing. In a recent study (paywalled, bioRxiv pre-print) by Jingkun Zheng et al. in Nature such benign enzymes are dropped for Cas12a2, which turns a detection event into the release of a DNA-destroy enzyme as the molecular equivalent of a guided missile.

The pitched use case here is the detection of cancer-cell specific mutations in the DNA, following which the tumor cells will be instantly shredded from the inside. This could theoretically provide a cure for many cancer types, but should we expect to see this kind of therapy approved any time soon?

The Original CRISPR

What we call CRISPR is quite literally what the name says: clustered occurrences of repeats with spacers made of genetic code fragments in the prokaryotic DNA. These can be considered to be the memory of the prokaryotic immune system, with genetic sequences from e.g. invasive viruses and bacteriophages embedded in the organism’s own DNA as these spacers.

In prokaryotic organisms like bacteria these CRISPR arrays are accompanied by multiple CRISPR-associated systems (CAS, or Cas): genes that are translated into proteins which are associated with these CRISPR arrays.  Of these, CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) is a protein that that performs double-strand DNA cutting action when provided with a transcribed RNA copy (crRNA) of the CRISPR spacer in question after it has been attached to a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM). This PAM ensures that the original sequence in the CRISPR locus is not attacked.

Directly attacking the genetic material of an intruder in this manner is somewhat more aggressive than the comparable system eukaryotes called RNA interference. This merely silences target mRNA genes, which incidentally is a problem with mRNA-based vaccines and thus require a special coating of the mRNA particles.

Cas12a2

Although we could conceivably use Cas9 for an anti-cancer therapy as well by damaging the DNA with a double-strand DNA break and pray it’s enough, the Cas12a protein lineage offers us an even more suitable protein, since it’s less complex and yet much more versatile than Cas9. The first step remains the same, with a transcription of the target RNA fragment containing the mutated gene’s signature with PAM used to track down any affected cells in the patient’s body.

The variant of Cas12a that has received a lot of attention lately is Cas12a2, which as Oleg Dmytrenko et al. reported in 2023 induces cell death. This effectively means that the infected bacteria commits suicide if it detects via Cas12a2 that it has become infected, destroying itself before it can be used by e.g. a bacteriophage to replicate itself and infect the rest of the colony.

How Cas12a2 exactly achieves the shredding of the host cell’s DNA is elucidated in a 2026 study by Paul Scholz et al. in Nature. The simple version is that rather than performing a targeted cut of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), Cas12a2 continues making cuts to the host’s dsDNA and chromatin until said cell enters apoptosis.

Crucial here in the context of using Cas12a2 for cancer treatments is that it accurately recognizes the crRNA sequence and does not have a high off-target activation rate. In this study by Scholz et al. in human cells they found minimal off-target activation. This finding makes sense in that bacteria wouldn’t want to needlessly self-terminate due to a Cas12a2 nuclease having a bad day.

TP53

With the above background information we can now understand the June 2026 study by Jingkun Zeng et al., with the most interesting aspect of their study being the chosen target gene for an anti-cancer treatment. This being the tumor protein 53 (TP53) gene, also known as p53.

This particular gene is a regulatory transcription factor that is classified as a tumor-suppressing gene. It does this through multiple mechanisms, including:

  • Activating DNA repair proteins in case of DNA damage.
  • Halting the cell cycle upon damage to allow for repairs.
  • Initiating apoptosis if the damage is too severe.
  • Pushing cells into senescence once the telomeres have become too short.

It’s known that this particular gene is mutated in a variety of ways in about half of all analyzed cancers, making it a solid target once you know the specific mutation via a biopsy or such method. In this study an in-vivo study was also performed using mice models featuring lung tumors.

By using the same liquid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulation method referenced earlier for e.g. SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines, the Cas12a2 protein was encoded as mRNA and injected into the mice, with the designed target on TP53 packaged alongside it in the LNP. Theoretically the LNPs would deliver the mRNA to the cells, whose cellular machinery would then assemble the Cas12a2 protein, following which the targeting information would then allow the protein to scan and assess the cell for the particular TP53 mutation.

Not Quite Prime Time

Few things are easy or straightforward in medical sciences, with this being sadly no exception. Although in the in-vivo experiment the mouse tumors got suppressed compared to the controls – indicating that the Cas12a2 mRNA and tagging payload were being delivered and working – the ultimate effect was more suppressive than curative.

Especially for advanced tumors the lung tumor burden wasn’t noticeably reduced, which could be due to a variety of reasons. For this reason this study should probably be treated as yet another step forward in what could one day become another very effective anti-cancer treatment, right along with e.g. immunotherapy.

Perhaps the biggest take-away here is that within the realm of molecular biology there are many fascinating constructs and mechanisms that are just waiting for us to discover and use them, whether it is to cure diseases or to fix genetic defects including very lethal ones.

item.title: Simulating and Visualising the Central Limit Theorem - Hack a Day
item.description:
Statistics is one of those fields which people tend to love or hate when they’re confronted with it during their school time. Although incredibly useful and even essential in many fields, including finance and engineering, it’s not always easy to grasp even the basics such as those pertaining to distributions. The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) is an essential element there, which [Greg Foletta] tried to make easier to comprehend using some code samples and visualizations.

The essential summary of the CLT is that if you take the mean of each sample in a set, once you have enough (>30) samples, the distribution of the sample means approaches a normal distribution. This is quite the theorem to put out there, with the supporting proof and explanations on e.g. Wikipedia being very mathematics-heavy.

We’d be remiss not to also mention the excellent [3Blue1Brown] video on the topic, which has even snazzier visualizations if you’re more into learning in that fashion. Even if you don’t think that you need to learn statistics and how distributions work, chances are that you’ll come across a situation where it could have come in handy, or at least have deepened your understanding of a topic like the probability of something happening.

item.title: Have You Ever Heard Of the Lobo MAX-80? - Hack a Day
item.description:
[Adrian Black]’s enthusiasm is palpable as he shows off something truly unusual: a Lobo MAX-80 computer from 1982. To call this machine rare would be an understatement, as the company folded soon after its release. The one shown here is the first one [Adrian] has ever seen, never mind that he had never even heard of it before.

The MAX-80 was a Z80-based computer that was CP/M and LDOS compatible. As [Adrian] puts it, many companies and innovative products came and went during this time period. There was so much, and most of it has simply disappeared.

He was able to find information about the Lobo MAX-80 from advertisements, media coverage, reviews, and more (and he has thoughtfully uploaded everything, see the video description for links) and even pieced together a short history of a company that got its start making TRS-80 and Apple II disk drives before transitioning to producing their own machine. The MAX-80 was released in 1982, but sadly the company didn’t last much longer.

After sharing what history he was able to dig up, [Adrian] opens the unit he has and goes through diagnostics. It’s actually in remarkably good shape, and he’s eventually able to get it to actually boot into CP/M.

There’s still more work needed before he can put it through its paces, but getting a formerly completely unknown machine from the 80s operational is pretty wild. Watch the whole thing in the video below.

item.title: Hacking the Sidekick in 2026 - Hack a Day
item.description:
The early 2000s saw a Cambrian Explosion of form factors for mobile devices, and one of the most feature-rich phones of the time was the Danger Hiptop, better known as the T-Mobile Sidekick. [ashe] wanted to get the phone going again, which took some sleuthing.

While not advertised as such at the time, the Hiptop was primarily a client for web apps from the Danger servers. So, when Danger was shuttered, so were most of the phone’s features. [ashe] was able to track down the SDK for the device’s Java-based OS, but to get any programs running on an actual device, they needed a developer key. After finding a few more clues, they were able to use CADO-NFS, a general number sieve, to crack the 512-bit encryption scheme for the system’s developer key and generate a new one for their device.

[ashe] ported a visual novel to their Sidekick 3 with their new key, saying “Endings arrive as real Sidekick text notifications, using an emulated modem.” Work continues on the Re:Danger server to bring other functionality back, including plans to spin up a GSM network to connect an actual Sidekick. The server replication only works with an emulated Sidekick so far. They did include a Sidekick emulator on their site if you’d like to try it yourself.

If you’re a fan of the form factor but would like something with a bit more power, we’ve seen a UMPC inspired by the Hiptop/Sidekick a few years back.

item.title: Robotic Car Charger Locks On With Suction - Hack a Day
item.description:
Not only does [Mew463]’s robotic car charger take care of plugging in his vehicle for him, it has some really clever features that are great to see in action.

We’ve seen a rover-platform-based robotic car charger before, but what’s different here is that [Mew463]’s robot isn’t particularly husky. It’s designed to be low-profile, snug right up against the vehicle during use, and park itself against the wall when not.

As an added touch, one doesn’t even have to manually open the car’s charge port door. The robot uses API calls that — once it confirms the vehicle is parked and not in use — unlocks and opens the charge port remotely. People used to be able to pop the charge port with a plain old wireless replay attack, but an API is the better way to go about it.

Four Mecanum wheel and LiDAR get the robot into more or less the right position, then fine-tuning happens with the help of an onboard camera and a ChARuco board pattern on the car just under the charging port.

Once things are lined up just right, the charger moves forward to plug into the car. Here’s where [Mew463] had to get clever, because plugging in a car charger actually takes a decent amount of force, and the robot is not particularly heavy. The solution is two suction cups that anchor the robot to the car as a gear assembly pushes the charger home. We really like how the robot snugs right up, so while the car is charging there isn’t a big thing in the way.

Disconnecting is the reverse of the process, and for the robot to park itself again it simply swivels the camera backward so it can see the marker on the wall without the whole robot having to turn around. It’s all very slick, and you can watch it in action in the video embedded below.

item.title: Free Your Harley From The Dealer - Hack a Day
item.description:
Vehicles have come with diagnostic ports for many years now, and there are a host of easily available tools to interrogate them. Despite that, there are still proprietary aspects that remain out of reach. For one of them there may be a way to know more though, as [Daniel Henzulea] has made what he describes to us as a dealer-grade diagonostic tool for Harley-Davidson motorcycles. These machines don’t come with the familiar OBD-II port.

The Harley diagnostic port is a custom six-pin socket that carries a CAN bus. Into this is plugged a CAN transceiver, and to that is connected one of the Xtensa-based ESP32s. The magic then is in the software, which exposes and makes accessible every function. What used to be closed source and prohibitively expensive, is now open to all.

You might not be surprised to read that this isn’t the first time we’ve featured a project diving into a Harley-Davidson’s data bus.

Header: Reinhold Möller, CC BY-SA 4.0.

item.title: From Phone, To SDR, No Extra Hardware - Hack a Day
item.description:
One of the more exciting recent developments has been the discovery that many radio chips used in common and cheap wireless network interfaces, microcontrollers, LoRa interfaces and others can be persuaded to give access to their baseband data streams This gives them full SDR functionality, which on cheap devices is hugely interesting. Continuing that trend and taking it to a new height is [Logan Zarov], who’s converted an LG D325 Android phone into a wideband receiver with very minor modification indeed.

The phone is rooted and runs LineageOS as you might expect, and there’s a modem firmware update to supply the SDR baseband magic. There’s also a mod for an antenna wire. Where this becomes especially interesting is in its receive frequency range. The modem talks in the GHz, but this radio receives in the MHz, it can pick up shortwave. This is achieved by using the Bluetooth radio as a local oscillator, oddly in a similar manner to that we suggested a few weeks ago.

This is hackery at its most epic, we love it, and look forward to the similar hacks which will certainly follow. There’s a video below the break, and you can see it doing its thing.

item.title: UDP Broadcasting Meets the More Focused Multicasting - Hack a Day
item.description:
After previously exploring the basics of UDP broadcasting, why IPv4 subnets are an exciting feature that you really want to dive into, as well as the contentious topic of IPv6, there are still plenty of elephants to admire and cans of sardines to crack open. One of them being the topic of broadcasting versus multicasting, which at first glance sounds rather similar and may even have some wondering why you’d even bother with multicasting if you can just send-and-forget with IPv4 broadcast address.

Of course, we already found out that IPv4 broadcast addresses come in a few flavors, and that’s before you start even considering the implications of subnets and routing limits. When we then consider that in IPv6 broadcast addresses were dropped completely in favor of link-local multicast addresses, and that IPv4 also supports multicast, then this raises the question whether using IPv4 multicast’s own take on ‘link-local’ doesn’t make more sense.

Or perhaps more succinctly put, is IPv4’s take on link-local broadcasting as straightforward as IPv6’s?

CIDR

Before diving into multicasting, there is one important topic that has been absent from the IPv4 discussions so far. This being that of CIDR, which stands for Classless Inter-Domain Routing. This forms part of IPv4’s evolution, with CIDR in 1993 replacing the previous classful network architecture, with the goal to slow the growth of routing tables and with it IPv4 address exhaustion on the Internet. It’s also the reason for some of IPv4’s quirks.

The most obvious implication of CIDR is that it is the reason why we write IPv4 addresses the way that we do today, yet the classes from classful networking have left their traces to this day, including the reason why some companies hold large chunks of classful allocations. This is where Class A, B and C addresses come from, with Class D address being the multicast range.

A lot of IPv4 addresses were incidentally wasted with the classful system because the three available classes provide blocks that are effectively always unfortunately sized. CIDR addresses this with subnets, creating CIDR blocks that can thus be more appropriately sized to the target application or customer instead of handing a company a small 8-bit Class A or a very large (216) Class B block.

Although I would never claim to be an expert on this subject matter, CIDR would seem to be a solid improvement here that probably postponed the death of IPv4 to – at this rate – probably a few days after the heat death of the universe. It’s apparently such a good idea that even IPv6 uses CIDR.

IPv4 Multicast

If we now look at the IPv4 multicast addresses, a lot becomes suddenly clear. The main thing probably why IPv4 multicast addresses all are in the 224.*.*.* to 239.*.*.* range, as this is the pre-CIDR multicast range.

Next it’s important to note that these multicast address are sub-divided into blocks, either with a specific function or left as simply Reserved. Unless we have any pressing business outside of doing multicast things outside of a local subnetwork, the multicast address range we are interested in is thus the 224.0.0.0 to 224.0.0.255 range.

The next question then is what we can do with all of these addresses, essentially what the special meaning is that has been assigned to each of these.

That too is defined in the above referenced Wikipedia page, though one’s eyes may slide casually over to the Pv6 side to see how different it is. At first glance it would seem that in either case you can just mash in the ‘all hosts’ multicast group address, or link-local as IPv6 calls it. For IPv4 this thus means that sending a message to the 224.0.0.1 multicast address should reach every single node on the same network, with routers happily not routing it to other network segments.

To Broadcast Or To Multicast

With these findings in mind, this then leaves us with the question of why we’d bother with IPv4 broadcasting at all. Is this simply an archaic legacy from a time before multicasting became fully implemented by IPv4 software stacks, considering that it’s a technically optional feature?

Looking around for an overview of why to prefer one over the other I could not find any direct comparisons, with multicast on IPv4 seemingly almost always being used for sending to a specific group of receivers using the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP). This is quite useful for e.g. video streaming to multiple receivers and similar applications where it’s much more efficient to just duplicate the same packet a few times as it’s being routed.

IGMP contrasts with IPv6’s Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD), which is an integral part of ICMPv6 rather than an IP encapsulation protocol, so one could presume there to be some more overhead to IPv4 multicast compared to its broadcast features.

IPv4’s Three Options

Thus, after all is said and done we end up with a grand total of three options in IPv4 if we want to do UDP broadcasting for service discovery or other purposes:

  • Determining the interface’s broadcast address and broadcasting on that.
  • Use the local broadcast address 255.255.255.255.
  • Use the multicast address for all nodes: 224.0.0.1.

It would seem that the first option is what most guides seem to suggest, though many also will happily tell you to always assume a /24 network, so your mileage will vary heavily there.

The second option is obviously braindead simple, and actually is another fun pre-CIDR legacy item as the standard broadcast address, established before directed broadcast became a thing. This is probably why there’s the implicit threat that a sysadmin will kick in your door if you so much as think about using it.

Finally multicast to all nodes as the IPv4 take on link-local multicast would seem to be much closer to the local broadcast address in its basic usage. Of course, this all assumes that IGMP is supported and functioning correctly.

Take-Away For Now

After spending some time researching all of these options I cannot say that from a software developer point of view I feel very reassured about which option is ‘the best’. While in IPv6 it’s very much a ‘take it or leave it’ kind of deal with its take on broadcasting, in IPv4 you get the legacy option, the directed ‘legacy’ option and the shiny new IGMP-based multicast option, all of which seem to come with their own set of issues, advantages and potential complications.

In a way I would say that a directed broadcast option is the preferred approach for something like service discovery, to which I can also add that there’s been a response to my bug ticket on the Poco Project tracker regarding it not reliably returning an interface’s netmask, never mind its broadcast address. This issue should be addressed in the upcoming 1.16.0 release, with a workaround possible until then.

Directed broadcast has the definite advantage that you know which interface you’re sending the broadcast on, which makes it easier to sort through responses. This is also rather part of the original design of NyanSD, so retaining that feature without in-depth refactoring is a nice benefit.

Of course, it’s quite possible that I misunderstood something here, and multicast in IPv4 is actually the cat’s pajamas. Feel free to sound off in the comments with your thoughts on your favorite IPv4 broadcast method.

item.title: The Sounds of the World, One Random Album at a Time - Hack a Day
item.description:
In the streaming era it’s easy to forget that there’s still a lot of stuff being broadcast over the radio for anyone who cares enough to dial in their receiver. Give me an antenna big enough and a tower on which to place it, and I shall listen to the world.

Of course, so you can’t actually listen to everything being blasted out all over the planet yourself. But if you’d like to at least have a little taste, check out Impermanence Series A — a project by [Sam Scorsby] that randomly combines bits and pieces of audio pulled down from shortwave and FM broadcasts with some web streams, live microphones, and even a bit of the Internet Archive each day into a one of a kind album. We’re not sure we’d call it music, exactly. But it’s certainly fascinating to listen to, a bit like randomly spinning the dial on a planet-wide radio receiver.

[Sam] has shared the Python scripts that pull together each day’s album, and he’s not shy about the fact that the project was created with the help of artificial intelligence tools. In fact, that’s sort of the point. [Sam] puts himself somewhere in the middle when it comes to the current debate over AI, and acknowledges that while computers are good at processing raw data, it still takes a human touch to put it all into context.

So each day [Sam] will listen to the latest computer-generated album and pick his favorite tracks, and once the project has run its course, he’ll put together a human-curated “Best Of” collection. Man and machine working together, each doing what they do best.

We know something of opinionated folks on the Internet, and our experience tells us that Impermanence Series A is unlikely to change anyone’s minds when it comes to AI. But we do appreciate the thoughtful approach [Sam] has taken with the project, and look forward to hearing what he comes up with in the end.

item.title: Is This The Only Instrument You Need? - Hack a Day
item.description:
When working on an electronic project it’s likely you will find yourself working with a variety of different instruments, be they logic analysers, oscilloscopes, or whatever. These can take up a lot of space, not to mention cost a bundle of cash. [Max.K] came up with PicoLab as a solution, it’s an all-in-one box containing a four-channel oscilloscope, eight-channel logic analyser, GPIOs, a data logger, and serial, SPI, and i2C interfaces. There’s even an adjustable power supply!

Behind it all is an RP2350, in its larger package with more pins, coupled to some custom interface and protection circuitry. Perhaps the cleverest part is its interface, which it serves as a web site on the network card it exposes through the USB port. Any OS that supports a web browser and USB networking can thus use this thing. You can find all the code in a GitHub repository, should you wish to have a go at building one yourself. We like this idea.

item.title: Putting a MiSTer Marquee on a Better Display - Hack a Day
item.description:
Some MiSTer users put a small secondary “marquee” display on the FPGA board that can show information about the system such as the currently loaded core and what game it happens to be running. Generally these take the form of a small monochrome OLED display, likely the one most of us have sitting in a parts bin somewhere.

But [Erico Mendonca] wanted a something with a bit more style, so he’s come up with a firmware for the ESP32-C3 that connects to MiSTer’s existing secondary display protocol but works with slightly more visually impressive panels such as the round GC9A01 that so many hackers have been playing with as of late. If the whole circular display thing isn’t your…thing, you can even run the firmware on the Cheap Yellow Display for a turn-key rectangular experience.

Because [Erico] didn’t want to fiddle with anything on the MiSTer side of the equation, his firmware has to do the heavy lifting when it comes to the art that shows on the display. So there’s a web-based editor that lets you put together your own artwork to show on the marquee based on what command the MiSTer has actually sent out. Flashing the firmware on the ESP32 can be done through the browser as well, as is becoming increasingly common these days, making it relatively easy to get this project up and running.

With this project it’s also possible to control multiple client displays over WiFi from one system, just in case you wanted to show off what console you were booting up in multiple places.

We’re fans of the round display here at Hackaday, so it’s been great to see more folks putting them to use as of late.

item.title: Replicating the Color-Changing Effect of the Lycurgus Cup - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although most archaeological finds from ancient civilizations aren’t quite as exciting as what you might expect from the movies, occasionally you come across something that’s truly special. The Lycurgus Cup is one of those, with the 3rd or 4th century CE glass cup and its incredible detail surviving likely because it ended up in church treasuries after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Now its almost magical dichroic glass effect has been recreated in a modern take by researchers at the University of Sheffield.

Dichroic glass takes on a different color depending on the lighting conditions, with the Lycurgus cup appearing to be green glass when lit from the front and red when light passes through it from behind. This serves to give the portrayed scene – of the demise of King Lycurgus from Greek mythology – an extra boost with the right lighting.

The cause of this dichroic effect in this ancient marvel of glass work was unknown for the longest time, but research on a fragment of the glass revealed that it contains nanoparticles of both gold and silver. Since then a number of researchers have recreated this dichroic glass, with [Lars Kool] et al. using FDM 3D printing to create objects embedded with the same nanoparticles that also display this effect.

Where this work by the University of Sheffield differs is in that it creates the effect not only in glass, but also creating a piece of art in the form of a modified Atlas statue to use it. The resulting dichroic effect is rather similar, which isn’t too shocking since unlike over 1,600 years ago we can now literally see and measure nanoparticles in glass, while adding exact amounts of each to pure glass.

Here’s to raising a dichroic glass cup to bridging the millennia with recreated luxury glass recipes.

item.title: An Attempt at a Useful Desktop OS For Microcontrollers - Hack a Day
item.description:
We’re living at an interesting time here in 2026, when microcontrollers are becoming powerful enough to surpass the capabilities of “real” computers from a time when those real computers were starting to become useful. We’ve seen plenty of microcontrollers emulating machines from the 1990s, but what if instead they were giving all their power to the OS? It’s a question [Thomas] is trying to answer with SylphideOS, a general purpose GUI operating system aimed at multiple microcontroller platforms.

On the surface it has a GUI that appears to owe a lot to the early Macintosh machines, but underneath it has the FreeRTOS kernel, something that has been around for quite a while. You can argue among yourselves as to whether this make it an OS in its own right or a FreeRTOS distro. Aside from driving a screen through a framebuffer it also has the hardware interfaces you’d expect, for keyboard and storage. There’s support for RP2350 and selected ESP32 platforms so far, as well as an emulator.

We have already seen a few operating systems for microcontrollers that provide a user interface for a binary bootloader rather than persisting under whatever programs are running, so this marks an interesting departure. Only time will tell if it becomes a success, but perhaps it’s one to watch.

item.title: Emulate the 486 in Your Browser - Hack a Day
item.description:
You might fondly remember the days of the Intel 486, but you probably don’t have one on your desk anymore. If you’d like to emulate that classic hardware, you can now do it in your browser, thanks to [Jan de Jager].

What [Jan] has built is a 100% browser-based emulator for an Intel 80486DX2-66 PC. Obviously, it’s not just a CPU that’s being emulated here—[Jan] has gone so far as to throw in the motherboard and ISA/VLB adapter card emulation necessary to make this a real and functioning computer that runs inside a solitary browser tab.

It’s all written in ES6 JavaScript. It will happily run SeaBIOS, VGA BIOS, FreeDOS 1.3, and a whole bunch of classic games, like Wolfenstein 3D, Duke Nukem, and DOOM. There’s even a control panel where you can configure the PC how you like, from storage to expansion cards and all the rest.

Once upon a time an emulator was an application you had to download and run, hoping all the while that your new machine had enough grunt to emulate the classic hardware of your desires. These days, we have endless piles of CPU cycles to throw at everything and you can do it all within a browser. Or even on a tiny microcontroller, if you feel like it!

item.title: SLAM Navigation For an Arduino Powered Car - Hack a Day
item.description:
There are plenty of “robot” projects out there that are really just a small remote control platform of some sort. We often like to think of robots of having some sort of autonomy though. [Luca Fagioli] demonstrates a great example of this with his explorer robot that uses Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) to navigate its environment.

The robot is a built on a small plastic chassis, with one gear motor per drive wheel. Running the show is an Arduino Uno R4 Wi-Fi, paired with the Sensor Shield 5.0 and an L298N motor driver board. There’s also an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor module onboard, mounted atop an SG-90 servo motor so it can be panned around. The ultrasonic sensor determines the range between the robot and surrounding walls, and a map is constructed at the same time as the robot is localizing itself within it. There are also infrared sensors on the bottom of the robot for detecting tape marks on the floor for checkpointing purposes.

Often, SLAM mapping is done with advanced laser rangefinders or time of flight sensors, but there are many ways to go about it as this project demonstrates. We’ve even seen it done in a distributed manner with coordinated drones combining their efforts. Overall, it’s a highly useful technique for robot navigation and wayfinding.

item.title: Hacking a Marine Radio Dish - Hack a Day
item.description:
Having watched some fun videos on repurposed satellite dishes on YouTube, [Melan] wanted to get in on the action, managed to source an Intellian i4 — a dish built for marine use — and set about hacking it.

[Melan] first needed to convince the antenna that it was still on a boat by using an RP2040 microcontroller and an RS-422 module to send NMEA sentences. This was necessary to tell the i4 the “heading” of the “boat”, even though [Melan] was really using the rig stationary on land. From there, a simple email to the company itself sufficed to get the Intellian software running on the antenna.

But could it be controlled without the software?. Sniff the communications between the software and the Antenna Control Unit, and decompile the code. This done, it was relatively straightforward to put together a protocol description and figure out how to command the antenna where to point simply by issuing commands for azimuth and elevation.

We’ve featured other great bits of satellite equipment before, like this truck tracker teardown from a few years ago. If you’ve got some nice equipment on the bench that listens in on (or transmits out to) birds in space, don’t hesitate to let us know on the tipsline.

item.title: Airborne Particle Monitoring, the BIG way - Hack a Day
item.description:
Airborne micro particles can be a significant health hazard in a workshop, and thus it’s important to maintain a high standard of ventilation. But monitoring their concentration is also important, and thus there exists a range of sensors to help keep you safe. [WeSpeakEnglish] has taken this idea to the MAX, with a PM2.5 sensor that drives a very large wall mounted display. You’ll never be uncertain what the level is now!

The standout feature of this thing is a huge addressable LED seven segment display PCB, upon the back of which sits a tiny Seeed Studio Xiao board to which the particle sensor is hooked up. The software displays the particle count, and handily changes the colour as the number creeps upwards. Meanwhile should you wish to log the readings, the USB exposes a serial port upon which they are placed.

We can see this is a useful project for anywhere that is likely to have a high particle count, but it’s worth noting also that a large 7-segment display with an ESP32 board attached could have plenty of other uses. Meanwhile this is a nicely finished air quality monitor, but it’s certainly not the first we’ve seen.

item.title: How a Single University Project Started Everything - Hack a Day
item.description:
If we care to cast an eye over the history of ubiquitous personal computing as we know it today, we might immediately point at the original IBM PC. After all, for most of us our machines share backward compatibility in some form through multiple generations back to that original box from 1981.

But if we look at the things we use today and take for granted, from laser printers to graphics cards to the routers which power most of the Internet, they’re not from IBM at all. At the recent Vintage Computing Festival Berlin, [Michael Engel] delivered a talk naming a surprising progenitor for much of that technology, none other than Sun Microsystems.

It all starts with [Andy Bechtolsheim], famously Sun’s co-founder, when at the end of the 1970s he was a postgraduate at Stanford University. Working on the Stanford University Network — SUN — project he designed a computer to be used as a workstation on the network. The processor of choice then was Motorola’s 68000, but it lacked the MMU that would be required to run UNIX. His design had an MMU implemented externally to the 68000, with a bank of SRAM serving as the page table. This design would form the CPU board of the first Sun workstation.

The story might end there, were it not that many other companies had the same requirement, and Sun could supply them a CPU board. Silicon Graphics, the distant ancestral progenitor of your GPU, was one of them, so the first SGI workstation also had the same CPU as the first Sun. It appeared in the early Imagen laser printers too, as well as commercial AppleTalk to Ethernet bridges. Perhaps the biggest surprise is that because the original Stanford board had also been used as a router, the software for that became part of Cisco’s first product.

The video is below the break, and it’s a fascinating watch.

item.title: Where Did Your Mouse Come From? - Hack a Day
item.description:
Many readers will be familiar with Douglas Englebart’s 1968 so-called “Mother of All Demos”, in which he described many of the devices and technologies we would be using two or three decades later. Among these was a primitive computer mouse, but while famous it was by no means the earliest pointing device. At the recent Vintage Computer Festival Berlin, [Dmitriy Kostiuk] delivered a fascinating lecture of the history of the pointing device.

It’s a long video that we’ve placed below, and it’s an exhaustive examination of the topic from the earliest examples to the 1990s when mice became commoditized. It’s a surprise to find that the first pointing device was a trackball built for a 1950s Canadian warship, with a surprisingly modern-looking optical encoder. Englebart’s 1966 wooden block with its pair of wheels and potentiometers had a less-well-known and much more stylish competitor in the same year from Telefunken.

We visit the various design iterations as the form of what we’d call a mouse today took shape. It’s unexpected to find that those Sun mice with the spotty mouse pad weren’t from Sun at all, they were from Mouse Systems. The first mice from Microsoft and Apple make an appearance, as do some awful designs for 8-bit computrs. Remembering those in particular perhaps it’s as well we didn’t have the cash to buy such a disappointing product for ourselves.

The video is long, but interesting. Give it a watch.

Header image, Douglas Englebart’s prototype, Michael Hicks, CC BY 2.0.

item.title: SIMD-accelerated Machine Vision on an ESP32-S3 - Hack a Day
item.description:
Recently [shraiwi] decided to have a bit of good nerdy fun and implement the FAST machine vision algorithm on an ESP32-S3 using its SIMD ISA. This involves using the assembly instructions for the ISA, making for an exciting opportunity to become familiar with this part of this Xtensa Lx7-based twin-core MCU.

The Features from Accelerated Segment Test (FAST) algorithm is a corner detection method that can determine with reasonable accuracy and in real-time whether a given input frame contains said corners which thus may correspond to objects and other characteristics worthy of note. This is essential for machine vision, with machine learning able to bump up its recognition accuracy even more.

Implementing this algorithm on the ESP32-S3 proved to be a bit of a challenge due to somewhat limited SIMD ISA. Missing instructions included things like comparisons between unsigned byte values, and there is no support for direct misaligned reads.

All of these required some creative coding to work around, but in the end the ESP32-S3 running at 240 MHz was able to process a VGA stream in real-time at 30 FPS. This means about a 2x speed-up over a naive implementation using only non-SIMD instructions.

If you want to play along at home, the Platform IO project is made available on GitHub.

item.title: The Oldest Windows App To Still Run On WIndows 11 - Hack a Day
item.description:
In the open source world we are used to software being compiled from source for our particular distro, so while in a few cases an ancient release may still be in use, it’s just going to run on the latest distro version. But in the Windows world it’s rare for software to come with the source, so you’re left with a binary that will only run if your Windows version has the right APIs for it. Since the more recent versions of Windows dropped 16-bit support a while back, that means there must be a hard date set on the earliest Windows GUI application that can still run today. [Enlyth] decided to investigate.

Given that the earliest API supported in WIndows 11 is the 32-bit version, the hunt led straight to either the first Windows NT release and ancestor of Windows 11, or the Win32s extension for WIndows 3.1. Thus a 1993 Win32S version of Freecell runs happily, but that want’s the end of the trail. Somewhere in the pre-release builds of Windows NT 3.1 would be the requisite binary, but there’s a snag. Early Windows NT 3.1 APIs were incompatible with later ones. This led through a lot of crashing binaries to a November 1992 version of the CD player app, that ran because it called a DLL which happens to still be present. The need for another DLL to emulate a CD drive speaks volumes about the progress of the PC world, back then they were the last word in storage but who’s got one now?

That’s the earliest official binary to run, but the story’s not quite over. Windows 11 may not have a VDM to run 16-bit apps, but there’s a WINE VDM for that. Behold, Reversi from Windows 1.01 in November 1985, in Windows 11. Your ancient software may yet be saved.

item.title: In Praise Of A Legendary Power Transistor - Hack a Day
item.description:
There are some devices which achieve electronic immortality, it’s likely that you have used a few of them yourself. The 555 timer of course, or the 741 op-amp. [ElectronicsNotes] is here with another candidate that might not have been on your mind as you read the previous sentences, and it’s a transistor. The 2N3055 is an NPN power transistor, no, THE NPN power transistor, that has found its way into an astounding array of devices over the last six decades or more.

For such a ubiquitous device one might imagine that there’s not much new to know, but the video delivers on that front. Here as well as probably for you the 3055 has always been an epitaxial device whose quirks you likely know well, but originally it was something different. It used the hometaxial construction process on its launch in the early 1960s, but in the mid 1970s it was replaced by a version with the same capabilities but using the epitaxial process. The consequent higher Ft required modifications to circuits using the device to stop unwanted oscillation.

Where this is being written there are several 2N3055s, in the by now rather old office audio amplifier, in a bench power supply, and probably elsewhere too. It’s been superseded in many ways and its TO3 case now feels antiquated, but it will probably never entirely go away. Meanwhile if you’d like to read about another iconic 1960s device that never went away, we have you covered.

Header: a really early example. Eule4404, CC BY-SA 4.0

item.title: Enable Resizable BAR on Unsupported Motherboards - Hack a Day
item.description:
Recently [Rod Burlamaqui] released the arc-rebar project on GitHub, enabling Intel GPUs to work significantly more efficiently if the system’s mainboard does not support resizable BAR. It does require a Debian or Ubuntu installation and of course a supported Intel GPU.

Although the resizable base address register (ReBAR) feature has been part of the PCIe specification for a while, its use was quite limited until Intel released its Arc series of graphic cards. These use this feature to map much more of the GPU’s video RAM (VRAM) into the PC’s address space than the standard 256 MB, assuming that the system is capable of decoding addresses above 4 GB, i.e. allow for 64-bit BARs.

For GPU manufacturers like AMD and Nvidia this wasn’t so much of an issue as their GPU designs developed in a world where ReBAR didn’t exist, while Intel’s new GPU generations were designed with ReBAR as a core feature, which naturally cripples performance if the mainboard does not have it enabled during PCIe bus enumeration.

This initramfs-based fix runs before the GPU driver loads and performs the requisite BAR configuration. In testing with an Intel Arc B580 GPU on a 2015-era Intel Xeon mainboard the difference between the default and the fixed bandwidth was a bump from a pitiful 15 GB/s to a respectable 392 GB/s, showing how this one fix can breathe new life into older systems.

item.title: Practice Japanese on an Inkplate 4Tempera eInk Device - Hack a Day
item.description:
Learning a new natural language can be a daunting proposition at the best of times, with repetition and immersion generally considered to be the best ways to build up not only vocabulary but also that innate sense for grammar and cultural details that sneak into every spoken language. Flash cards are one way to help with vocabulary and sentence building, such as [Peter Hraska]’s Enkiplate project that uses the Inkplate 4Tempera being an  interesting alternative to lugging a stack of cards with you.

Although the software also works in the browser, using the Inkplate or similar device means that you can keep it with you while it keeps track of your progress in learning the shown cards, with a starting pace of 12 cards per day to learn. It also shows you calendar items for that day and the weather using an online weather service.

Starting from basic kana, i.e. the two phonetic writing systems, the difficulty is slowly ramped up to cover kanji and then sentences. Due to the limitations of the 4Tempera’s ESP32-WROVER-E module’s local storage up to 16 flash cards can be stored at a time, with an application on a PC being necessary to obtain new cards.

item.title: Arduino Engine Runs Many Games - Hack a Day
item.description:
A few years ago, [Smashcat] ported a ZX Spectrum game called Manic Miner to the Arduino Uno. The Arduino has less memory than the original Spectrum did, so doing all this on an 8-bit microcontroller was no easy lift. Since then, parts of this original port have been adapted to produce a game engine, allowing [Smashcat] to port several other games to the Arduino Uno as well.

The engine is able to host a 2D map with the ability to scroll, at a resolution of 256×256, as well as up to nine sprites at the same time. The graphics are locked to 50 FPS, but only with a real Arduino Uno that has a crystal oscillator. Some replica boards do not have a timekeeping chip accurate enough to replicate the video signal, which is done without a framebuffer. That signal, as well as two PWM audio channels, are still generated directly as well, with only a few resistors needed to hook everything up to a monitor and a controller, including the option of using an NES controller.

With all of that running on the Arduino and it hooked up to the daughterboard that provides the controller interface as well as the resistors for the video signal to function and a driver for a speaker, the system now runs the original Manic Miner as well as three other games: Scramble, Space Invaders, and Pac Man.

The engine and the rest of the code are available on a GitHub page as well, and there’s even a WebAssembly version available to run various pieces of the software without the specific hardware. The original ZX Spectrum was an interesting machine too that still inspires builds like this, despite it being well over 40 years old now.

item.title: Hiding Virtualization From Other Software - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) allows Linux systems to function as hypervisors without needing any extra software, but VMs created with it don’t behave exactly like real hardware does. Sometimes that’s important, though, so [sandwich] built a tool called vfio-native that obscures the fact that software might be running in a virtual machine.

There are plenty of the ways that virtual hardware differs from bare metal. The VM may behave slightly differently for obscure instructions in ways that are measurable, it may take slightly longer to perform some tasks, or the hypervisor may simply announce itself directly. vfio-native includes some kernel patches that solve some bugs which address the different behaviors, changes the way that the kernel identifies itself, and attempts to force the CPUs to behave in ways that real hardware would behave. With all of this applied to the virtual machine, it scores a 1/85 against a VM detection tool, with a standard KVM virtual machine scoring 10/85.

For anyone looking to test this out, it’s available in the AUR for Arch Linux. Also, it’s probably worth mentioning that there are more reasons to use this than cheating at Counter-Strike. For example, security researchers testing malware need to know how that software behaves when it thinks its on real hardware, and some may behave in benign ways when confined to virtual machines. Some licensed software also may disable itself when it detects its running in a VM, which can be a nuisance for things like software controlling industrial tools which only run on operating systems that are no longer maintained or hardware that can’t be found anymore. Some other tools we’ve seen before perform similar tasks as well.

item.title: Hairy Armor For Combat Robot? It’s Not Terrible! - Hack a Day
item.description:
[Angus] of Maker’s Muse enjoys combat robotics, in which contenders zip about in an arena, attempting to disable one another with weapons that lift, spin, and smash. He got a funny idea a short while ago and wondered whether a stiff mane of bristles could serve as lightweight, ablative, impact resistant armor?

Just to set the stage, [Angus]’s new robot competes in the plastic antweight (or “plant”) division, in which robots are limited to 150 grams with both chassis and weapons made of plastic. In such circumstances, one can see how a mane of thick, rigid “hairs” might actually punch above its weight, so to speak.

Nothing settles a question like a good experiment, so [Angus] sat down and redesigned his latest robot to replace its outer shell with a thick wad of bristles, in the style of a 3D printed lion’s mane. Filament is bridged between the model and an outer support structure, which is cut away afterwards to expose the “hairs”.

How well did it perform? Well enough to merit further study! Where past robots got their outer shells broken up, the hairy robot seems to have come through quite intact. It seems the idea might not be as silly as it first seemed, at least in the plastic antweight division.

3D printers have been fantastic in the field of combat robotics. First they were great because they made custom parts easier and more accessible to hobbyists, but things have evolved more since then. Now folks compete by putting motors and electronics inside almost entirely 3D printed robots. There’s never been a better time to get into combat robotics, and experiment with unorthodox designs.

If you want to try a hairy robot for yourself, be sure to watch the followup in which [Angus] improves the hair-generating process considerably.

item.title: Building a Swashplate-less Helicoper Rotor - Hack a Day
item.description:
A helicopter blade uses a swash plate and a set of linkages to change the angle of the blades. Not only does it vary the collective pitch to increase or decrease thrust, but it varies each blade’s pitch throughout each rotation, letting it produce more lift on one side of the rotor. This presented a problem to [worked in theory] — he’s building an RC helicopter from scratch, and this mechanism added both complexity and weight. Instead, he started looking for a way to get around the problem.

There were two options to eliminate the linkages: a linkage-less swashplate design used in Black Hornet drones, and an under-actuated design using angled hinges to control the blade angle. [worked in theory] started with the Black Hornet design, which has the end of each blade run along the swashplate on wheels, while a central spring presses them down. Friction in the hinge and wheels proved too high, and it stopped responding at higher speeds. A second, lower-friction design seemed promising, but it still required actuators, and thus weight, to control the swashplate. [worked in theory] therefore moved on to the under-actuated approach. In this design, the blades are mounted on angled hinges — by varying the motor’s speed throughout each rotation, inertia causes the blades to swing backwards or forwards, changing their pitch.

[worked in theory] tested two such rotor designs: one with one hinge per rotor, and one with one hinge for both rotors. The design using a single hinge seemed less sensitive to friction, was more responsive in testing, and had a more linear control response, so he used that. To actually make the blades, [worked in theory] 3D printed them as flat blanks, then thermoformed them using printed molds. During testing, the blades needed weights added to pull them back toward the standard angle under constant rotation; fortunately, though, this had the side effect of damping out unwanted vibrations.

There’s still a long way to go before the helicopter’s finished, but this is quite an impressive start. This is the second under-actuated propeller we’ve seen recently, both inspired by [Tom Stanton]’s original design.

item.title: Transforming a Tungsten Ditelluride Monolayer into a Transistor - Hack a Day
item.description:
In the world of silicon semiconductors, the process of creating transistors and similar structures involves various rounds of modifications and additions in order to create the requisite functional layers. A less involved approach would simply create these structures in-situ, with research the past years having focused on transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) monolayers to do exactly this. Recently [Seok Young Min] et al. reported (paywalled, Phys.org summary) on creating transistors in-situ in a tungsten ditelluride (WTe2) monolayer.

By selectively changing parts of the top layer into tungsten oxide (WOx) as an insulator and other sections into n-type WS2 and p-type WSe2 the researchers were able to create functional MOSFETs, without the normally requisite grafting on of different materials. An obvious advantage of this is that this can be done at an atomic scale, potentially achieving densities significantly higher than with industry standard silicon semiconductor technology.

WTe2 is not the only TMDC that could be viable here, of course, with other researchers investigating the use of MoSe2 for a similar purpose, as in this research by [N. Lu] et al. from 2014. This being the creation of 2D semiconductors, referring to the thin layers of these monolayer TMDCs, along with potentially other materials such as graphene.

item.title: A 3D Printed Marble Clock, but it’s Scrolling Text - Hack a Day
item.description:
With the topic of marble clocks having been quite well explored at this point, it raises the question of how easy it would be to take the basic principle and create a text display using black and white marbles. As [Ivan Miranda] found out in a recent marble text scroller project, this is far from easy.

The reason why a scrolling text display was picked comes down to not wanting to be limited to a fixed number of digits. This resulted in a round wheel design, with inner steel ball bearings and a stepper motor on both the wheel and an inner selector mechanism. These respectively align the marble channels and pick the right color of marbles to be dropped into any of the wheel’s slots, creating the right sequence of marbles for the target text.

Perhaps the most amazing thing about it is that it’s an absolutely massive structure, yet it’s all 3D printed and bolted together. It took a number of trial-and-error cycles, and debugging issues like the IR sensors getting confused by daylight, but it now mostly seems to work all right.

There are still some remaining issues, such as having to manually home the wheel before starting, and the ratio of black vs white marbles can cause unexpected gaps in the final text. Despite this the text is quite legible and definitely infinite.

item.title: Mesh Network Telephony Over Bluetooth on Android Phones - Hack a Day
item.description:
Telephony is a bit of a mixed bag. On the one hand, being able to talk to people in far off places is kind of neat, at least in theory. On the other hand, you’re usually reliant on a centralized network, which isn’t ideal to the mindset of most hackers.[Gautam]’s MeshLive project deals with that last one, offering a decentralized mesh network solution based on Bluetooth for Android phones that can handle both voice and video.

Rather than relying on dedicated hardware, this particular mesh piggybacks on your phone, and exists only as an Android application. Calls are end-to-end encrypted for both voice and video — though two-way video calling is still experimental. More testing has gone into video broadcasting, where a stream goes out one-way. The capability is available for voice, as well.

Each user has a unique identifier that can be scanned to create contacts, but it isn’t otherwise clearly identifiable to everybody. You’ll only appear with a random name that changes every 15 minutes to other users in range who aren’t your contacts. Range is of course the Achilles heel of this project, since it’s using the Bluetooth hardware of ordinary smartphones. It’s possible to extend the range of Bluetooth significantly with the right hardware, but we imagine most folks aren’t carrying directional antennas around with them. While every phone does forward the signal to as many others as it can, it can only do so for about 20 meters.

Of course LoRa remains the protocol of choice for mesh networking, though it’s normally used for text messages only. We have seen voice packets over LoRa, but anything LoRa requires dedicated hardware while this only requires an app.

item.title: Meshtastic Pet Tracking - Hack a Day
item.description:
Most commercial pet trackers require a subscription or network connection to function. [Jon G Aguado] wanted a better way and designed LIA, a Meshtastic collar tracker.

LIA uses a custom PCB containing a ESP32-S3, LoRa radio, GPS/GNSS receiver, and a charge controller for the 18650 or 5023450 pouch Li-ion cell powering the device. Everything fits inside a 3D printed enclosure, and the device is charged via a magnetic 4-pin USB pogo connector to increase weather resistance.

One of the neat features of this particular tracker is that [Aguado] gave it two different power modes. High power gets a location fix every 30 seconds and has a pair of bright LEDs for visual assistance, low power only gets a fix every minute or so, and it can also be set to off, which is something we wish more device manufacturers remembered should be an option.

We hope anyone planning on using Meshtastic and LoRa in the US is aware of the issues surrounding FCC compliance, and if you want to track your pet another way, maybe KineFox is an option?

item.title: An Analog TV Station For Anyone - Hack a Day
item.description:
If you’re a collector of older TVs, you’re probably facing the problem in some form of having no transmissions to tune in to. With many sets you can use a SCART or other A/V input, but nothing beats using the thing as it was intended. [BorisDigital] had exactly this problem, and since he worked in a TV transmitter control room in the 1990s, he’s made a small TV station that looks and operates like the real thing.

It’s a 10 inch rack stuffed with goodies, each of which replicates the function of a piece of broadcast gear which would have cost a small fortune back in the day. At the top is a transmitter, a relatively inexpensive board from China. Below it a clock and audio monitor powered by a Pi Pico, then a vectorscope, waveform monitor, and monitor powered by a set of Pi 5s with USB video digitisers, a pair of SD card video record/play units — yet more Raspberry Pi — and at the bottom, an automatic scheduler powered by another fruity board from Cambridge. If you’re not into TV the construction may be worth a second look. Those neat looking rack front panels are 3D printed with different filaments for the lettering, and are both robust and stylish. We can already see how this could be used in our work.

We miss analogue TV, partly because it was a wonderfully intricate technology that, beautifully, just worked. it’s a few years now since we reported on the last gasp of analogue TV in the USA, about a decade after it was turned off where this is being written.

item.title: Pushing Bluetooth out to 12 Kilometers - Hack a Day
item.description:
Bluetooth is a short-range protocol that’s great for peripherals and finding your keys, but it’s limited range is mainly a product of how it’s usually implemented. A recent video from [nktbuilds] demonstrates this by extending its range out to 12 kilometers, or around 7.5 miles.

The secret is twofold: one is the antenna, a parabolic unit that captures far more than the dinky dipole in your phone. The other is a very sensitive receiver with a much lower noise floor. What you won’t see here is any extra power than you get stock out of one of those generic coin-sized Bluetooth tracker tags. It’s kind of obvious, in retrospect: grab more signal, lower your noise floor, and get a better result. Still, it certainly wasn’t obvious it would work out to 1200 m, and it’s an impressive feat by [nktbuilds]. We’re going to have to keep it in mind next time we lose our keys.

Of course this doesn’t mean you should jump to Bluetooth for distance communications. You’re still better off sticking with something like LoRA for that, especially since it’s good to hundreds of miles if you can get line-of-sight — or even tens of thousands with the right setup.

item.title: Remembering the Weirdest Nintendo DSi Accessory - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Nintendo DSi was released in November 2008, and boasted a new feature not formerly seen on the brand’s handhelds—it had two cameras, inside and outside. It let the console take photos, a feature rather fitting given it was an era in which phone cameras had become the norm. Only, it wasn’t so good out of the box. However, [gavff] recently found an accessory from way back when that aimed to make the DSi’s camera somewhat more capable.

For some reason, the console accessories company Nyko decided that that the Nintendo DSi deserved an 8x optical zoom lens. Never mind that the console’s cameras were limited to a resolution of just 640 x 480 pixels, it was deemed important that the handheld have the ability to capture images of things that were somewhat farther away. The lens mounted to a specially-designed case that fit around the original DSi’s shell. It’s not particularly clear what the intended use case was, but if you wanted to expand the capability of your DSi camera, this was one way to do it. You could get some pretty sharp photos if you knew what you were doing, as [gavff] demonstrates in the video.

The video then takes things farther, putting an even larger, sillier telescopic camera lens on the DSi. [gavff] used it to capture a photo of the Moon, with the benefit that unlike modern smartphones, there’s no AI faking the results. The video also touches on the goofy Mad Catz flash accessory that used the DSi’s charge port.

We love seeing silly lenses on cameras that were never supposed to host them. Also, isn’t it wonderful that our ancient “Nintendo DS Hacks” category is getting some love again after all this time? We’ve actually published a bunch of DS hacks this year.

item.title: lighting the skies - computers are bad
item.description:
Someone stated in the early days of the war, a feeling that was reciprocated by the soldier in khaki and the sailor in blue, that a mechanical device would be the determining factor in ending the world conflict, favorably, of course, for the United States and her allies. 1

One of my common topics is the history of nuclear weapons. The "atom bomb" is a rich vein of history because its impact has been as much cultural as technical. Dramatic depictions like Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer have recently enforced, perhaps even revived, the perception of nuclear weapons as an innovation that forever changed warfare. More quietly, historians and strategists tend to wonder if that is still true today, or if it was ever as true as was supposed—the conventional firebombing of Tokyo probably claimed as many victims as the nuclear attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, for example. Besides, it's not unusual to hear people overstate the significance of nuclear weapons to WWII in a way that is obvious with a brief inspection of the timeline. The technology became available only very late in the war, and for that reason if no other, it must have had less of an impact on the outcome than other revolutionary wartime developments like radar.

Why is it that radar, a complex technology that fundamentally changed the landscape of aerial combat, seems so pedestrian? Perhaps because the technology has far more non-military applications, and so is more familiar to our everyday lives. Perhaps because the development of radar was scattered between countries and institutions without the involvement of such intriguing figureheads as J. Robert Oppenheimer (although one wonders if this is because we have not looked as close; certainly radar figures like Henry Tizard had colorful lives as well). Perhaps because radar just isn't as exciting: it does not put on anything like the show of a nuclear detonation.

Today, we consider another such step in military technology. This is an invention that forever changed the battlefield, and it's one that does put on a show. In fact, that has become the technology's main purpose. From the 1870 siege of Paris to the modern used car lot, searchlights have marked many of history's great conflicts—and great deals.

The concept of electric light has been known since the very early 19th century. An electric arc lamp, or at least one of their ancestors, was demonstrated in 1806. Because of the widely known story of Thomas Edison's incandescent lamp, most people know that electric light had a very difficult journey from idea to practical device. That path was not as simple as what we are taught in schools: besides the several other inventors with a good claim to the lightbulb, incandescent lights were just one of a few technologies that developed in parallel.

Before controlled incandescence, the principal form of electric light was still an arc. Arc lamps also did not fall to incandescent bulbs as quickly as you might think. Arc lamps remained the preferred choice for very bright, high-CRI lighting into the mid-20th century, and reached what will likely remain their ultimate form in the late 1960s, as the 15 kW Xenon arc lamps used by IMAX projectors. Along the way, arc lamps displaced many of the early forms of artificial lights: Oxy-hydrogen candles, known as "limelights," fell out of theatrical use. "Moonlight towers" began the displacement of gas lights for street lighting.

And the military—the military readily adopted this new form of reliable, practical, powerful lighting.

Calling In Light

The effect of artificial lighting on military tactics could fill a book. I will focus on one narrow part of this story, but it will be helpful to set the stage with a few of the earlier developments. For much of the pre-electricity era of military history, artificial lighting was mostly a disadvantage. Fires, torches, and other practical sources of light were bright enough to reveal one's location but not bright enough to search anyone else out. Ironically, the main interest that military researchers had in light was often to suppress or conceal it.

The chemical light technology developed for theaters and displays had promise, though. One of the first recorded uses of a powerful light for a military venture (and, as far as I can tell, the very first recorded use of a searchlight) came in the context of the American Civil War. The Union Navy sought to economically attack the Confederacy by maintaining a persistent blockade on southern ports; the Confederacy sought to maintain trade, often by sending out "blockade runners" under cover of night. A Union ship, perhaps frustrated by firing aimlessly into the dark, improvised: a theatrical light was mounted to a crude reflector, forming the first naval searchlight. It wasn't a very good one, it was dim and unfocused and the sailors struggled even to keep it lit under maritime conditions. It was good enough, though. By first following the sound, and then casting the light, the Union ship was able to engage the Confederate vessel even on a moonless night.
