Amusingly, while this incident is widely described in histories of military signals and lights, I have found none that state the outcome. Perhaps it was unfavorable to the victors.

Electric arc lamps were far more suitable to military use: simpler to operate (although not as simple as we might today expect), more flexible in their placement, and by the end of the Civil War brighter. The 1870 Siege of Paris, part of the Franco-Prussian War, was a bellwether in the history of military aviation. Cut off on the ground, the French made extensive use of balloons (a technology they had pioneered in the 18th century) to move people and mail. In the process, several records for aerial travel were set. The French enjoyed air superiority and had little need for air defense, but the situation on the ground was much more troublesome. Prussian forces mounted lengthy artillery bombardments, causing devastation limited mostly by the range of their cannons. For the soldiers manning Paris's fortifications, it was important not only to keep attackers outside of the city, but to keep them as far away as possible.

Paris, not for nothing known as the "City of Light," had seen demonstrations of arc lamps back to 1850. The invention of the arc regulator (which advanced the carbon rods to keep the arc intact) and improved batteries made the lights more practical by 1870, and during the early days of the siege "electricians" were hastily recruited to the city's defense. They manned a variety of arc lamps installed around the city, limiting the cover of darkness for nighttime assaults. At the summit of Montmartre hill, a position with a clear view over one of the most vulnerable parts of the city's defense, they installed one of the most impressive lights ever built. Not only was it larger than the others, it could operate for longer: the power supply was not a battery, but a dynamo powered by a steam engine. Besides that leap into modern design, the Montmartre light also presents an early example of "tipping and cueing" in intelligence gathering. French intelligence agents, having caught wind of a surprise attack, sent a message to Montmartre where the light's skilled operators aimed it by heading and elevation before applying power to catch the enemy in quite a compromising position.

A decade later, the military searchlight had become a standard technology. The Royal Navy regularly equipped ships with dynamo-powered, carbon-arc searchlights starting around 1882. They found that, besides their role in aiming weapons, searchlights could be something of a weapon on their own. Aiming searchlights back at coast defense artillery positions not only exposed them to incoming fire, it also dazzled the gunners and frustrated their efforts to accurately aim at the ships. This principle was memorably demonstrated by a 1903 US joint maneuver exercise, in which the Navy's Atlantic Fleet mounted a simulated attack on Long Island Sound. All together, on cue, the ships trained their searchlights on the main defensive battery at Fort Michie. The soldiers at the fort didn't manage a single shot, they were so blinded by the lights—and limited in their ability to even move around the battlements, since they could so plainly be seen (and fired upon).

As the military developed searchlights, they were quickly applied to civilian use. Limited availability of electricity, and limited need for such powerful lighting, meant that searchlights wouldn't yet become part of the urban landscape. They were reserved for special events, especially those with an emphasis on technical demonstrations. Of course, such events were bounteous around the turn of the century in the form of various world fairs and expositions. Perhaps the first use of searchlights as a device for entertainment came at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, which was extensively lit by electricity. A total of 17,000 horsepower of steam engines (so, yes, presumably steam horsepower, a curiously different unit from the one we are familiar with today) powered thousands of arc lights.

Most of these were for illuminating the fairgrounds and its many monuments, but some were installed for the sake of light itself. On the roof of the Liberal Arts Building, a searchlight claimed to be the most powerful yet made could light a newspaper well enough to comfortably read at a distance of eight miles. Of course, it was more than just a book light—it was a way to attract attention. Unlike the military context, civilian searchlights were deployed specifically to be seen. Rooftop searchlights became a common feature of large expositions, and by lazily searching the sky they established an atmosphere while guiding curious onlookers to the site of the event.

Even this early, it was known that searchlights could be a powerful form of advertising. At the Chicago World's Fair, the upstart Cloud Projector Company demonstrated a searchlight with a lens system that could focus a slide onto the cloud layer. It was literally a cloud projector, in the modern sense, and giant words floating ethereally in the sky announced the fair's upcoming special events.

In 1901, the Pan-American Exposition was underway at Niagara. Among the attractions was a demonstration of electrical arcs produced by a 40 kV transformer recently installed at the Niagara Falls power station. Alongside that light show, a second, more controlled form of arc was displayed: searchlights. These were described as an application of military technology, and specifically of military signaling technology. Searchlights were installed atop the "Electric Tower" at the exposition grounds, and at a viewing tower erected at Niagara Falls proper. At night, the two lights—22 miles apart—were each plainly visible from the other tower. The military was, of course, well aware of this potential use and as soon as searchlights had been installed on Navy ships they came into use as a means of communication.

Extensive newspaper coverage of the Exposition means that we know more details of these machines. The searchlights used for the tower demonstrations had 30" reflectors, and consumed 80 amps at about 50 volts for 4 kW give or take. This was indeed a very bright light for the time, and at the Exposition, the searchlights were swung around among various targets. "As the beams of the projectors sweep across country," The Virginian-Pilot wrote, "the residents of the villages and country places will enjoy the illumination." Excitement for the lights was such that newspapers throughout the region published Morse code tables, in the hope that anyone in the region could decipher news bulletins that were sent from the signal lights.

Watching the Skies

Electric light is far from the only invention to make a dual appeal to spectacle and the military. From the Wrights' first controlled flight in 1903, it only took about seven years for the Navy to envision the aircraft carrier. The 1911 Italo-Turkish war featured armed biplanes, and as the hostilities of the First World War opened the US Army flew airplanes into Mexico, in pursuit of Pancho Villa. In 1915, the Austro-Hungarian Aviation Troops bombarded the Serbian city of Kragujevac from biplanes. Serbian soldiers fired on them with small arms, but had no success. A private, though, got a lucky shot with an artillery gun. This was the first instance of ground-air combat, and the first use of air defense.

By the latter part of WWI, aircraft were in routine use as both bombers and fighters. One tended to lead to the other: our 1915 takedown notwithstanding, bombers and reconnaissance planes enjoyed almost complete freedom of the skies in the first few years of the war, until Germany's fighters presented meaningful resistance. Ground-based air defense lagged behind, but in an interesting turn of aviation history, the held-over use of tethered balloons as observation posts provided a key motivation for improved anti-air artillery. These balloons were conspicuous and almost defenseless, so ground-based escorts accompanied them.

Balloons—and in the case of the Germans, Zeppelins—remained an important part of WWI air units. Besides their ability to hang around for an extended period of time, airships could carry much larger payloads than early bombers. Zeppelins occasionally loomed over London, raining down the era's most sophisticated destruction, from 1915 to 1917. These lumbering vessels had their vulnerabilities, though. Big, slow, and flammable, they were easy to take out with artillery fire if you could spot them. German air raids were conducted at night, and by the end of the war Zeppelins were being painted a non-reflective black.

By 1916, a network of 258 searchlights across England hunted the skies for airships. There were as many anti-aircraft guns, using the pencil-beams of the searchlights as aiming guides. Air defense was so new at the time that little military doctrine had developed around it, and Britain's first searchlight units were found in the Royal Engineers. As in France, the searchlight operators were known as electricians, specifically the Electrical Engineers.

These units had actually formed prior to the outbreak of WWI, for the purpose of coastal defense. None other than Chief Scout Lieutenant-General Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell (yes, the 1st Baron Baden-Powell) had improvised the use of a chemical searchlight to keep ships away from a besieged town during the Second Boer War; the Electrical Engineers had relieved the use of chemical lights in South Africa when they arrived with arc lights. By 1914, the Electrical Engineers had six companies in London as part of the Territorial Army. With the outbreak of the World War they were immediately put into service, as were other Anti-Aircraft Searchlight companies across Britain. Soon, other companies were deployed closer to the front in Europe.

1910s carbon arc search lamps were not always easy to operate. Most military searchlights by that time were built on the back of trucks, with combustion engine dynamos as a power supply. A typical WWI searchlight unit had three lights, five trucks, and 28 soldiers. Searchlight units became a natural home for other air defense technologies then under development, so that by the end of the war some units had acoustic reflectors (for detecting aircraft by sound) as well.

One of the lessons learned during the First World War was that searchlights were quite flexible. Portable searchlights could be used for air-defense, or could be positioned on a hill to light the battlefield (and even dazzle attackers). A technique called "artificial moonlight" took advantage of the enormous output of carbon arc lamps by pointing a searchlight up at clouds and letting the clouds reflect the light back to earth. This dim illumination could help an infantry unit move at night; commanders had the moon on demand.

On the other hand, searchlights were vulnerable. Experiments in mounting searchlights on airships to light the ground were of limited success, the lights made the position of the airship obvious and it would quickly be shot down. Similarly, as air-ground combat techniques evolved, searchlights became the first target for incoming enemy aircraft. Destroying the searchlights meant that anti-air guns were firing blind.

Even after the First World War established searchlights as a defensive technology—their sweeping beams portending destruction—the public didn't lose its affection for a bright display. In an apparent homage to the use of arc lamps for both stage plays and film projectors, Hollywood's Egyptian Theater had searchlights atop its facade from its opening day. Perhaps inspired by the 1895 installation of an ex-Chicago World's Fair searchlight in Pasadena, the Egyptian Theater's lights announced premieres by sweeping the sky—promotional searchlights learned from air defense, and ironically, the post-WWI fashion for major events was to aim lights upwards, rather than downwards at terrain as had predominated before the war.

Grauman extended the concept to his other theaters, with both permanent and portable lights often used at the Chinese Theater. In 1930, for the opening of Howard Hughes's "Hell's Angels," 200 searchlights lined Hollywood Boulevard. The scene could have easily been mistaken for a major air raid, but instead it became part of Hollywood culture. Three years later, 20th Century Pictures adopted its memorable emblem, surrounded by beams of light.

Hollywood's searchlights spread beyond just theaters. In 1931, Fisher Motors De Soto-Plymouth on Hollywood Boulevard opened under sweeping lights. Auto dealerships always wanted attention, and searchlights were the perfect combination of electrical modernity, show business spectacle, and mystery.

Synchro Searchlights

Searchlight technology advanced incrementally between the First and Second World Wars. Carbon-arc lamps remained the underlying technology, but features like automatic carbon regulators (that "fed" the carbon rods towards the arc as they burned away) and foot switches for easy control became standard. A common searchlight at the beginning of WWII might range from 8 to 24 kW, and by the end of the war the largest units reached over 100 kW.

The greater innovation of that war was the integration of searchlights into electromechanical fire control systems. New electrical technology, specifically a clever device called a "synchro" or "selsyn," revolutionized searchlight units. A synchro is a way of electrically transmitting a position. Two devices, similar to AC motors, are coupled by a three-phase circuit such that rotating one will rotate the other in proportion. The two "ends" of the synchro will always have the same relative position, so that by putting a synchro transmitter in one place and a synchro receiver in another, you can remote control the position of a device like a searchlight.

Synchros were immediately applied to "distant electric control," still a common term in marine searchlights. One of the main problems with the searchlight has always been its tendency to attract enemy fire. Early searchlights often had two operators sitting on chairs to the back or side, cranking wheels for azimuth and elevation. These two operators were often killed early in the engagement. By the use of distant electric control, a searchlight's operators could hide some distance from the searchlight or even operate it from a fortified position like a bunker. This turned out to be a superior way of using a searchlight anyway: operators directly beside later searchlights were practically blinded by the light reflected back by dust and vapor in the air. An operator some distance to the side had a much easier time seeing what was at the end of the beam.

Many US air defense searchlights offered a backup, as well: a control crank at the end of a metal arm, called an extended hand control. Were the electrical control system to fail, a searchlight operator could at least stand ten or so feet off to the side and be that much further from incoming fire. Practical use of searchlights for air defense by WWII required adaptation to the better ground-attack capability of aircraft. Searchlights might be stored in a concrete bunker and rolled out on tracks for use, by soldiers who would quickly retreat from the searchlight to a hidden control point. If the searchlight was struck, the operators at least survived, and a well-equipped unit would have a second light ready to go. The purpose of the concrete searchlight shelters was mostly to ensure that a "spare" searchlight would survive the shrapnel from an attack on the one in use.

The synchro could also integrate searchlights with other air defense equipment. Early in WWII, radar had not yet been fielded, and acoustic locators remained the state of the art. But they were now part of a unified system: two operators on a set of acoustic listening horns would spin cranks to adjust horizontal and vertical position until the sound of an airplane's engines was loudest. By synchros, this position was transferred to a searchlight control station. These stations resembled a large pair of binoculars on a sort of articulated mount. The base of the control station had readouts for the azimuth and elevation from the acoustic locator, and the operator started by turning wheels to aim the remote searchlight where the locator indicated an aircraft should be present.

Once the aircraft was caught in the beam, the searchlight operator threw a transfer switch that placed the searchlight under control of the synchros in the articulations of the binocular mount. From this point on, they tracked the aircraft through the binoculars, and the searchlight followed automatically. The azimuth and elevation from the binoculars could be sent by yet other synchros to readouts at an anti-air control station or even directly to a firing computer that aimed guns.

All of this required adjusting for the different locations of each of these components. A combination of old fashioned fire control techniques (placing each station along a common base line) and analog computers did that trick, already well-established technologies since similar computations were needed to aim guns in consideration of gravity and wind.

Speaking of a common baseline, it is also worthwhile to discuss the use of searchlights in coast defense during WWII. For a period of the war, the US feared a naval attack, particularly on the West Coast. Similar systems were widely deployed for firing artillery at attacking ships. A set of observation stations, placed along a common baseline, took azimuth readings to enemy ships. Those readings were reported by messenger, and later transmitted by synchros, to a plotting room where a mechanical and later analog computer determined the position of the ship. Yet other computers, at fire control points, determined how to aim the guns.

Because this whole system relied on baseline stations visually spotting ships through theodolites, it was much less effective at night. Searchlights were added to many installations, remote controlled by synchros from the baseline stations. Like the azimuth-indicating spotting scopes, two searchlights trained on a ship from a well-surveyed baseline gave enough information to compute a firing solution.

Advancing technology obsoleted the whimsical acoustic locating horns. Infrared heat detectors, looking much like searchlights but operating more or less in reverse, were the first electronic means of detecting aircraft in the night. They soon gave way to the first radar sets. The SCR-268, introduced in 1940, was the US Army's first fielded radar system. Its huge beam antenna had three operators on a bench hanging from the back, spinning cranks to adjust the antenna position until oscilloscopes showed the strongest possible return. The SCR-268 was a drop-in replacement for the acoustic locators in searchlight units, but it was far more effective. Skilled radar operators could place an aircraft accurately enough that it was centered in the searchlight beam before the light was turned on. Besides giving enemy pilots quite a surprise, this gave them little time to evade or return fire before anti-aircraft guns were zeroed in from the searchlight.

The British developed a more refined version of the SCR-268 called the Searchlight Control Radar. It is notable for its far more compact design, small enough that its antennas were mounted directly to the searchlight under control. The result is almost cyberpunk, a 1.5 meter light bristling with antennas, operators hanging from the sides. The SLC is said to have raised the chances of spotting an inbound aircraft with the searchlight from 1% to 90%.

I put a lot of time into writing this, and I hope that you enjoy reading it. If you can spare a few dollars, consider supporting me on ko-fi. You'll receive an occasional extra, subscribers-only post, and defray the costs of providing artisanal, hand-built world wide web directly from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

Consider a typical World War II searchlight, the GE Model 1942, introduced the year that its model number suggests. This 60" searchlight came on a trailer, with a second trailer up to 600 feet away for the 12 kW diesel power plant and the control station up to 300 feet away. What we might now call accessory interfaces allowed the searchlight to receive synchro signals from a locator and send them to a firing computer. These searchlights still required quite a bit of maintenance, and they provided features to ease that work, like a work light inside the searchlight drum for replacing the carbon rods.

The Second World War also brought about a renaissance in aerial searchlights. Mostly abandoned in the First World War because of their tendency to attract fire, searchlights returned to aircraft for a decidedly nautical use. Submarines, all diesel-electric during WWII, typically surfaced at night to run their engines and charge their batteries. The first submarine-hunting aircraft used compact carbon arc searchlights to pick submarines out of the dark. The system was remarkably effective, and prompted a change in strategy for diesel submarines, which had to rely on their own anti-aircraft weapons rather than mere stealth.

Radar complemented the searchlight, but only for a short time. Radar locators for searchlights were basically an interim measure, making the best use of early radar sets that were sensitive enough to detect aircraft but lacked the spatial resolution to locate them precisely. Radar engineers, especially in Britain, made rapid improvements. For anti-submarine warfare, for example, shortwave radar systems were far more sensitive. It wasn't long before radar could directly guide anti-aircraft weapons, as well.

Military searchlights had a role to play all the way through the Korean War, but a much reduced one. Anti-aircraft detection and firing is now firmly the domain of electronic warfare: radio waves, not light beams, search our skies.

Surplus Light

The declining relevance of searchlights to the military proved an enormous boon to their civilian use. Searchlights were tremendously expensive, so promotional use had been limited to major events like world's fairs. During the war, on the other hand, the Army had built thousands of them. Afterwards, through the War Surplus Administration, it parted with most of them at bargain rates.

Entrepreneurial spirits, many of them veterans of the war, purchased secondhand air defense searchlights and offered them for advertising. Just about any auto dealership could afford to hire a searchlight for a sale, and many did. In California, it became traditional for dealerships to bring in searchlights to announce the new model year.

There is a bit of moth in every human being, operators of giant searchlights have found. Whenever a searchlight is probing into the night sky, motorists are apt to go blocks, even miles out of their way to track down the source. [^2]

Growing up in Portland, I remember seeing strange lights in the sky and searching for their origin. The searchlights utterly fascinated me, even if the source inevitably turned out to be another car lot. In New Mexico, promotional searchlights are rare, although not unheard of. The predominant weather may be a factor, since cloud cover makes searchlights more obvious. But it's mostly a matter of geography: the largest concentration of military searchlights was on the West Coast, and many overseas units were returned to West Coast ports. Los Angeles became the capital of the searchlight because they were cheapest there.

There are still WWII military surplus searchlights in promotional use, but far fewer than there once were. Parts are hard to come by, and the operation of carbon arc lamps is a less familiar skill. Most of these searchlights are eighty years old, and built to designs that would have been familiar one hundred years ago. Because of radar's dominance, the military has little need for such powerful lights and no longer buys them in quantity. Promotional searchlights have once again detached themselves from air defense, developing as a separate industry.

Modern searchlights use Xenon lamps, similar to carbon arcs in their use of an electrical arc as the light source, but far more refined. The arc is confined in an environment of Xenon gas, which practically eliminates electrode wear. Companies like Luminator make several-kW Xenon searchlights that can be mounted to aircraft, the main remaining use of searchlights for tactical purposes. Promotional systems have become much more specialized: Sky Tracker makes a popular system that mounts four 2 kW or 4 kW Xenon searchlights in the bed of a pickup truck. The four lights are attached to a common cam that rotates them in a "clover leaf" pattern, quite nonsensical for the historic application of air defense. Nonetheless, that clover leaf or vortex pattern is probably what most people now think of when searchlights are mentioned.

Fixed searchlights, of the type that graced so many World's Fairs, are now rare. The most famous in the US, if not the world, is the Luxor Sky Beam in Las Vegas. Often said to be the brightest light in the world, the tip of the Luxor pyramid contains 39 7 kW Xenon searchlights for a total of over a quarter of a megawatt, all fixed straight upwards. Even that light may be in its twilight years: since 2008, it has operated at only half power.

Today, concerns of light pollution, impact on aviation, and a general sense that auto dealerships should not lay claim to the sky have led to a decline in searchlight advertising. We are perhaps fortunate that the Cloud Projector Company's plans for on-cloud advertising didn't pan out; our present advertising industry is dystopian enough. Still, I am but a moth, or at least I have the impulses of one. There's nothing quite like a searchlight.

  1. "The Daily Item," Lynn, Massachusetts, May 7 1919 p. 9. [^2]: "The Plain Dealer," Cleveland, Ohio, July 11 1961 p. 46↩

item.title: 2026 Retrocomputing Challenge: I Would Do Anything For Serial Data - Hack a Day
item.description:
These days we take high-speed networking for granted, but it can be difficult to get vintage computers talking to modern machines. To help solve this problem [jaime] came up with Meatloaf which can provide files to a Commodore regardless of their location or medium of storage.

Meatloaf is an ESP32 device at its core, which plugs in to any of several Commodore computers through their IEC serial port. Many similar systems exist to bridge the gap between the modern world and the now-retro one, but this one connects to a dedicated service which points towards files no matter where they’re stored. There is some local storage, but it can also retrieve files from any active URL, and Meatloaf retrieves the files and then sends them to the Commodore over that serial link.

Part of what makes this unique is that the user doesn’t need to configure Meatloaf in any particular way, everything is done from the Commodore as long as the URL is known to the user. The system can even parse nested files like archive file types and send them along to the computer just like it would if they were on a period-correct floppy drive. There’s a GitHub project page as well for anyone looking to get into the weeds of this serial data interface.

item.title: That Weird 7-Pin S-Video Port on Old Laptops - Hack a Day
item.description:
Even though laptops from around the early 2000s came with just about every conceivable port on them, they still would often feature a somewhat unusual combined video output port. While at its core this was just a 4-pin analog S-video output, the three additional pins on the mini-DIN connector provided some more features. Of course, as [VWestlife] found out during his archaeological research, not every manufacturer used the same pinout here.

The naming for this specific port differs, with the name ‘S-video+’ appearing regularly, yet many descriptions glossing over the additional pins and only mentioning that it can be used with a 4-pin S-video connector. As it turns out, most manufacturers used roughly the same pinout, matching the shown Dell one. This adds composite output, along with two S/PDIF digital audio pins that could be routed out with an adapter into their full-sized ports.

Of course, the Apple PowerBook G4 had to be that exception again, with it omitting the audio pins and putting the composite signal on pin 5. This left the last two pins completely unused, but serving to completely confuse anyone who thought that they could get more out of the port with an adapter for those uncouth PC systems.

As to the remark at the end about how the transition to ‘just USB ports’ has made everything better, we’d challenge the average person to look at a random USB-C port and tell based on its appearance which standards it actually supports.

item.title: A Walkie Talkie Interface For Claude - Hack a Day
item.description:
[Bookmari] had a problem — working as a delivery driver, they wanted to work on various projects with Claude Code while out and about. Unfortunately, it simply wasn’t practical to write prompts and read answers on the job. Thus, they whipped up Walkie Claudie, so they could use their voice instead.

The concept is simple enough, it’s an interface that lets you talk to Claude using speech recognition, and lets Claude talk back to you with a text-to-speech engine. It runs on a smartphone, with a direct network connection to the PC running Claude, though you can use a VPN if you’re distantly located. [Bookmari] has a push-to-talk setup so that pushing a button on their Bluetooth earbuds lets them talk directly to Claude. There’s also a special mode to keep the channel active during long pauses if you need a while to collect thoughts and vocalize them. Just for fun, the interface is styled like an old-school walkie LCD, and there’s fun little details like synthesized squelch and channel-switch noises and so on.

If you’re looking for a way to stay hooked up to your AI assistant at all times, this could prove useful to you. Alternatively, consider if maybe it’s worth taking a break sometimes, or check out other Claude Code projects we’ve seen of late.

item.title: Using an Unmodded GBA as a Music Synth - Hack a Day
item.description:
The style and sound of older video games is unique enough that they’re still copied in relatively modern games like Undertale, Celeste, or Shovel Knight. There’s also a vibrant chiptune community making music on the older hardware directly. Often this involves hardware modding or otherwise finding chips from older gaming systems to replicate that unique retro gaming sound authentically. But disassembling older systems is not always necessary. Take a look at this Game Boy Advance synthesizer which uses the GBA hardware with no modifications at all.

The key to making this work is the GBA’s multiboot feature, which allowed these systems to send executable code over a link cable to other consoles which didn’t have cartridges. This meant that friends could play multiplayer games without each one needing their own cartridge, but it also means that nowadays people can send their own custom software directly to the console’s RAM without much extra effort. To run the synthesizer software, the GBA is connected to a computer, the software is started, and then when the GBA is powered on the snythesizer is automatically loaded into its RAM. The audio output is played over the headphone jack, and various controls are available on the computer and on the console.

In the video linked below, [Andy] is using the GBA with some other musical hardware and the sounds he’s getting from the unmodified console are impressive. It could certainly be a go-to for anyone interested in getting started in this style of music or who doesn’t want to do something like take apart an original Sega Genesis for the audio circuitry.

item.title: RepRapMicron Uses Fibre Optics To Print Tiny Benchy in Resin - Hack a Day
item.description:
The RepRapMicron (also µRepRap) is pretty much the microscopic take on what RepRap did for more macroscale manufacturing, with the most recent innovation being a UV print head, called the PIKA UV Head. What this does is use off-the-shelf optical fiber and UV LED modules to create 3D structures in-situ in a UV resin, allowing for pretty small structures to be printed, down to a resolution of about 9 µm.

More photos of prints can be found on the blog page with links to YouTube videos. It’s naturally somewhat tricky to get clean photographs of a 3D print that’s small enough to lose forever if you so much as sneeze or breathe too loudly.

For the UV head assembly a single mode fiber optical cable was used in the form of a regular patch cord that got trimmed a bit with a hacksaw. This was used in combination with a “3W” UV LED module, which may or may not be its true rating, but it was definitely able to cure the SLA resin. The used resin was regular eSun Standard Resin.

Afterwards you have to do the typical SLA post-processing, including cleaning off of liquid resin – both the part and fiber – and curing the part. So far results are pretty decent, with overhangs still being a weak spot that will be addressed in future revisions.

item.title: Automatic Coil Winder Takes the Tedium out of Actuators - Hack a Day
item.description:
Anyone who’s ever built their own motors knows how tedious winding the coils soon becomes; in [Larry]’s case, the issue was even worse. He’s building his own flip-dot matrix display, and each dot uses two electromagnetic coils to flip a magnet in the dot. Rather than wind each of these by hand, therefore, he built his own coil-winding machine.

The coil winder uses two stepper motors: one to wind wire onto the bobbin, and one to move the wire guide carriage back and forth, distributing the wire evenly across the bobbin. The bobbin is held in place by a retainer, which doubles as a tie point for the end of the wire. The spool of wire rotates on a pair of bearings, and the wire is fed between two pieces of foam to provide adjustable tension. The housing is mostly 3D-printed, with some metal rods, bearings, and belt drives fleshing out the structure. On the electronics side, a Teensy controls the winder, with an OLED display and a rotary encoder for control. Before beginning on a coil, it homes the guide carriage against an end-stop switch, then winds on layers, keeping track of the number of layers applied.

We’ve seen a few coil winders here in the past, including a 3D printer adapted to winding stators. For more on this winder’s application, check out [Larry]’s flip-dot design.

item.title: Reconstructing the Ancient Chinese Storm of Crows Weapon - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Chinese had been using large crossbows – akin to Greek and Roman ballistae – for warfare for many of the same reasons that European armies loved them. Their single, large arrow was effectively unstoppable, though this also was rather useless against large groups of infantry unless they were so kind to neatly line up. Old Chinese records mention a special kind of ammunition, called a cup arrow, or ‘storm of crows’, which involves launching many smaller arrows instead of a single large one, a feat that [Tod] really wanted to try and recreate.

In itself this doesn’t sound too complex: just grab some arrows, loosely tie them together in a bundle and slap them on the crossbow. Yet with the immense forces applied on this bundle it clearly turns out that the engineering challenge isn’t quite that straightforward, as the arrows love to scatter wildly in all directions or otherwise be rather unpredictable.

Although we can find historical references to multiple bolt siege crossbows being used, details are sparse on how the Chinese engineers addressed these aforementioned issues, so [Tod] tries a range of approaches to try and make it work on his own siege crossbow. Unfortunately he wasn’t able to make it work reliably, but he says he’ll be back with a range of improvements, with the community invited to pitch in their own ideas.

These type of weapons were very commonly used in China and surrounding nations from hundreds of years BCE to around the 16th century CE, when black powder was used to launch projectiles like fire arrows from a Huo Che or the Korean equivalent of the Hwacha, effectively multiple rocket launchers, not unlike the MLRS units seen in militaries today.

item.title: Running a Philips CD-i Off USB-C - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Philips CD-i is a console with many shortcomings, and those include the power supply. For whatever reason, the engineering team decided it should use an 8P8C connector just like Ethernet. Thus, just like your Ethernet cables, it has that annoying problem of the tab snapping off all the time. [MattKC] wondered if the CD-i could benefit from a USB power upgrade instead, and set about making it a reality.

The plan was simple enough—get the CD-i running off of USB-C instead of the ungainly original power supply that shipped with the unit. Given the console runs almost exclusively off of 5 V power, it should have been pretty easy. Only, the original spec adds one little detail that makes things a bit harder. The console is designed to draw up to 3 A from the 5 V line, while also having a -5 V line at 0.2 A. If not for that negative supply, it would have been easy to run the unit off any old 15 W USB-C charger spitting out 5 V. That extra negative line complicates things, because while the negative line could be created with some supporting electronics, it’s hard to find that extra watt from most chargers. While there are plenty of higher-wattage USB-C chargers, the majority tend to use higher voltages to deliver the additional power, capping the 5 V output at 3 amps.

Thus, it was necessary to work a little harder. [MattKC] decided to build a board that would negotiate with a USB-C charger for 9 V operation to get the power budget necessary. This would then be stepped down to 5 V, while there would also be an inversion step to supply the -5 V line, too. A CH221K chip does the job of negotiating a 9 V USB-C power supply, while a TPSM84538 steps the voltage down to 5 V with the capacity to supply up to 5 A. An LT3580 chip then inverts this voltage for the 5 V line. There’s also a power switching circuit on board because the CD-i included some of that functionality in the original power brick.

If you’ve got a CD-i and you’re sick of fussing with the original power supply, this could be a great upgrade. We’ve also explored USB Power Delivery in detail before, if you need a primer.

item.title: When You Can’t Pick Between Electric and Jet Power, This Buggy Has You Covered - Hack a Day
item.description:
Technically, what [Macona] built with a surplus Solar T-62 turbine is not a dune buggy, but a sand rail, but it does have the delightfully rare combination of electric and turbine drive that is absolutely worth wading through a 53-page forum thread to learn about.

The turbine came bare as surplus, but [Marcona] used a pair of Kia/Hyundai HSG water-cooled motor-generators to turn it back into something very much like the APU it likely started out as. That’s APU as in “Auxiliary Power Unit” in this context, the little generator that keeps the lights on when your plane is sitting on the tarmac. That went into the sort of frame you’d once have put a VW bug engine in — and the 150 HP off the shaft of the turbine beats anything you’ll get with Wolfsburg’s little boxer motor, even after losses in the generator and motors. Even better, the whole assembly, which uses the electric motor from a Mitsubishi Outlander, likely doesn’t weigh any more than the internal combustion engine and transmission, so whatever you call this little off-roader it ought to move well. It certainly seems to in the demo video embedded below.

What it doesn’t do is sip fuel, the T-62 being rated at 19.3 gallons/hr at full load. Fuel efficiency is definitely not the motivation here. He’s absolutely not saving money, especially not with what jet fuel costs these days. It’s one of those projects done purely for the joy of it — where if you have to ask why, you’re barking up the wrong tree. The vehicle isn’t yet street legal, but [Marcona] is working on it.

If you do like the idea of this kind of series hybrid drive, Edison Motors of Canada is working on bringing it both to semitrucks and heavy trucks, and that is motivated by fuel savings.

item.title: DOOM Ported to a $30 Clamp Meter - Hack a Day
item.description:
DOOM. Boil it, mash it, stick it in a stew, it’s the game that runs on anything and everything. Now, the classic shooter is running on a rather unlikely target—a cheap clamp meter of very limited resources, thanks to the work of [Artur Bieniek].

The clamp meter in question is the FNIRSI DMC-100, which can be had for the low price of just $30 or so if you know where to look. It’s a far cry from the many thousands of dollars you’d pay for a heavy old 486-based machine back in 1993. [Artur] got the doomgeneric engine running on the Artery AT32F415 chip that runs the clamp meter.

The chip is pretty capable, with its 150 MHz clock speed, though the 32 KB of RAM posed rather a big limitation to the project. It may be one of the lowest RAM DOOM ports out there. Even with this limit, [Artur] was able to get Episode 1 of Freedoom: Phase 1 loaded on to the thing, including E1M1 to E1M9 along with the title screen, intermissions, the finale, the menu, and four save slots. Color graphics are displayed on the meter’s 320 x 240 screen, and there are even sound effects on the built-in buzzer. Controls are mapped to the rather curious choice of a DJI RC-N1 drone controller.

We’ve seen DOOM running on everything from desk phones to completely custom CPUs. These days you have to try pretty hard to find something it hasn’t already been ported to.

item.title: Restoring a Soviet ES-4001 Mainframe Control Panel - Hack a Day
item.description:
Recently the [Chornobyl Family] got their hands on an ES-4001 control panel for a 1970s-era Soviet mainframe, with the intention to restore it to full working order. Not just because they’re really into cool old Soviet technology, but also because of the connection that this control panel holds to the Chernobyl nuclear accident that was so instrumental to the area in modern times.

During the 1970s the USSR felt that it could not be left behind in the race to create better digital computers. This led them to not only create a few original designs, but also effectively clone the IBM System/360 and System/370. This resulted in the ES EVM-series of mainframes, with an ES-1060 finding itself installed at the Duga-1 early warning radar system near what is now the Chornobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine.

Although the radar arrays are the most well-known feature of the Duga-1, below it is the computer center where the ES-1060 was installed. It was never put into service following the ChNPP Unit-4 accident — all that remains of a once pinnacle of Soviet engineering are the picked-over carcass of the mainframe and its control panel.

The control panel in question was obtained was from the early 1980s, serving a more gentle service life in a datacenter and looks to be in a mostly good condition. That said, there was still enough to be done to make it work and undo the damage of its violent removal from the mainframe. Along the way we also learn how the system was used and how the control panel works.

Although similar in some ways to the System/370, it’s still very different, and with only about 300 of these mainframes produced, it’s worth saving whatever elements still remain today, along with the surviving documentation.

item.title: NASA Batteries Survive Extreme Cold and Heat - Hack a Day
item.description:
One of the major limits of mass-produced batteries is the electrolyte. From lead-acid to lithium ion, there’s some temperature where the electrolyte will freeze and cause all sorts of problems, from cracked casings to various non-favorable chemical changes in the battery itself. But if there’ a solid electrolyte available, many of the downsides of charging and discharging batteries in extreme cold disappear. These batteries developed by NASA, for example, can survive some wild temperature swings.

The electrolytes used for these batteries are either a ceramic or polymer electrolyte, both of which are solid. In testing, the batteries could meaningfully operate at temperatures of -60° C and up to 80° C on the high end. Further, the solid electrolyte helps protect them even outside of these temperature ranges. Bringing the battery temperature down to -170° C was not enough to damage the battery at all, and using a small heater to bring the temperature back up to its operating range showed no capacity losses or other issues.

These batteries are eventually intended for use in some of the coldest places outside of Earth still accessible to humans (in theory) such as the south pole of the Moon where the temperatures regularly get that cold and stay cold for long periods, especially in permanently-shadowed craters or places on the Moon we might want to put some telescopes eventually. There are other terrestrial situations where these batteries might be useful as well, since they don’t need as much thermal management as other battery types.

item.title: An Open Source Linear Capacitive Encoder - Hack a Day
item.description:
If you’ve ever pulled apart a set of digital calipers, you’ve probably marvelled at the capacitive encoder that does all the measuring work. There’s nothing stopping you from using the same techniques yourself, as [Nick] demonstrates with an open-source capacitive encoder of his own design.

The sensor PCB works by by having a grid of eight transmitting antennas, etched into a PCB, beneath a larger receiving antenna. The transmitting antennas pulse out a pattern as the sensor PCB moves, with the signals bouncing back from the reflector PCB which is fixed in place. The varying capacitance caused by the position of the reflector elements relative to the sensor PCB varies the strength of the pulses hitting the receiving antenna. A microcontroller—in this case an STM32—can read those pulses to determine the displacement of the sensor PCB relative to the reflector down to a very fine degree. In this case, to an accuracy of 40 micrometers. Not bad!

If you need ultra-fine linear tracking for something you’re building, you might find this project very useful. Files are available on Github for the curious, along with a great explainer on exactly how the capacitive coupling becomes a positional reading. You can also study previous teardowns we’ve featured on cheap digital calipers, just to round out your education further. If you’re working on your own impressive workshop equipment, or subcomponents of such things therein, don’t hesitate to let us know on the tipsline!

item.title: Keeping Old Wi-Fi Radios Alive With Stream Conversion - Hack a Day
item.description:
There are plenty of Wi-Fi radios out there that were built over the last two decades or so. However, many older models are now becoming less useful because many internet radio stations are switching to newer streaming formats that they don’t support. [Clifford Farrugia] has been working on a little project to save these appliances from the e-waste bin.

The HLS Radio Converter is the result of that work. It’s a small open-source tool that converts modern HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) protocol streams into regular old HTTP MP3 streams that older internet radio appliances are built to decode. You can run the tool on something as simple as an old Raspberry Pi. To make it work, you just give the tool the URL of the stream you’re looking to convert, and it then spits out a new URL to point your radio to which has the stream in the old-school format instead.

It’s a simple tool, but one that should prove very useful if you have a beloved old internet radio that can’t handle modern streams. We’ve featured lots of fun projects in this vein before, too, like this ultra-tiny internet radio build. If you’re working on your own projects in this space, be sure to let us know via the tipsline.

item.title: Floating-Point Addition and Subtraction on Intel’s 8087 - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although you can do basic floating point format operations like addition and subtraction just fine on any CPU, having specialized hardware for it can provide a significant speed boost. Here Intel’s 8087 was the first mainstream floating-point coprocessor to provide this option to a wide audience, with [Ken Shirriff] recently reverse-engineering using an 8087 die how these basic operations were implemented.

The real-world speed-up of even simple operations like adding two floating point numbers compared to the 8086 CPU was on the order of a hundred times, which is very relevant the moment you start doing interesting things with spreadsheets, not to mention rendering 3D scenes in CAD software or even games.

As always, the devil is in the details, with sneaky infinities and edge cases also providing the biggest potential for speed-ups in dedicated silicon, along with the large circuitry spent on the shifter. With floating point values being very much about aligning values with shifting by a number of bits, this circuitry along with the detecting of over- and underflows is the key element why the 8087 and its successors were so crucial in making floating-point operations at all feasible in PC applications.

How this shifting works in theory is detailed in the article by [Ken], along with how the 8087 implements this in its circuits. Naturally, a large part of this is implemented in microcode, the listing for which is also provided. From this it’s quite clear how what seems like a simple set of operations is actually quite complex, making even the now much maligned x87 ISA an improvement over doing it all in integer-based software.

item.title: Trying to Get Linux Running on a Nokia E6 - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Nokia E6 is a smartphone from back in the old days when Symbian was a thing. [fluffleswaffled] has been doing the work to get the ancient handset running Linux instead, because that’s ultimately cooler than what the phone shipped with out of the box.

There isn’t an unlocked bootloader on the E6, so instead, [fluffleswaffled] used an altogether different route to boot Linux. A Symbian app is used to load the kernel and device tree into RAM, at which point the MMU and caches are turned off and the device jumps into Linux. It’s a one-way trip, from which there is no way back to Symbian without a power cycle. The setup nets a terminal on the phone’s own screen, and the hardware keyboard and touchscreen are functional. The display is controlled by a Broadcom VideoCore III, with [fluffleswaffled] capturing messages from Nokia’s original display driver to create a custom kernel driver that replays them.

There’s an issue, though. The phone doesn’t stay in Linux land for long — it always resets within a couple minutes of booting into the alternative OS. [fluffleswaffled] believes this is because the phone’s baseband chip is supervising the application processor, and killing things once it’s detected that the Symbian mobile stack has stopped running. They’re hoping that someone with experience with Nokia basebands or the relevant hardware can point them in the right direction to get this hack running for more than 3.5 minutes at a time.

There probably isn’t a great deal of utility in getting Linux running on a 2011 smartphone, but we love the hustle nonetheless. We’ve seen this done before, though, and it’s always interesting to learn what it takes to get the OS booting on a new platform. If you’re whipping up similar hacks in your home lab, don’t hesitate to let us know on the tipsline.

item.title: Reading QR Codes by Hand - Hack a Day
item.description:
QR codes can be a handy way to send a link or contact details without all that tedious mucking about with typing in a link, but they aren’t very useful without a smartphone to decode them. [Noel Friedrich] wondered if there was a way to do it by hand.

If it all seems a bit daunting at first, [Friedrich]’s write-up helps you work through copying a QR code to paper and then decoding it, as long as it’s version 1-5. Slashes in the template tell you where error correction has been applied to the code and you need to flip the bit back to what it was.

[Friedrich] then goes into some more details with a practical example of how the error correction works and how to exploit the ways QR codes are generated and read to make artistic QR codes. This even works to make human readable codes (without the worksheet), although the quality of the text still makes it somewhat challenging.

This isn’t the first time we’ve featured reading QR codes without a computer, but once you learn, maybe this QR code clock will be a bit more useful!

Thanks to [InstantArcade] for the tip via Discord!

item.title: Making a Five-Segment Display with Platinum-Titanium Cathodes - Hack a Day
item.description:
Before the advent of effective semiconductor LEDs many display types existed to display things like numbers and other characters. The Nixie tube is a well-known one, along with VFDs and there are also lesser known ones such as Burrough’s Panaplex, which all saw plentiful use in everything from calculators to audio equipment. The design that [Witchcraft and Alchemy] made appears to lean heavily on this Panaplex design.

Rather than neon, this uses argon as the gas. The anode is formed by the indium-tin oxide layer on a piece of glass, with the cathode sputtered onto the other side in the form of first a titanium layer followed by platinum. This combination helps to prevent the latter from flaking off due to incompatibilities between the molecular matrices of the glass and platinum.

Since this is an early prototype, only five segments were sputtered onto the glass and driven with a 74141 Nixie driver IC, creating the expected purple glow in a vacuum chamber. Following this a self-contained prototype was created, but this proved to be less successful, with the prototype quickly failing to light up as expected.

For a next attempt no tape or epoxy for sealing the device will be used, but rather a gasket instead of gluing the front glass onto the device. The use of conductive vias should make the device’s vacuum more permanent, and enable those last two segments to make it a seven-segment display. The final change should be to use a Penning mixture instead of pure argon.

item.title: Every Type of Current Sensor Explained - Hack a Day
item.description:
Measuring electric currents is an essential element of many electrical systems, but doing so in a way that is as nonintrusive as possible is not an easy problem to solve. Due to this we got a wide variety of current sensors to choose from for any given application, with [ElectrArc240] running us through these variants in a recent video.

The fairly low-tech, cheap and quite reliable method of using a shunt resistor is first demonstrated. This sees a lot of use in fairly low-voltage and low-current applications, with for example videocards using it to limit the amount of power the GPU can use, a feature that modders will happily bypass. Here simply the voltage drop across a known resistance value is measured, from which the current can be derived.

Of course, you got higher voltage and higher current applications too, as well as direct- and alternating current, with the latter especially allowing for easy current measurements simply from the electromagnetic field, or flux. Anyone who has used a clamp meter can attest to that such contact-free current sensing works, even for DC applications.

Beyond the basic transformer type you got many variants including Hall-Effect, TMR and fluxgate sensors, as well as the fiber-optic current sensor that uses an interferometer to measure the phase-change induced by the magnetic field – the Faraday effect – to the transmitted electromagnetic radiation. These more exotic types will improve resolution, at the cost of a rapidly increasing void in your project budget.

These various sensor types and their construction are demonstrated and discussed in the video, including when you’d want to use a specific type, and what the potential gotchas are with each type. Even if for many applications a simple shunt resistor suffices, it’s a good idea to know these different types, as well as their underlying theory of operation.

item.title: Sega Genesis Controllers on the Philips CD-i - Hack a Day
item.description:
The Philips CD-i was not popular upon its launch in 1991, and is barely acknowledged today. In the opinion of [MattKC], it had a particularly poor selection of controllers, too, and it’s often hard to find used examples anyway. To rectify this situation, he whipped up an adapter to let him use Sega Genesis controllers instead.

The benefit of the Genesis controller is that it uses DB-9 connectors that are readily available, and it’s got a simple pinout that is compatible with the Atari joystick port, too. It makes interfacing the controllers supremely easy. Converting the controllers required using a Arduino Pro Micro to read the Genesis pad and translate it into something suitable for the CD-i.

On the Sega controller side, the microcontroller just has to strobe one pin while reading the state of others to determine what all the buttons are doing. The CD-i, however, expects a serial data stream from the original Philips controllers. Thus, the microcontroller is set up to poll the Genesis controller, and then translate this into the serial commands for the CD-i. It gets a little complicated, because the CD-i wasn’t really built for game controllers, but mouse-like inputs instead. But it’s not too hard to get things working once you understand what the weird Philips console is looking for.

There aren’t really any good games on the CD-i, so this isn’t a project that the retro gaming masses will be flocking to. Still, if you have a CD-i and you want to hook up some controllers on the cheap, this might come in handy. Alternatively, you could also try the BlueRetro project.

item.title: Knitting Yarn and Filament with FilaLoom - Hack a Day
item.description:
We don’t generally think of 3D printing and knitting in the same sentence. One uses threads and fine motor control, while the other requires great knowledge of pressing buttons and plastics. That said, they both entail stacking material over and over until a finished product emerges. So why not blend the two crafts together? [Joram de Haas] decided to work on just that in the form of FilaLoom.

This isn’t the first time we have seen additional elements embedded into 3D printed parts here on Hackaday. However, this particular implementation has some extra features which allow the embedded structures to grow larger than most examples prior. Instead of placing any implements directly into a structure by hand, all thread is placed by a tool head not so different from tool-changer printers. Using both the 3D printing tool head and the thread tool, some truly interesting properties can emerge from the finished product. If you aren’t interested in the weird webbing properties themselves, you surely could appreciate the possibilities demonstrated by the 3D knits.

You might not have a specific use case for thread printing, but why not check out some other fancy 3D printing techniques? Here’s a group of various design techniques that will certainly make you think twice in your next design!

View this post on Instagram

Thanks [Sam Smith] for the tip!

item.title: A Stereo Vision Board For Hardware Hackers - Hack a Day
item.description:
It’s plenty easy to do lots of vision tasks with a single camera, but using two cameras gives you lots of magical abilities, like depth perception! If you’d like to experiment with stereo vision, you might enjoy this board that [machinehum] built specifically for hackers.

The project came about because [machinehum] was particularly excited about the Rockchip RV1103, a 1.1 GHz single-core ARM chip. It comes with 64 MB of DDR2 RAM and a has a MIPI CSI-2 bus on board, which comes in handy for interfacing cameras. Thus, it was the perfect part to whip up a stereo vision board with on-board compute capability and Linux support right out of the box. The processor is paired with two OV9281 global-shutter cameras, as well as a LI2HH12 3-axis accelerometer to provide motion sensing. There’s also 4 MB of flash memory thrown on board, as well as a 10/100 Mbit Ethernet interface for good measure. [machinehum]’s write-up also lays out the software stack and how everything works in concert with Video4Linux2.

If you’re new to experimenting with stereo vision, you might find this to be a useful platform for getting started. Design files are on GitHub for the curious. We’ve seen similar projects built using the Raspberry Pi before, too, which itself is essentially just a fast ARM powered computer with useful camera interfaces built-in. Funny that.

item.title: 5 GHz Drone Video, With An ESP32 - Hack a Day
item.description:
With the ESP32 series of microcontrollers having had hidden software-defined radio (SDR) facility revealed, we’re now moving on from the announcement into projects making use of the finding. [Twotoz] has one using an ESP32-C5, to receive and demodulate analog FM video.

You might think that video is something which has largely gone away in 2026, with TV transmissions having made the switch more than a decade ago, and home entertainment appliances having used HDMI for longer. But it’s still very popular in the world of drones however, where it exists as 5 GHz FM transmission. There’s no digital cliff-edge to lose your picture if you fly into somewhere with bad propagation of radio waves, and perhaps more importantly, it has an extremely low latency. This receiver uses a Seeed Studio Xiao ESP32-C5 board with a simple resistor-ladder DAC to produce the video. It has a simple button channel interface, and a serial link for more in-depth options.

It’s good to see these projects appear, especially as this one’s 5 GHz and shows those chips work too with the hack. We’d be interested to know whether the latency of the SDR affects its usability though. You may be interested to know this isn’t the first time we’ve seen an SDR do video.

Thanks [Ink] for the tip!

item.title: Using Ultrasound and Microbubbles to Make Tiny Devices - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although we generally do not look at bubbles in fluids as more than a curiosity – if not an outright annoyance – in certain contexts they can be very useful. If you can namely control their formation and position, you can use them in small systems to control actuators and dynamically affect acoustic systems. The main issues here are that controlling their formation, lifetime and controllability remain hard to solve. This is what [Zhiyuan Zhang] et al. sought to address, with a recent study published in Science Advances covering their approach using ultrasound-driven, electronically programmable microbubbles.

There’s also a Cornell press release article about their findings, which uses a new device that produces hydrogen bubbles along a grid of electrodes, before using ultrasound to steer them around. Using this chip-like device they claim to be able to control the 10-100 micron sized bubbles, with the ultrasound matching the resonant frequency of the target bubble. With each bubble size having its own resonant frequency, this allows for individual control by varying the induced oscillations.

Although in the demonstrated 2D setup this microbubble approach works well, it still requires a fairly bulky bench top setup around it which would need to be scaled down to be more practical. There is also the issue that the chamber geometry affects the movement of a bubble, which becomes especially important to further research when using complex (3D) chambers with this technology.

item.title: Lazarus and the Free Pascal Compiler Gain Dynamic Package Support - Hack a Day
item.description:
If you have developed in Pascal or Delphi in the past decades, you’re probably familiar with the Lazarus IDE that provides an interface to the Free Pascal Compiler (FPC), much like Delphi’s IDE. For users of Lazarus IDE there’s now an exciting new development, with the announcement that FPC and Lazarus now support dynamic packages.

The upshot of this is that you no longer need to rebuild the IDE if you want to add components, controls and Lazarus extensions. In addition you can use this same dynamic package feature in your own Pascal applications this way.

Naturally this is a great improvement, and it’s good to see more improvements to such a venerable programming language. Not only is it still being used today for just about anything, including web development, but there is a good case to be made for using Pascal today as it’s no longer the language it was half a decade ago.

We’d also be remiss to not mention the legacy of [Niklaus Wirth], who not only created Pascal, but was also instrumental in the development of Object Pascal together with Apple. This effort ultimately led to everything from Turbo Pascal to Delphi, FPC and so much more, making it a heartening sight to see this legacy being kept alive today.

item.title: Going Whole-Hog on a First Satellite Ground Station - Hack a Day
item.description:
When most radio enthusiasts start trying to pick up signals from satellites, they might put together a quick-and-dirty Yagi antenna and try to catch a repeater as is passes overhead, or they might grab a small unused dish from a satellite TV service and point it up at a weather satellite by hand to try to decode some of the data coming down. But [Cranktown City] had a different approach. He found an eight-foot dish online and built a massive articulating base station out of it as his first exploration into the world of satellites.

The first problem that needs to be solved with a dish of this size is its mounting location. This installation uses a large post and concrete foundation with a custom-fabricated metal base at the bottom. The metal base houses all of the electronics not just for receiving signals from the dish, but also for orienting it properly. That includes a large metal gear driven by a wheelchair motor to control its azimuth and a linear actuator to take care of its elevation. Getting the large dish onto the frame was its own ordeal, complicated by the fact that it’s not uniform in its shape and has to be mounted in a specific orientation.

With everything assembled, the circularly-polarized antenna installed, and the computers up and running, the dish is able to track satellites across the sky and download data from things like GOES weather satellites. [Cranktown City] also built in a system that detects wind and points the dish vertically when it goes above a certain speed. This level of effort is impressive, and absolutely not required to listen in on plenty of sattelite activity out in the sky, but this installation will certainly give [Cranktown City] a lot of mileage and possibly even work for some radio astronomy.

item.title: NASA’s Lunar Grounding Challenge is a Real Buzz - Hack a Day
item.description:
One could make a joke about how an astronaut walking on the lunar surface is rather akin to a cat walking on the carpet in the living room, but out in space the resulting triboelectric discharge can do a lot more damage than just some stinging fingers and a bemused looking cat.

The problem that NASA and other space agencies are dealing with is that the charge that builds up on a lunar-walking astronaut is very hard to equalize with something like a lunar lander. For this reason they have now set up the Lunar Grounding Challenge to consult the public whilst dangling $150,000 of rewards in front of anyone ready to pounce with a good idea.

Here on Earth we have many ways in which we can get rid of unwanted charge: dry winter weather, for instance, demonstrates effectively that humidity is a crucial factor here. With no real atmosphere on the Moon, each astronaut becomes a walking capacitor, which is worsened when said astronaut ventures outside of the sunlit areas and then returns to the slightly positively charged lander.

The challenge here is to equalize the astronaut and lander, with a design specification of a -100 kV or higher astronaut and about 100 V lander. A resulting current should not exceed 1 mA, ideally less than 0.2 mA to remain below human perception levels. If an arc exists it should not contact the suit or astronaut.

Of course, the most low-tech solution would be to use a resistor to limit the current, but at those voltage ranges it would take an awful long time to bleed off, in an environment that’s basically a perfect insulator. It definitely seems like a fun challenge to sink one’s fangs into.

item.title: Super Mario Galaxy Now Runs on the GBA - Hack a Day
item.description:
Joining the ranks of fresh backported Nintendo games is Super Mario Galaxy for the Nintendo Game Boy Advance (GBA), courtesy of [Tobias Friedly], AKA [Tobi]. In a recent video he announces the release of this game, along with the release of the source code of the engine and all the game’s code in a GitHub project.

Naturally none of the original Wii game’s assets are provided to appease Nintendo’s vicious lawyers, so you’re expected to bring your own super-legally acquired ISO image or equivalent to fill in these blanks when you build your ROM for the GBA.

This is a mostly complete port, even integrating the star pointer despite the GBA’s limited number of controls compared to the Wii. In some situations it’s opted to have star bits automatically collected to work around this limitation, which is probably a quality-of-life improvement that many SMG players will appreciate.

For the game’s logic a lot of code was borrowed from the recently decompiled version of the original game, which saved a lot of time even if the GBA’s hardware is no match for the Wii’s. From the gameplay in the video it definitely looks like a playable version of the game, with an acceptable frame rate that looks to be worth a try.

item.title: Visualize Regular Expressions with Marbles - Hack a Day
item.description:
If you are one of those people who visualize things physically better than in the abstract, then Regex Marble Run by [bottomless] might be for you. You enter a test expression and a string, and the site generates a virtual marble machine that lets you see the regular expression pick apart the string in a physical way.

Click this link, and you’ll see the regular expression “^[hH]ack.[dD][^0-9]*$” which, if you aren’t a regular expression user, might seem a bit cryptic. However, it is fairly simple if you take it bit-by-bit.

The caret character tells it to match the start of the string. So “^dog” will match “dog” and “dog food” but won’t match “food for a dog.” The following bit “[hH]” will match either “h” or “H”. Then there is “ack” which is just what you think it is. So a string starting with “hack” or “Hack” might match (depending on the rest of the expression.

The period means match any single character. Then there’s another “[]” but this time with “dD” to match any kind of D. The next “[]” character class is a range from 0-9, but since there is a caret, the match is negated. So “[^0-9]” means match anything except a digit from 0 to 9. The “*” means we can have zero or more of these. So “HackxD” matches, but so does “HackxDXYZabc” for now. Trick question: Does “HackxDXYZabc123” match? So far, yes, but it only matches to the lowercase “c” character.

The final character, “$” means end of string. So now “HackxDXYZabc123” does not match because we are still in the middle of the string. However, “HackxDXYZabc” will match since the previous “*” “ate” the rest of the string.

Head spinning? The site will let you see each letter of a test string as a marble that falls through the different parts of the regular expression. Balls that pass wind up in the left-hand box, while failures are in the right-hand box. Will it help you? We don’t know, but it is fun to watch.

Want a refresher on regular expressions? Or perhaps you want some practice?

item.title: Birduino Plays Bird Calls on Demand with NFC-enabled Cards - Hack a Day
item.description:
All [Hannah Robertson]’s Birduino needs is for one to tap an NFC-enabled card to the reader, and the device plays one of the vocalizations associated with the bird shown on the card. It ties together a few different components into a whole, and acts as a good reference design for similar work. There are a few time-saving construction tips worth keeping in mind, too.

The major components are an Arduino Nano, an RC522 RFID reader, and an MP3 player module. Using hardware modules and breakout boards means simpler wiring and being able to take advantage of existing libraries and sample code. There are also a few other things in this build that avoid re-inventing the wheel.

Rather than design, print, and cut a set of bird cards, [Hannah] found a set of bird-themed playing cards with a different North American bird on each. The back of each card gets an NFC sticker off a big roll purchased online. The result? A set of NFC-enabled bird cards with a minimum of work and fuss. The RC522 RFID reader doesn’t fully support NFC, but it works well enough to read the ID off the stickers.

When the user touches a card to the reader, the device plays one of the vocalizations from a collection of sounds for each bird. Creating the manifests and linking each card’s ID to them was a lot of manual work, but the result is great. The sound themselves come from the Cornell Guide to Bird Sounds of the United States and Canada, a $20 USD curated compilation of vocalizations from a staggering 908 bird species of North America. In a way, the biggest bottleneck is the card deck itself. At 52 cards plus two Jokers, it contains only a small subset of the total birds in the Cornell collection.

The enclosure is laser-cut clear acrylic, and here [Hannah] offers some time- and money-saving advice for anyone looking to glue acrylic to acrylic in a way that doesn’t frost or cloud the clear acrylic: Clear Gorilla Glue Gel. There are of course other glues made for this purpose, but Clear Gorilla Glue Gel (the one in a squeeze tube) is something one should be able to find in just about any hardware store. Another tip: double-check before buying, because many Gorilla Glue products are very similarly named despite being significantly different products.

Watch (and listen to) the video embedded below. If birds and their vocalizations are something that intrigues and inspires you, Cornell also has a resource for identifying birds by sound alone — we’ve seen it implemented with a Raspberry Pi and USB microphone.

item.title: Making Photovoltaic Solar Cells with a Microwave - Hack a Day
item.description:
Although solar panels may seem like a kind of magic, they’re really quite simple devices, in their silicon form featuring nothing but the p-type silicon wafer and an n-type layer doped with e.g. phosphorus. Because of this simplicity it’s quite possible to make your own solar cells at home using only a few basic, off-the-shelf ingredients and a kiln, which in this recent video by [Dr. Semiconductor] uses a microwave kiln and thus justifies the video’s title.

Even the silicon wafer that you start with can be easily purchased online, though you have to be careful that it’s a bare wafer, without existing etchings on it. On this you need to get a phosphorus-rich layer, which is done by creating a delicious mixture of 1 mL of tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), 0.3 mL of 85 wt% phosphoric acid, 5 mL of ethanol and 0.25 mL of distilled water. After low heat boiling this for 30 minutes, it is spincoated onto the cut square of silicon wafer using a spinning platform, like a PC fan.

Next, you shove the coated silicon into the kiln and put it into the microwave to bake at a fairly low power level for half an hour. In the video it took less than 50% power of the microwave to not melt the silicon, so remember that those microwave kilns get pretty hot.

With the delightful smells of freshly baked silicon now teasing your nostrils, you can then take out the doped silicon to sand or etch off the thin layer of glass that’s formed around the new PV cell. On the clear spots you can now put a gallium-indium contact on the p-type Si side and a wad of indium on the newly doped Si-P side, which are now your contacts for the PV cell.

The full recipe along with many of the issues discussed in the video can also be found on the blog article, though the video conclusion notes that many improvements are still possible. The created PV cell in the video reaches an efficiency of about 5%, but this could be improved through changes like the use of a clean-room, adding an anti-reflection coating and improving the contact with the cell.

item.title: Meshtastic Sniffer for DragonOS - Hack a Day
item.description:
Meshtastic has gained a lot of popularity over the last few years thanks to its low barrier of entry. No licenses are needed and the hardware is dirt cheap, at least when compared to a lot of ham radio gear. But while that physical barrier is low, there is a bit of a learning curve. Part of that comes from the fact that there are a lot of channels and modes that people could be communicating on, and unless the user knows that information up front it can be hard to find where the conversations are happening. [cemaxecuter] noticed this problem and built a Meshtastic sniffer into his radio-forward Linux distribution, DragonOS.

The sniffing software is built in C and comes as a complete standalone binary and does not rely on GNU Radio. With DragonOS up and running and the software loaded, it can look at the entire bandwidth that Meshtastic operates on and detect any traffic and decode it (as long as the key is known). [cemaxecuter] is using a HackRF as a software-defined radio for this project, which he notes doesn’t quite have enough bandwidth to cover every Meshtastic operating frequency, but it can get most of them. After firing up his own node, the software quickly detects it and shows its details in the terminal.

Software like this opens up a lot of opportunities for things that would be tedious, difficult, or impossible to do with with a standard Meshtastic node. Besides finding places where conversations are happening more easily, [cemaxecuter] also suggests that it could be used for wardriving and for locating or finding other networks much more easily. For those who still haven’t tried it out, take a look at this 2023 treatise on the protocol and hardware and then dive right in.

item.title: An Open Micro-Maniplulator Improved - Hack a Day
item.description:
If you need a micro-manipulator, you probably already have a good idea of what it does. For example, you might be moving a probe over an IC die or wafer. You might be looking at something through a microscope. The key is moving something in very small, precise increments along three axes. An open-source design for a micro-manipulator has seen significant improvements lately. You can see several videos about the device below.

The device uses stepper motors, parallel kinematics, and miniature ball joints to achieve precise motion. The recent version 4.0 update fixes a few problems. According to the GitHub page:

  • Self-collision during homing fixed.
  • Connection of the ball joint block with screws only was not well constrained and could be rotated a bit.
